## FOREWORD
Under the leadership of the Royal Government of the 7th Legislature of the National Assembly of the Kingdom of Cambodia, the Ministry of Health pays high attention to the health and well-being of the entire population. The Ministry of Health is strongly committed to ensuring the provision of equitable, safe and quality patient-centered health services for the Cambodian population in line with the Health Strategic Plan 2025-2034 and the Royal Government Roadmap Towards Universal Health Coverage in Cambodia 2024-2035.
This Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPG) for General Medicine provides national guidance on the management protocols of priority health problems with a focus on diagnosis and care, including curative and preventive care, as well as follow-up of health problems.
The Guidelines, published for the third time in Cambodia in three parts, Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3; was developed by the Technical Working Group of the Ministry of Health with participation from various stakeholders and individuals, including experts from relevant fields ranging from clinicians working in hospitals at all levels to district health officers, Provincial Health Departments, national programs, health professional associations, as well as partner organizations.
The Guidelines is intended for use by health professionals and other relevant professionals, especially health care providers, including doctors and other health practitioners in both public and private health facilities as well as trainees, policymakers, relevant individuals, professional councils and professional associations.
The Ministry of Health guides all health professionals and relevant individuals to use this Guidelines in their professional practice with the aim of improving effectiveness, efficiency and quality in patient care and safety, as well as contributing to human resource capacity building.

## INTRODUCTION
## I. BACKPROUND
The Ministry of Health of Kingdom of Cambodia is committed to improving the health and well-being of all Cambodian population through the provision of quality, safe, acceptable, equitable and affordable healthcare services. Implementing evidence-based, appropriate, and cost-effective health interventions within care packages at various levels of the health system, guided by contextually relevant best practices in clinical practice guidelines (CPGs), can significantly enhance population health.
Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPGs) are essential diagnostic and care tools in achieving UHC by ensuring that healthcare services are provided timely, effectively, safely, continuously and with patient-centeredness. The guidelines provide evidence-based and or up-to-health services at different levels of the health system. They ensure that health problems are appropriately diagnosed and clinical decisions are based on the best available evidence and experiences, leading to improved patient diagnosis and care outcomes as well as more efficient use of resources. By adhering to CPGs, healthcare providers can offer consistent, high-quality care that meets national and international standards.

The 1st Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPGs) for Medicine and Pediatrics were published in 2013. They are the only existing CPGs in Cambodia. Since then, many new developments have taken place, especially in the area of laboratory tests, medical imaging, diagnosis tools and treatment options. Regularly reviewing and updating the CPGs offer up-to-date and more evidence-based recommendations for health services and interventions tailored to Cambodia's current and future needs. Updating the clinical practice guidelines aims to enhance both quality and coverage by providing a solid evidence-based foundation for changes in services. This includes the diagnosing, treatments, and support necessary to deliver these services as defined in the essential packages of care under the CPA guidelines.

## II. DEVELOPMENT PROCESS
This Clinical Practice Guidelines was formulated by “Technical Working Group of Clinical Practice Guidelines for General Medicine “of the Ministry of Health through face-to- face and online meeting of the working group and small group meeting and discussions with guidance and endorsements from the Steering Committee for National Medical Care and Therapy of the Ministry of Health mainly through its meeting .The development process of the guidelines was actively participated by various stake holders and individuals, including experts from related fields ranging from clinicians working in hospitals at all levels, district health officers, Provincial Health Department, national institutes, national programs, health professional associations as well as experts and officials partner organizations . Each health section follows standard format except in few cases. These guidelines contain three parts-Part I, Part II and Part III with each separate volume presented in its hard copy division and publication. The guideline covers 174 topics/diseases/conditions within 11 specialized chapters. The guideline do not cover the national programs topics/diseases/conditions such as HIV/AIDS, TB,
Malaria, Dengue, Schistosomiasis and vaccine preventable diseases. The list of the protocols/guidelines of these national programs are included in the annex B of the CPGs.

## III. PURPOSE AND USERS
The main aim of these guidelines is to assist health care providers and practitioners make informed decisions on clinical diagnosing and treatment based on recommended protocols based on systematic review of evidence and an assessment of the benefits and harms of alternative care options. The guidelines is used for health professionals and relevant stakeholders in both public and private sectors, including doctors, related health professionals, trainees and medical students, policy makers, professional societies, in both public and private health facilities and institutions, including Provincial and district hospitals, private clinic, training and research institutions.
The main end users of the CPG are clinicians, managers and other health professionals practicing in patient care settings in both private and public sectors, particularly at referral hospitals and private clinics to support the delivery of consistently safe, quality and cost effective and equitable health care. They should be harmonized with the CPA guideline, IPC guideline, AMR guideline, Cambodian Hospital Accreditation Standards (CHAS) and Quality Enhancement Monitoring Tool (QEMT) and other MoH guidelines to motivate and facilitate their relevance and use. CPG can also be used by other relevant bodies and people such as in training and research institutions as well as by other organization or institutions as per the relevancy of their mandates.

Dr. HUN Vanasola, Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Asst. TAING Sovanna, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha,

## I. INTRODUCTION
Patients who present to the Emergency Room (ER) are typically unselected on arrival. A critical function of all ERs is to have reliable processes that can sort patients, in accordance with their clinical need. This process is termed “Patient Assessment” which is an important part of emergency patient evaluation. Even though it may seem time-consuming, it is necessary to properly and completely examine the patient to determine what care the patient requires. It is required not only to detect life-threatening conditions and correct them as quickly as possible but also detect problems that may become life-threatening if they go unnoticed.
## II. TRIAGE
- Triage is a French verb meaning to sort.
- Most patients entering an emergency room (ER) are greeted by a triage nurse, who will
perform a brief evaluation of the patient to determine a level of acuity or priority of care.
## Priorities of Care and Triage Categories:
- Standardized triage categories are usually developed within each ER.
- Most common triage systems consist of five levels of acuity:
- Triage Level I - Resuscitation
- Triage Level II - Emergent.

## Triage Level II - Emergency:
- Conditions requiring nursing assessment and physician assessment within 15 MINUTES
of arrival.
- Conditions include:
- Head injuries
- Severe trauma
- Severe asthma
- Lethargy or agitation
- Severe allergic reaction
- Chest pain
- Back pain
- GI bleed with unstable vital signs
- Stroke with deficit
- Abdominal pain in patients older than 50
- Severe headache
- Vomiting and diarrhea with dehydration
- Any pain greater than 7 on a scale of 10
## Triage Level III - Urgency:
- Conditions requiring nursing and physician assessment within 30 MINUTES of arrival.
- Conditions include:
- Alert head injury with vomiting.
- Mild to moderate asthma.
- Moderate trauma.
- Abuse or neglect.
- GI bleed with stable vital signs.
- History of seizure, alert on arrival.
## Triage Level IV - Less Urgency:
- Conditions requiring nursing and physician assessment within 1 HOUR.
- Conditions include:
- Alert head injury without vomiting.
- Minor trauma.
- Vomiting and diarrhea in patient older than age 2 without evidence of
dehydration.
- Minor allergic reaction.
- Corneal foreign body.
- Chronic back pain.
## Triage Level V - Non-urgent:
- Conditions requiring nursing and physician assessment within 2 HOURS.
- Conditions include:
- Minor trauma, not acute.

## III. ASSESSMENT
The primary and secondary assessment ensure that life-threatening conditions can be identified and treated early, in order of priority.
## 1. Primary Assessment:
- Primary assessment is meant to identify life-threatening conditions and treated early, in
order of priority.
- It is an initial, rapid, A-B-C-D-E (airway, breathing, and circulation, neurologic disability
and exposure). It should be performed in the first 5 minutes and repeated whenever a patient’s condition changes or worsens.
- A problem discovered (A-B-C-D-E) must be addressed immediately before moving on to
the next step.
Figure 2: Acute Life-Threatening Conditions
## A (Airway):
- Can the patient talk normally? If YES, the airway is open.
- If the patient cannot talk normally:
- Look to see if the chest wall is moving and see if there is air movement from the
mouth or nose.
- Listen for abnormal sounds (such as stridor, grunting, or snoring) or a hoarse or
raspy voice that indicates a partially obstructed airway. Stridor plus swelling and/or hives suggest a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis).
- Look and listen for fluid (such as blood, vomit) in the airway.
- Look for foreign body or abnormal swelling around the airway, and altered mental
status.
- Check if the patient is able to swallow saliva or is drooling.
## B (Breathing):
- Look, listen, and feel to see if the patient is breathing.
- Assess if breathing is very fast, very slow, or very shallow.

- Look for signs of increased work of breathing (such as accessory muscle use, chest in
drawing/retractions, nasal flaring) or abnormal chest wall movement.
- Listen for abnormal breath sounds such as wheezing or crackles.
- With severe wheezing, there may be limited/no breath sounds on examination because
narrowing of the airways may be so severe that breathing cannot be heard.
- Listen to see if breath sounds are equal on both sides.

section: Assessment the Patients in Emergency Room
content:
- Check for the absence of breath sounds and dull sounds with percussion on one side
(large pleural effusion or hemothorax).
- If there are no breath sounds on one side, and hypotension, check for distended neck
veins or a shifted trachea (tension pneumothorax).
- Check oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter when available.

section: Assessment the Patients in Emergency Room
content:
## C (Circulation):
- Obtain a blood pressure (in both arms if chest trauma is suspected).
- Look and feel for signs of poor perfusion (cool, moist extremities, delayed capillary refill
greater than 3 seconds, low blood pressure, tachypnoea, tachycardia, absent pulses).
- Look for both external AND internal bleeding, including bleeding: into chest; into
abdomen; from stomach or intestine; from pelvic or femur fracture; from wounds.
- Look for hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds that might indicate
pericardial tamponade.
## D (Disability):
- Assess level of consciousness using the AVPU scale:
- A: The patient is aware of the examiner and can respond to the environment
around them independently. The patient can also follow commands, open their eyes spontaneously, and track objects.
- V: The patient's eyes do not open spontaneously. The patient's eyes open only in
response to a verbal stimulus directed toward them. The patient can react to that verbal stimulus directly and in a meaningful way.
- P: The patient's eyes do not open spontaneously. The patient will only respond to
the application of painful stimuli by an examiner. The patient may move, moan, or cry out directly in response to the painful stimuli.
- U: The patient does not respond spontaneously. The patient does not respond to
verbal or painful stimuli.
- In trauma cases, check consciousness using the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS).
- The AVPU scale correlates to distinct GSC ranges, as outlined below

section: Assessment the Patients in Emergency Room
content:
- GCS Score 15 - Alert
- GCS 12 to 13 - Verbally Responsive
- GCS 5 to 6 - Physically Responsive
- GCS 3 - Unresponsive
- Always check glucose level in the confused or unconscious patient.
- Check for pupil size, whether the pupils are equal, and if pupils are reactive to light.
- Check movement and sensation in all four limbs.
- Look for abnormal repetitive movements or shaking on one or both sides of the body
(seizure/convulsion).

section: Assessment the Patients in Emergency Room
content:
## E: Expose/environmental control
- Examine the entire body for hidden injuries, rashes, bites or other lesions.
- Rashes, such as hives, can indicate an allergic reaction
- Other rashes can indicate infection

section: Assessment the Patients in Emergency Room
content:
This is a detailed clinical assessment diagram based on the ABCDE approach to emergency patient evaluation. The diagram is structured as a 5-row by 5-column grid, with each row corresponding to one of the five primary categories: Airway (A), Breathing (B), Circulation (C), Disability (D), and Exposure (E). Each column represents a step in the assessment process: LOOK, FEEL, LISTEN, MEASURE, and DO.

The diagram visually organizes assessment criteria and interventions for each category:

---

**Row A: AIRWAY**

- **LOOK**: Look for airway obstruction (e.g., foreign body, vomit, blood, edema).
- **FEEL**: Feel breath on your cheek to assess airflow.
- **LISTEN**: Listen for signs such as patient talking, inspiratory stridor, or gurgling.
- **MEASURE**: Not applicable for airway (no specific measurable parameters listed).
- **DO**: Interventions include giving oxygen (10–15 L/min), suctioning, head tilt, chin lift, jaw thrust, nasopharyngeal airway, and oropharyngeal airway.

---

**Row B: BREATHING**

- **LOOK**: Observe for cyanosis, asymmetric chest, abnormal movements, use of accessory muscles, and absent abdominal respiration.
- **FEEL**: Assess for chest wall instability and subcutaneous emphysema.
- **LISTEN**: Auscultate for percussion and breath sounds.
- **MEASURE**: Measure respiratory rate (target: 12–20/min) and saturation (SAT); target SAT is 94–98% / 88–92%.
- **DO**: Position the patient, perform bag-mask ventilation, obtain arterial blood gas (ABG), and order chest X-ray.

---

**Row C: CIRCULATION**

- **LOOK**: Check for visible blood loss and skin color changes (e.g., pale, red, mottled).
- **FEEL**: Assess pulse, capillary refill time (CRT), sweating or cold skin, and tender distended abdomen.
- **LISTEN**: Listen for heart sounds.
- **MEASURE**: Monitor heart rate, blood pressure, ECG monitor, and urine output (0.5 mL/kg/h).
- **DO**: Establish IV/IO access, perform 12-lead ECG, apply Trendelenburg position, insert urinary catheter, and conduct FAST/FATE exam.

---

**Row D: DISABILITY**

- **LOOK**: Assess pupils.
- **FEEL**: Check for neck stiffness.
- **LISTEN**: Ask if patient is alert and oriented.
- **MEASURE**: Evaluate AVPU/GCS score and blood glucose level (with reminder: “Don’t Ever Forget Glucose!”).
- **DO**: Place patient in recovery position.

---

**Row E: EXPOSURE**

- **LOOK**: Inspect for bruising, rash, infection, injury, and peripheral edema.
- **FEEL**: Determine if patient is cold or warm.
- **LISTEN**: Not applicable (no listening component listed).
- **MEASURE**: Measure temperature.
- **DO**: Uncover or cover patient as appropriate, and order relevant blood tests.

---

The diagram uses color-coding for visual clarity: yellow for LOOK, pink for FEEL, orange for LISTEN, light blue for MEASURE, and green for DO. Each section is clearly labeled with bold headers and bullet-pointed items for easy reference during rapid clinical assessments. This tool is designed for use in emergency medicine settings to guide systematic patient evaluation.

## 2. Secondary Assessment (F-G-H-I-J):
- Do not begin the secondary assessment until the primary assessment is complete and
resuscitation procedures have been initiated as indicated.
- Continue to monitor ABCDE during the secondary assessment. If any life-threatening
problems arise, return to the primary assessment and intervene as indicated.
- Prioritize and initiate interventions for injuries or conditions discovered in the secondary
assessment after the entire head-to-toe examination is complete.
- Perform the secondary assessment using a systematic: the mnemonic F-G-H-I-J
- F: Full set of vital signs/Five interventions/Facilitate family presence
- Full Set of Vital Signs
- Obtain a full set of vital signs including blood pressure, heart rate,
respiratory rate, and temperature.
- Obtain blood pressure in both arms if chest trauma is suspected.
- Five interventions
- Pulse oximetry to measure the oxygen saturation.
- Indwelling urinary catheter (do not insert if you note blood at the meatus,
blood in the scrotum, or if you suspect a pelvic fracture).
- Gastric tube (if there is evidence of facial fractures, insert the tube orally).
- Laboratory studies frequently include type and crossmatching, hemoglobin
and hematocrit, urine drug screen, blood alcohol, electrolytes, prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time, and pregnancy test if applicable.
- Facilitate family presence
- It is important to assess the family's needs.

section: Assessment the Patients in Emergency Room
content:
- If any member of the family wishes to be present during the resuscitation,
it is imperative to assign a staff member to that person to explain what is being done and offer support.
- G: Get monitoring devices and Give comfort measures.
- Do not forget to give comfort measures to the family during the resuscitation
process.
- Follow the mnemonic L-M-N-O-P when obtaining resuscitation monitoring
devices and supports.
- L= Laboratory studies: ABG analysis, lactic acid level, type and
crossmatch if indicated
- M= Monitoring (Cardiac): arrhythmia may indicate a blunt cardiac injury
- N= Nasogastric or orogastric tube: to relieve gastric distention, optimize
lung inflation and prevent vomiting and aspiration. Avoid in patients with a suspected head injury or mid-face fractures.
- O= Oxygenation and Ventilation: Assess SpO2 by pulse oximetry and
plethysmography if any doubt, Monitoring ETCO2 via capnography
- P= Pain assessment and management: using pain assessment scale then
initiate pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic as indicated.
- H: History and Head to Toe examination.
- Obtain prehospital information of the incident or illness. A helpful mnemonic M-
I-S-T:
- M: Mechanism of injury:
- It is helpful to understand the mechanism of injury to anticipate
probable injuries. It is particularly helpful in motor vehicle accidents to know such information as external and internal damage to the car and the period of time elapsed before the patient received medical attention.

section: Assessment the Patients in Emergency Room
content:
- I: Injuries sustained or suspected:
- Ask prehospital personnel to list any injuries that they have
identified.
- S: Signs and symptoms before arrival
- T: Treatment
- What treatment did the patient receive before arriving at the
hospital and what was his response to those interventions?
- Obtain the patient’s history. A helpful mnemonic is S-A-M-P-L-E.
- S- Signs/symptoms associated with the injury or illness
- A- Allergies and tetanus status
- M- Medications currently used, especially anticoagulants
- P- Past medical history (including hospitalizations and surgeries)
- L- Last oral intake and output (last menstrual period if female of
childbearing age)
- E- Events and environmental factors related to the illness or injury?
- Assess the patient from head to toe (Physical Examination)
- I: Inspect posterior surfaces
- In the injured patient, obtain assistance to maintain cervical spine alignment and
support injured extremities while log rolling the patient to the side.
- Avoid rolling the patient onto an injured extremity or side if possible. If
necessary, for adequate assessment of posterior surfaces, roll the patient to both sides.

section: Assessment the Patients in Emergency Room
content:
- The log roll maneuver can result in spinal and pelvic movement. Carefully
consider the risks and benefits of performing this maneuver, especially if the potential for spinal cord injury or pelvic fracture is significant.
- When spinal or pelvic injuries are suspected, radiographs are recommended before
logrolling the patient.
- Inspect the posterior surfaces for wounds, deformities, or discolorations. Palpate
all posterior surfaces for wounds, deformities, or muscle spasms.
- Remove the backboard or transferring device as indicated.
- J: Just keep reevaluating
- Continue ongoing monitoring and evaluation of the patient. Reevaluation should
include the primary survey, vital signs, level of pain and any injuries identified. A helpful mnemonic is V-I-P-P:
- V = vital signs
- I = injuries sustained and interventions
- P = primary survey
- P = level of pain

tongue, mucosa

## IV. ANAGEMENT
## 1. A = Airway management
If the patient is unconscious and not breathing normally and:
- NO TRAUMA: open the airway using the head-tilt and chin-lift maneuver.
- Place one hand on the patient’s forehead and the other under the chin.
- Tilt the forehead back whilst lifting the chin forward to extend the neck.
- CONCERN FOR TRAUMA: maintain cervical spine immobilization and open the
airway using the jaw thrust maneuver.
- Identify the angle of the mandible
- Place two fingers under the angle of the mandible (on both sides) and anchor
your thumbs on the patient’s cheeks
- Lift the mandible forwards
- Place an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway to maintain the airway.
- If a foreign body is suspected: – If the object is visible, remove it– be careful not to push
the object any deeper.
- If the patient is able to cough or make noises, keep the patient calm and encourage
coughing.
- If the patient is choking (unable to cough, not making sounds) use age-appropriate chest
thrusts/ abdominal thrusts/back blows.
- If the patient becomes unconscious while choking, follow relevant CPR protocols.
- If secretions or vomit are present, suction when available, or wipe clean. Consider placing
patient in the recovery position if the rest of the ABCDE is normal and no trauma is suspected.
- If the patient has swelling, hives or stridor, consider severe allergic reaction
(anaphylaxis), and give intramuscular adrenaline.

## 2. B = Breathing Management
- If unconscious with abnormal breathing, start bag-valve-mask ventilation and follow
relevant CPR protocols.
- If not breathing adequately (too slow for age or too shallow), begin bag-valve-mask
ventilation with oxygen. If oxygen not immediately available, DO NOT DELAY ventilation. Start ventilation while oxygen is being prepared. Plan for rapid handover/transfer.
- If breathing fast or hypoxic, give Oxygen.
- If wheezing, give salbutamol.
- Repeat salbutamol as needed.
- If concern for severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), give intramuscular adrenaline.
- If concern for tension pneumothorax, perform needle decompression immediately and
give IV fluids and oxygen. Plan for rapid handover/transfer.
- If concern for large pleural effusion or hemothorax, give oxygen and plan for rapid
handover/transfer.
- If cause unknown, remember the possibility of trauma.
Figure 8: One-Hand bag mask ventilation technique
## 3. C = Circulation Management
- For cardiopulmonary arrest, follow relevant CPR protocols.
- If signs of poor perfusion, give IV fluids and oxygen and:
- For external bleeding, apply direct pressure or use other technique to control.
- If internal bleeding or pericardial tamponade are suspected, refer rapidly to a
center with surgical capabilities.
- If cause unknown, remember the possibility of trauma: Bind pelvic fractures and splint
femur fractures, or any fracture with compromised blood flow.

## 5. E = Exposure Management
- If snake bite is suspected, immobilize the limb, 20mn WBCT, give appropriate antivenom
if available.
- Remove constricting clothing and all jewelry.
- Cover the patient as soon as possible to prevent hypothermia by using warm blankets,
overhead warmers, and warmed I.V. fluids. Acutely ill patients have difficulty regulating body temperature.
- Remove any wet clothes and dry patient thoroughly.
- Respect the patient and protect modesty during exposure.
- If cause unknown, remember the possibility of trauma: Log roll if suspected spinal injury.

## OXYGEN THERAPY AND RESPIRATORY SUPPORTS
Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda,
Prof. Asst TAING Sovanna, Dr. Pen Phallkun, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha , Dr. TES Sovannara ,
Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya
## I. DEFINITION
The administration of supplemental oxygen is necessary when a patient has low blood oxygen levels, termed hypoxemia. Untreated, acute hypoxemia can lead to tissue hypoxia (low level of oxygen at the cellular level), organ dysfunction and death. Delivery of oxygen to tissues also relies on adequate cardiac output and hemoglobin to carry oxygen to the tissues.
Oxygen therapy improves oxygen delivery to the tissues by increasing oxygen content in the blood. Oxygen content in the blood is frequently measured indirectly by pulse oximetry as oxygen saturation (SpO2).
- oxygen content in arterial blood (CaO2) = 1.34 × (Hb) × SpO2 + (0.003 × PaO2) Arterial oxygen partial pressure (PaO2) measured in mmHg by arterial blood gas analyzer.
- Oxygen concentration (% O2) from the oxygen source (i.e. wall outlet, bedside concentrator…) is the purity of oxygen produced by the device. It can range widely depending on the quality of the source but generally should range from 0.82–1.0 (82– 100%).

- Fraction of inspired oxygen (% FiO2) is the oxygen concentration that is inspired by the patient, usually a result of mixing the oxygen source and ambient air and can range from 0.21–1.0 (21–100%). This varies depending on the delivery device and the patient’s respiratory drive.
Oxygen saturation (% SpO2) and oxygen partial pressure (PaO2) are the measured oxygen levels in blood, the former measured by pulse oximeter and the latter by blood gas analyzer.

## II. INDICATIONS FOR OXYGEN THERAPY
- Respiratory distress
- Sepsis with hypoperfusion or shock
- Alteration of mental status
- Hypoxemia
The following conditions may require airway management in addition to oxygen.:
- obstructed or absent breathing,
- severe respiratory distress,
- central cyanosis,
- shock,
- coma and/or convulsions
Supplemental oxygen therapy should be provided immediately to achieve the following SpO2 targets:
- SpO2 ≥ 90% in adults and children
- SpO2 ≥ 92–95% in pregnant patients
- SpO2 ≥ 94% if child or adult with signs of multi-organ failure, including shock, alteration of mental status, severe anemia, and/or during resuscitation.
- Once stabilized, resume target SpO2 ≥ 90%.
## III. RESPIRATORY (VENTILATION) SUPPORT
Respiratory failure type 1 or hypoxic-respiratory-failure, as well as patients who have dyspnea and low SpO2 need supplemental oxygen therapy. Most of the time, the standard oxygen delivery devices (nasal cannula, mask) or HFNC can help. When patients have also hypercapnia (respiratory failure type 2), then NIV is more helpful. In cases where the oxygenation disorder is

severe (e.g., in ARDS with PaO2/FiO2 <150), often, only invasive mechanical ventilation may help. Note that the NIV is the first-choice modality of ventilation support in Exacerbations of COPD and acute congestive heart failure.

## A. Oxygen delivery devices
a. In adult
b. In children
Nasal cannula is the preferred method of delivering oxygen to infants and children < 5 years of age with hypoxemia who require oxygen therapy.
c. Humidification
When oxygen is delivered at standard flow rate (0.5–1 L/min for a neonate, 1–2 L/min for an infant, 1–4 L/min for an older child) through nasal prongs, humidification is not necessary. Higher flow rates without effective humidification may cause drying of nasal mucosa with associated bleeding, airway obstruction and may cause bronchoconstriction in some conditions (e.g. asthma, COPD).
Bubble humidifiers reduce the dryness of the oxygen supplied by bubbling the gas through water at room temperature. They must be filled with clean water at least once a day (distilled water or tap water that has been boiled and cooled). The water level in the humidifier should be checked twice daily and topped up as necessary. The humidifier equipment must be washed and disinfected regularly to prevent bacterial colonization.
## B. Choosing the modality of respiratory support
- Standard oxygen therapy:
Simple mask and nasal cannula provided low FiO2, can be used on patients with mild hypoxia. FiO2 varies and depends on minute ventilation. Use cannula with O2 flow < 5LPM; simple mask needs the O2 flow 5-10LPM

Venturi-mask provides constant FiO2 as marked on the device, different color gives different FiO2. Usually, the color red gives FiO2=40% with O2 flow 10-12LPM, the green one gives FiO2 = 60% with oxygen flow 12-15 LPM.
Use a non-rebreathing mask with reservoir bag and the highest possible oxygen flow to the patient who is remarkable hypoxic (SpO2 <90%), It may provide FiO2 up to 80-95%
- High Flow nasal canula (HFNC):
The main use of HFNC is to provide relatively high FiO2 to patients with severe non- hypercapnic-hypoxemic respiratory failure. Most devices can provide maximum FiO2= 100%

and flow 60LPM. Sometimes HFNC can help hypoxic-respiratory-failure patient avoid intubation, but it is important to detect failure and move early to invasive mechanical ventilation if indicated.
The ROX score = SpO2/FiO2 ÷ RR,
may help to decide whether to continue HFNC or change.
score < 2.85 at 2h, or < 3.47 at 6h, or < 3.85 at h12 are predictors of failure Score ≥ 4.88 after 2h, or 6h, or 12h predicts the success, and HFNC may continue.
- Non-invasive ventilation (NIV):
NIV with a mask delivering continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) can increase minute ventilation, reduce the work of breathing, recruit alveoli, and improve hemodynamics.
Contra-indication of NIV:
 - Cardiac / respiratory arrest
 - Medically unstable (hypotensive shock, uncontrolled cardiac ischemia, or
arrhythmias)
 - Severe upper gastrointestinal bleeding
 - Unable to protect airway (impaired cough or swallowing)
 - Excessive secretions
 - Unable to apply mask due to facial surgery, trauma, burns, or facial deformity
 - Agitated or uncooperative
 - Undrained pneumothorax
 - Multiorgan system failure
NIV helps to improve oxygenation (increase PaO2) and ventilation (decrease PaCO2). Using ICU ventilator, in CPAP mode, CPAP = PEEP, in BiPAP mode EPAP=PEEP, delta P = PS, PS + PEEP= IPAP. (EPAP: expiratory positive airway pressure, IPAP: inspiratory positive airway pressure)
Initial setting usually PEE=5 cmH2O, PS=5-10 cmH2O

Increase level of PEEP usually helps to increase PaO2, and increase the PS usually decreases PaCO2.
- Mechanical ventilation:
Endotracheal intubation and controlled mechanical ventilation should be pursued aggressively when ventilatory support is needed and NIV is not expected to improve outcomes, such as for acute exacerbations of asthma and diseases that do not respond rapidly to medical therapy (e.g., pneumonia and ARDS).
Endotracheal intubation is an aggressive procedure that should be done by trained personals. Some anesthetic drugs (hypnotic, opioids, myorelaxant) often used during intubation and for neuro sedation. The intubation tube-cuff pressure should be between 20 - 30cmH2O. Modern ventilators have many settings and choices to adapt with patient conditions. The most frequent initial setting in emergency is:
- Mode: V-ACV (volume target-assist-control-ventilation)
- Vt: 6-8ml/kg (Ideal body weight), ~ 400ml for adult 60-70kg actual body weight.
- PEEP: 5 cmH2O
- FiO2: start 100%, then reduce progressively as condition improved
- Frequence: 12-18/min (varies to PCO2, increase Frequence if PCO2 high)
- Plateau pressure: < 30 cmH2O
- Trigger: -2 cmH2O, or – 2L/min

Most often, after putting on mechanical ventilation in ER, the patient was transferred to operation room or ICU where the team adapt the ventilation setting and follow up accordingly. The control of mechanical ventilation is guided by arterial blood gas analysis or PetCO2 and SpO2 measures, the surveillance of respiratory mechanic and clinical response. The main objectives of mechanical ventilation are:
(1) normalization of oxygenation and ventilation (2) Avoid or limit the complications of ventilation. And (3) wean patients from ventilator as soon as possible

## IV. OXYGEN SUPPLY
At the facility level, there are many considerations required to estimate oxygen demand, including:
- Oxygen source type:
- pressure swing adsorption (PSA),
- vacuum pressure swing adsorption (VPSA) plants,
- bulk liquid tank,
- bedside oxygen concentrators,
- distribution manifolds with high-pressure cylinders, or
- a combination of sources.
- Distribution system: Oxygen may travel from the source to the patient’s bedside in two main ways: pipe network or bedside high-pressure gas cylinders (or bedside concentrators). Accessories for monitoring and regulation of the medical gas should be included (e.g. pressure regulators and flowmeters).
- Delivery equipment and devices: This refers to biomedical equipment connected to the network (e.g. patient ventilators, or direct interfaces such as nasal cannula). Oxygen concentrator
There are multiple devices available and approved, with different power efficiencies and a range of minimum and maximum oxygen output between a minimum of 0.125 L/min to a maximum of 10 L/min. Few portable oxygen concentrators can deliver more than 10 L/min, and many oxygen concentrators may claim a wide range of flows but only with low oxygen concentrations.
## Oxygen cylinders

Many hospitals use oxygen cylinders, the pressure is in Bar. A full compressed cylinder is 120-130 Bar. A cylinder size J, has 47.2L water capacity, full compressed to 120 bar have oxygen = 47.2 × 120 = 5664L. A pressure release manometer is needed to reduce the outlet pressure to a constant pressure usually from 3.5-5 Bar to run the ventilator. Some model ventilators (e.g., Hamilton T1) can be connected also to low pressure O2 flow outlets.

This is a detailed clinical decision-making algorithm for the management of patients with pneumonia requiring oxygen therapy, progressing from initial assessment to escalation or weaning. The flowchart guides clinicians through oxygen delivery modalities based on patient response and presence of emergency signs.

---

**Decision Points & Branches:**

1. **Initial Assessment:**
   - Decision Point: “Are any of the following signs present?”
     - Clinical signs of pneumonia + any of:
       - Adults: RR > 30/min, severe respiratory distress, or SpO2 < 90%
       - Child: very severe chest indrawing, grunting, central cyanosis, inability to breastfeed/drink, lethargy/unconsciousness/convulsions.
     - YES → Proceed to oxygen delivery via Nasal Cannula.
     - NO → Continue monitoring and reassess (~q2–6 hr).

2. **Nasal Cannula:**
   - Flow: From initial “YES” branch.
   - FiO2 Limit: Max FiO2 ≤ 0.4.
   - Flow rates:
     - Neonates: 0.5–1 L/min
     - Infants: 1–2 L/min
     - Children: 1–4 L/min
     - Adults: 1–5 L/min
   - Decision Point: “Are emergency signs present?”
     - YES → Intubation and mechanical ventilation.
     - NO → Assess response: Increased distress or SpO2 < 90%?
       - YES → Simple face mask.
       - NO → Continue monitoring and reassess.

3. **Simple Face Mask:**
   - Flow: From “NO” at nasal cannula response.
   - FiO2 Limit: Max FiO2 ≤ 0.5.
   - Flow rate: 5–10 L/min.
   - Decision Point: “Assess response: Increased distress or SpO2 < 90%?”
     - YES → Non-rebreathing mask + reservoir.
     - NO → Continue monitoring and reassess.

4. **Non-rebreathing Mask + Reservoir:**
   - Flow: From “YES” at simple face mask response.
   - FiO2 Limit: Max FiO2 0.5–0.95.
   - Flow rate: 10–15 L/min.
   - May consider adding nasal cannula to augment FiO2.
   - Decision Point: “Assess response: Increased distress or SpO2 < 90%?”
     - YES → “Are emergency signs present?”
       - YES → Intubation and mechanical ventilation.
       - NO → Consider 1–2h trial of one of the following (based on patient & local context):
         - CPAP
         - High-flow nasal oxygen
         - NIPPV/BiPAP
     - NO → Continue monitoring and reassess.

5. **Emergency Signs (Listed separately):**
   - Obstructed or inadequate breathing
   - Central cyanosis
   - Severe respiratory distress
   - Signs of shock
   - Seriously reduced level of consciousness
   - Seizures
   - Acidosis (pH < 7.30)
   - Severe hypoxemia, P:F<100
   - If present, escalate to intubation.

6. **Trial Options (if no emergency signs after non-rebreather):**
   - **CPAP:**
     - Pressure: 5–10 cmH2O (infant and children); 10–15 cmH2O (adolescents and adults).
     - Max FiO2 ≤ 1.0.
   - **High-flow nasal oxygen:**
     - 0–10 kg: 2 L/kg/min
     - 10–20 kg: 1 L/kg/min
     - 20–40 kg: 0.5–1 L/kg/min (max 30)
     - >40 kg: 0.5–1 L/kg/min (max 60)
     - Max FiO2 ≤ 1.0.
   - **NIPPV/BiPAP:**
     - For COPD or left heart failure presented.
     - PS Δ5–15 / PEEP 5–15
     - IPAP 10–30 / EPAP 5–15
     - IPAP = PEEP + PS; EPAP = PEEP
     - Max FiO2 ≤ 1.0.

7. **Assess Response After Trial:**
   - Timing: ~q1 hr initially; q2–4 hr once stable or improving.
   - Criteria for worsening: Increased/continued distress, SpO2 < 90%, pH < 7.30, PaCO2 > 45, declining or altered mental status.
   - YES → Return to escalation path (e.g., intubation).
   - NO → Continue therapy.

8. **Continue Therapy:**
   - Wean if SpO2 > 90% and improved work of breathing.

---

**Treatment Goals (Reassess every 2–6 hours):**
- SpO2 > 90%
- Improving work of breathing
- pH > 7.30
- PaCO2 < 45
- Adequate mental status
- If not met, consider alternative therapies, escalation, or transfer.

---

**Intubation and Mechanical Ventilation:**
- Use lung protective ventilation or highest level of support available.
- Transfer to a ward or facility where mechanical ventilation can be done safely.

- FiO2: Fraction of inspired oxygen

- Failure to meet goals or deterioration → Escalate to higher levels of care (including intubation).
- Emergency signs → Immediate intubation and transfer.

## VI. SAFETY MEASURES FOR USING CYLINDERS
- Check cylinder pressure: Before use, verify that the cylinder has sufficient oxygen by checking the pressure gauge.
- Open valve slowly: When opening the cylinder valve, do so slowly to prevent rapid gas release.
- Use correct flow rate: Set the oxygen flow rate according to the patient's needs and medical prescription.
- Monitor patient: Continuously monitor the patient's oxygen saturation levels and adjust the flow rate as needed.
- Secure oxygen delivery device: Ensure the oxygen delivery device (nasal cannula, mask, etc.) is securely fitted to the patient.
- Close valve when finished: Close the cylinder valve when the oxygen is no longer needed. VII.
## MONITORING AND ADJUSTMENT OF OXYGEN THERAPY
- Assess response
Re-evaluate patient every hour initially, then every 2-4h once the condition is stable or improving. Check for:
 - Increased/continued distress?
 - SpO2 < 90%, pH < 7.30, PaCO2 > 45,
 - declining or altered mental status?
- Titration and SpO2 goal
 - SpO2 ≥ 90% in adults and children
 - SpO2 ≥ 92–95% in pregnant patients
 - SpO2 ≥ 94% if child or adult with signs of multi-organ failure
 - Avoid SpO2 > 96% to avoid ill effects of hyperoxia and to conserve O2 supply. VIII.
## SPECIAL CASES
A. Chronic Obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD),
 - Acute exacerbation of COPD
medical therapy including bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics when indicated.

For patients presenting to the emergency department, provide supplemental oxygen if the patient is hypoxemic, and perform an assessment to determine the optimal treatment setting and whether noninvasive ventilation is indicated (due to increased work of breathing or impaired gas exchange).
- Titrate oxygen to a target saturation of 88%-92% to improve hypoxemia and prevent worsening partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO2) levels.
- Carbon dioxide retention can occur, especially if higher saturations are achieved.
- Perform arterial blood gas (ABG) measurements 30-60 minutes after starting oxygen.
- Venturi masks (high-flow devices) are more accurate than nasal cannula but less likely to be tolerated.
- Use pulse oximetry or ABG to track or adjust supplemental oxygen and monitor for carbon dioxide retention and/or worsening acidosis
 - Post exacerbation long term use of oxygen
At least 2months after exacerbation, Check if patient need long term supplemental oxygen. Perform 2 times ABG check in 3 weeks apart.
Prescribe oxygen at least 15h/day for long time in patients with stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who have “severe chronic resting hypoxemia”, defined as any one of the following:

- arterial oxygen partial pressure (PaO2) ≤ 55 mm Hg
- oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry (SpO2) ≤ 88%
- PaO2: 56-59 mm Hg, SpO2= 89% or arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) ≤ 88%, if evidence of peripheral edema, right heart failure, P pulmonale on electrocardiogram (ECG), polycythemia (hematocrit ≥ 55%), or pulmonary hypertension.
Long term oxygen therapy (at home) should be initiated at a flow rate of 1 L/minute and titrated up by 1 L/minute increments until oxygen saturation measured by pulse oximetry (SpO2) is > 90%. Consider arterial blood gas testing after initial titration to SpO2 > 90% to confirm target resting arterial oxygen partial pressure (PaO2) ≥ 60 mm Hg has been achieved (If available).
Oxygen flow should be sufficient to achieve PaO2 > 60 mm Hg or 90% SpO2 without causing hypercapnia or acidosis (Strong recommendation).

## B. Patient with Central nervous System lesion (stroke, brain injury)
 - Patient with ischemic stroke
Patients with adequate ventilation should have their oxygen saturation monitored. Patients who are hypoxic should receive supplemental oxygen to maintain oxygen saturation >94%. Supplemental oxygen should not routinely be given to nonhypoxic patients with acute ischemic stroke.
 - Brain injury (traumatic)
- Pre-hospital: Patients who are not intubated should receive supplemental oxygen as necessary to maintain an SpO2 >90% to 93%
- In Emergency department: Endotracheal intubation should be performed at this time for all patients with a GCS score <9, inability to protect the airway, inability to maintain SpO2 >90 % despite the use of supplemental oxygen, or clinical signs of cerebral herniation. Adequate oxygenation (PaO2 >60 mmHg) continues to be a priority.
- Recent study found that, the lowest mean PaO2 observed to maintain PbtO2 (Oxygen partial pressure in brain tissue) above the ischemic threshold (20mmHg) was 94 mmHg. The authors' results suggest that the minimal PaO2 target to ensure adequate cerebral oxygenation during the first few days after TBI should be higher than that suggested in the Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines IX.
## OXYGEN TOXICITY AND COMPLICATIONS
- Oxygen toxicity — Oxygen toxicity is considered to be a harmful effect of inspired oxygen at pressures greater than atmospheric pressure (i.e., >0.21 inspired fraction of oxygen at sea level).

- Oxygen toxicity can be caused by hyperoxia and hyperoxemia and is generally responsible for parenchymal lung injury, the retinopathy of prematurity and bronchopulmonary dysplasia in infants.
- In general, patients at greatest risk of oxygen toxicity are those who are receiving mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure with a fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) greater than 0.6 for prolonged durations (e.g., >24 hours).
- Efficient oxygen usage should be:
 - Target Saturation Range: Oxygen should be prescribed according to a target
saturation range. For most acutely ill patients, the goal is to achieve normal or near-normal oxygen saturation.
 - Monitoring: Continuous monitoring of oxygen saturation using pulse oximetry is
essential. This helps ensure that the patient remains within the target range and allows for adjustments as needed.

- Controlled Administration: For patients with conditions like COPD, controlled or
low-dose oxygen therapy is recommended to avoid complications such as hypercapnia.

## I- INTRODUCTION
Patients seldom deteriorate abruptly, even though clinicians may recognize the deterioration suddenly.
In early stages, some signs may be subtle, and clinicians may not fully appreciate the severity of the clinical picture.
The physiologic deterioration precedes many cardiopulmonary arrests by hours, suggesting that early intervention could prevent the need for resuscitation, admission to the ICU, and other sentinel events.
## II- EARLY RECOGNITION OF PATIENT WHO DETERIORATES IN HOSPITAL
The NEWS-2 score
Assessment of vital signs correctly frequently plus observation of patient general condition may ensure good patient care. Based on the degree of change from normal range of the vital signs, the score NEWS (National Early Warning Score) categorizes the patient group who need more frequent assessment and escalation of management before they become urgent or critically ill. The NEWS provides the basis for a unified and systematic approach to the first assessment and triage of acutely ill patients, and a simple track-and-trigger system for monitoring clinical progress for all patients in hospitals.

The NEWS is based on a simple aggregate scoring system in which a score is allocated to physiological measurements, already recorded in routine practice, when patients present to, or are being monitored in hospital.
The NEWS-1 issue in 2012, was reviewed and updated in 2017 as NEWS-2
Six simple physiological parameters form the basis of the scoring system:
1. respiration rate
2. oxygen saturation
3. systolic blood pressure
4. pulse rate
5. level of consciousness or new confusion*
6. temperature.
*The patient has new-onset confusion, disorientation and/or agitation, where previously their mental state was normal – this may be subtle. The patient may respond to questions coherently, but there is some confusion, disorientation and/or agitation. This would score 3 or 4 on the GCS (rather than the normal 5 for verbal response), and scores 3 on the NEWS system.
A score is allocated to each parameter as they are measured, with the magnitude of the score reflecting how extremely the parameter varies from the norm. The score is then aggregated. The score is uplifted by 2 points for people requiring supplemental oxygen to maintain their recommended oxygen saturation.

- The chart has a dedicated section (SpO2 Scale 2) for use in patients with hypercapnic respiratory failure (usually due to COPD) who have clinically recommended oxygen saturation of 88–92%. (for general patient use scale-1 to score SpO2, use scale 2 only after discussed with doctor)
- Sepsis should be considered in any patient with a known infection, signs or symptoms of infection, or in patients at high risk of infection, and a NEW score of 5 or more.
- In identifying patients with sepsis (sepsis-3) outside of ICU, qSOFA_ (three criteria: altered mental status, systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg, and respiratory rate ≥22 breaths per minute. When any 2 were positive) have been proposed. Compared with NEWS-2, qSOFA is more specific but it is less sensitive than NEWS-2. So, when both are positive, it is more certain that patient has sepsis.
- Clinical response to the NEWS should be recorded. This will provide a continuous record of actions taken in response to variations in the NEWS and act as a prompt for escalating care if necessary.

The early stage of critical condition, mostly response well with the simple measures and techniques of management while late management in ICU is often costly, complex, less effective or fails to help.
Critical illness is often reversible. Identification is time-critical. Early identification of critically ill patients is key.
Prompt, time-critical care interventions are crucial to reversing the course of critical illness and saving patient lives.
Essential Emergency and Critical Care (EECC) was established around 2020, with its initial framework and guidelines developed through a Delphi process—a structured approach to building consensus among healthcare experts worldwide. Over 270 specialists from various regions and backgrounds collaborated on the design of EECC, focusing on practical, low-cost interventions that could be feasibly implemented in all hospitals, including those in low-resource settings. This initiative was partially driven by the need for effective care models during the COVID-19 pandemic, which highlighted critical care gaps globally.

The framework builds on WHO’s Basic Emergency Care principles and aims to provide consistent, essential care that can stabilize critically ill patients, regardless of their specific diagnosis or the availability of specialized intensive care resources. This model is being gradually implemented worldwide, especially in areas where access to advanced critical care is limited, to address preventable mortality among critically ill patients.

## B. The process of EECC
The purpose of EECC is to identify critical illness and provide the timely, lifesaving care patients need to reverse their course of illness.
Evaluating the 8 vital signs of EECC is core to this process
Providers must be able to determine normal vital signs. Knowing the normal enables providers to then recognize when vital signs are critically deranged.
When patient vital signs are in danger zone, the clinical management starts to stabilize the condition by using adapted basic life support techniques. If conditions are a common problem like post-partum bleeding, anaphylaxis reaction, poisoning, healthcare providers may start the initial measures and follow the EECC protocol.
## C. The EECC vital signs
There are 8 vital signs in EECC. Traditional 5 vital signs include:
1) heart rate,
2) blood pressure,
3) respiratory rate,
4) oxygen saturation, and 5) temperature.

All hospital patients should have their (8) vital signs assessed at initial presentation and at a minimum every 24 hours thereafter. EECC recommends that vital signs be reassessed for changes in condition and setting, for example when:
- When bedside providers, patients, or guardians become concerned the patient’s condition has worsened
- During and after surgery or anesthesia
- During and after transport/transfer of a patient at risk of critical illness
- Following treatment or action for re-evaluation
Even before vital assessments, providers must start to determine if the patient is experiencing a life-threatening process. This is done by assessing:
- If the patient is awake (level of consciousness), which can be assessed using AVPU
- If the patient is talking (airway) and their breathing is calm, easy and quiet, (breathing).
- If the patient is unconscious, providers must quickly determine if there is a palpable pulse (circulation)

## I. DEFINITION
Shock is a life-threatening, generalized form of acute circulatory failure associated with inadequate oxygen utilization by the cells. Circulatory shock leads to cellular and tissue hypoxia resulting in cellular death and dysfunction of vital organs. There is circulatory failure manifested as hypotension (= reduced tissue perfusion); however, it is crucial to recognize that a patient in shock can present hypertensive, normotensive, or hypotensive.
## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
Shock affects about one-third of patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Distributive shock is the most common type of shock, followed by hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock. Obstructive shock is relatively less common. The most common type of distributive shock is septic shock and has a mortality rate between 40 to 50%.
## III. TIOLOGY
Four types of shock are recognized: hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic and obstructive.

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Cellular hypoxia causes cell membrane ion pump dysfunction, intracellular edema, leakage of intracellular contents into the extracellular space, and inadequate regulation of intracellular pH. These processes progress to the systemic level, resulting in acidosis, and

endothelial dysfunction, as well as further stimulation of inflammatory or anti-inflammatory cascades. Compounding this process is further reduction in tissue perfusion from complex humoral and microcirculatory processes that impair regional blood flow.
Serum lactate levels have traditionally been used as surrogates for hypoperfusion and tissue hypoxia. Elevations in serum lactate level are useful risk-stratification tools in undifferentiated shock. Four types of shock are recognized:
- Distributive: is characterized by severe peripheral vasodilatation with decreased systemic vascular resistance and altered oxygen extraction (vasodilatory shock). For example, severe sepsis or anaphylaxis.
- Cardiogenic: is due to intracardiac causes of cardiac pump failure that result in reduced cardiac output (CO) such as due to acute myocardial infarction, end-stage cardiomyopathy, advanced valvular heart disease, myocarditis, or cardiac arrhythmias).
- Hypovolemic: is due to reduced intravascular volume from internal or external fluid loss (ie, reduced preload), which, in turn, reduces CO.
- Obstructive: is due to extracardiac causes of cardiac pump failure and often associated with poor right ventricular output (pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade, or tension pneumothorax).
Figure 1: Schematic Representations of the four main types of shock (From NEJM.org)

This medical image is a comparative diagram illustrating the four main types of shock: Distributive, Hypovolemic, Cardiogenic, and Obstructive. Each type is presented in its own panel with a schematic representation of the cardiovascular system (heart and major vessels) to depict the pathophysiological mechanism.

Detailed description by panel:

1. Distributive Shock:
   - Label: “Distributive shock”
   - Visual: The heart appears normal in size and function. The peripheral vasculature (arteries and veins) is shown with significant dilation.
   - Annotation: “Vasodilatation” points to the dilated vessels, indicating that blood vessels are excessively relaxed, leading to poor perfusion despite adequate cardiac output.
   - Clinical implication: Common causes include sepsis, anaphylaxis, and neurogenic shock.

2. Hypovolemic Shock:
   - Label: “Hypovolemic shock”
   - Visual: The heart appears normal in size. The vascular bed is depicted with reduced volume or “emptying,” suggesting loss of fluid.
   - Annotation: “Loss of plasma or blood volume” indicates decreased intravascular volume.
   - Clinical implication: Caused by hemorrhage, dehydration, or severe burns.

3. Cardiogenic Shock:
   - Label: “Cardiogenic shock”
   - Visual: The heart is shown enlarged and darkened, indicating failure. The ventricle appears distended and non-compliant.
   - Annotation: “Ventricular failure” points to the dysfunctional heart muscle, unable to pump effectively.
   - Clinical implication: Often due to myocardial infarction, severe arrhythmias, or cardiomyopathy.

4. Obstructive Shock:
   - Label: “Obstructive shock”
   - Visual: The heart appears normal in size but is shown with external pressure or constriction around the pericardium.
   - Annotation: “Obstruction” points to a physical blockage; specifically, “Pericardial tamponade” is labeled, indicating fluid accumulation in the pericardial sac compressing the heart.
   - Clinical implication: Caused by pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism, or tension pneumothorax.

Each panel uses consistent visual language: pink for the heart and vessels, white background, and black text annotations. The diagrams are simplified schematics meant for educational purposes to illustrate the core mechanism of each shock type. There are no decision points, drugs, dosages, or outcomes listed — this is purely a descriptive anatomical-pathophysiological chart.

## V. DIAGNOSIS
A diagnosis of shock is based upon a constellation of clinical suspicion, biochemical, and hemodynamic features.
a. Clinical Manifestation
The clinical findings associated with shock vary according to the etiology and stage of presentation (pre-shock, shock, end-organ dysfunction). A diagnosis of shock is based on clinical, hemodynamic, and biochemical signs, which can broadly be summarized into three components:
1. Hypotension:
- Absolute (eg, systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg; mean arterial pressure <65 mmHg, associated tachycardia (except for patients under beta blockers)
- Relative (eg, a drop in systolic blood pressure >40 mmHg)
2. Clinical signs of tissue hypoperfusion which are apparent through the three “windows” of the body:
- Cutaneous (skin that is cold and clammy, with vasoconstriction and cyanosis, findings that are most evident in low-flow states)
- Renal (urine output of <0.5 ml/kg/h)
- Neurologic (altered mental state, which typically includes obtundation, disorientation, and confusion).

3. Hyperlactatemia (>1.5 mmol/L)
A focused history should be obtained from the patient (if feasible) and/or patient's relatives (information regarding risk factors, medications, and trend of baseline vital signs including blood pressure, valuable clues regarding the patient's risk for shock and potential etiology). Clinical features and symptoms can vary according to the type and stage of shock. Also, features pertaining to the underlying cause of the shock can be present.
- Patients with hypovolemic shock can have general features as mentioned above as well as evidence of orthostatic hypotension, pallor, flattened jugular venous pulsations, may have sequelae of chronic liver disease (in case of variceal bleeding).
- Patients with septic shock may present with symptoms suggestive of the source of infection (example-skin manifestations of primary infection such as erysipelas, cellulitis, necrotizing soft-tissue infections)
- Patients with anaphylactic shock can have hypotension, flushing, urticaria, tachypnea, hoarseness of voice, oral and facial edema, hives, wheeze, inspiratory stridor, and history of exposure to common allergens such as medications or food items the patient is allergic to or insect stings.

- Tension pneumothorax should be suspected in a patient with undifferentiated shock who has tachypnea, unilateral pleuritic chest pain, absent or diminished breath sounds, tracheal deviation to the normal side, distended neck veins and also has pertinent risk factors for tension pneumothorax such as recent trauma, mechanical ventilation, underlying cystic lung disease.
- In a patient with undifferentiated shock, diagnostic clues to pericardial tamponade as the etiology include dyspnea, the Beck triad (elevated jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds, hypotension), pulsus paradoxus, and known risk factors such as trauma, the recent history of pericardial effusion, and thoracic procedures.
- Cardiogenic shock should be considered as the etiology if the patient with undifferentiated shock had chest pain suggestive of cardiac origin, narrow pulse pressure, elevated jugular venous pulsations or lung crackles, and significant arrhythmias on EKG. Point-of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS) is effective at identifying the cause of shock and identifying appropriate next steps.
b. Investigation
Laboratory evaluation:
- Complete blood count and differential
- A complete metabolic panel, including renal and liver function tests
- Serum lactate
- Blood gas analysis (arterial or venous)
- Coagulation studies and D-dimer level

- Cardiac enzymes (Troponin-I or -T) and natriuretic peptides (NT-proBNP) [cardiogenic shock]. C-Reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin, urine analysis, blood culture and/or urine culture (before administration of antibiotics) and other microbiology exploration [Septic shock]
Imaging:
- EKG
- Chest radiography
- Point-of care (POC) ultrasound (if available with trained personnel)
- Directed at etiology of shock

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Each class of shock (distributive, cardiogenic, hypovolemic, obstructive) is distinguished from the other by a collection of clinical features supported by etiology found, laboratory, imaging, and hemodynamic findings.
1. Hypovolemic shock
- Reduced preload in context of a suspected or known cause.
- Hypovolemia displaying signs of reduced skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, a
collapsible IVC on imaging.
2. Distributive shock
- Hypotension without clinical and hemodynamic signs of reduced preload (eg, normal skin
turgor, normal inferior vena cava on imaging) or fluid overload.
- A preserved or hyperdynamic left ventricle is typically observed on echocardiography. a. Septic Shock
i. Definition
Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
Septic Shock is defined as sepsis that has circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities. Clinically, this includes patients who fulfill the criteria for sepsis who, despite adequate fluid resuscitation, require vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥ 65mmHg and have a lactate > 2mmol/L (>18mg/dL).
ii. Evaluation
Patients who have sepsis have organ dysfunction that can be identified by using the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA):

b. Anaphylactic shock
- Clinical = Diagnostic
- Most common (90%) Cutaneous: Urticaria, erythema, pruritus, angioedema, flushing
- Danger sign:
- Respiratory: stridor, wheezing, dyspnea, increased work of breathing, persistent cough, cyanosis
- Cardiovascular: Hypotension, dysrhythmias, collapse, chest pain
- Gastrointestinal: Nausea, Vomiting
c. Neurogenic Shock
- Clinical: Hypotension without tachycardia, bradycardia, warm and dry skin 3. Cardiogenic shock
- Hypotension in association with pulmonary edema,
- Large dilated ventricles and poor left ventricle function, or valvular or septal abnormalities
on echocardiography.
4. Obstructive shock
- Hypotension associated with distended neck veins but usually without clinical signs of
fluids overload or reduced preload.
- Bedside ultrasonography or echocardiography is useful in this setting to detect pericardial
tamponade and pneumothorax.
- Clinical:
- Pulsus paradoxus (a drop on systolic BP greater than 10 mmHg on inspiration)
- Muffled heart tones (cardiac tamponade)
- Elevated JVD (depending on volume status)
- Unilateral absence of breath sounds (tension pneumothorax)
- Tracheal deviation (tension pneumothorax)

## VII. ANAGEMENT
Shock is a time-sensitive condition. All patients with shock must be early recognized and managed well without delay. The management of shock comprises of the following principles that include:
- Recognition of the pattern of shock
- Selecting appropriate treatment (resuscitation)
- Specific therapy for the underlying problem
- Monitoring clinical response.

1. Objectives
The objectives of intervention:
- Restore adequate tissue perfusion
- Prevent worsening or to help recover organ dysfunction (include coagulation disorders) and organ failure.
- Once identified, the cause must be corrected rapidly.
2. Critical Sign
- Anuria and acute renal failure
- Acidemia further depresses CO (pH <7.2)
- Hypotension becomes severe and irresponsive to therapy
- Hyperlactatemia often worsens
- Restlessness evolves into obtundation and coma.
3. Mortality risk factor
- Patient-related factors (age, comorbidities, immune status…)
- Shock-related factors (types, duration and severity, underlying causes, MOD…)
- Response to treatment (delayed appropriate treatment or failure to respond to initial
treatment)
4. Outpatient Management
All patients with shock cannot be managed in the outpatient setting.
5. First-line treatment Initial management (= ABC)
- Airway:
- Assess the signs of airway obstruction: “see-saw” respiration, central cyanosis, no breath sounds.
- Opening the airway using: Head-tilt chin-lift, Jaw-thrust maneuver, insertion of an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway. Tracheal intubation may be required if those maneuver fails.
- Breathing:
- All patients should receive supplemental oxygen.
- For patients with respiratory distress or who are hemodynamically unstable, noninvasive or invasive mechanical ventilation are typically needed.

- Goal: Arterial oxygen saturation should be restored to >94% and ventilation controlled to maintain a PaCO2 of 35 to 40 mm Hg.
- Circulation:
- IV access through large-bore peripheral venous lines.
- Central venous access is the preferred route for the long-term administration of vasopressor therapy and in assessing volume status (preload) and monitoring ScvO2.
- Passive leg raising above the level of the heart with the patient supine (useful in hypovolemic shock but not in cardiogenic shock).
- Internal bleeding: surgical consultation.
- External hemorrhage: direct compression, wound packing and extremity tourniquets.
- Isotonic Crystalloid solutions:
- 0.9% NaCl, Ringer lactate (use RL for all cases except brain injury that use 0.9% NaCl)
- 20 to 40 mL/kg given rapidly (over 10 to 20 minutes)

- Hemorrhagic shock: new concept in early intervention is to stop the bleeding source and early transfusion to minimize crystalloid or colloids use.
6. Treatment Adjustment A. Hypovolemic Shock
Notes:
- The presence or likelihood of severe, ongoing hemorrhage, Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP) in a 1:1:1 ratio of plasma to platelets to pRBCs is generally used.

- The goal is to remove the obstruction as quickly as possible.
- A cardiac tamponade requires a pericardiocentesis in which a provider inserts a needle or catheter into the pericardium to remove the accumulated fluid.

Algorithm 1: Management of shock

This is a clinical algorithm for managing shock states, structured as a decision tree starting from initial recognition of shock through to specific interventions based on etiology.

---

**1. Initial Shock Recognition**
- **Trigger**: “Shock State”
- **Clinical Signs/Symptoms**:
  - SBP < 90 mmHg
  - Tachycardia
  - Polypnea
  - Cyanosis
  - Mottled Skin
  - Cold extremities
  - Pale
  - Confuse

---

**2. Initial Monitoring & Support**
- **Monitoring**:
  - Blood pressure, pulse, SpO2
  - 2 large bore IV access
- **Oxygen Therapy**:
  - Goal SpO2 > 94%

---

**3. Contextual Clues (Differential Diagnosis Branching)**
Four parallel branches based on presenting signs/symptoms:

**Branch A: Chest Pain, Orthopnea, Arrhythmia, Right/Left ventricular failure sign → Cardiogenic Shock**
- **Interventions**:
  - Norepinephrine: 0.5 mg/h +/- Dobutamine: 2–20 mcg/kg/min
  - Pulmonary Edema Management:
    - Furosemide: 1 mg/kg
    - Risodan: 1 mg/h
- **Additional Treatments**:
  - Treat tachy or bradyarrhythmia
  - Revascularization
  - ECMO
  - Fibrinolysis

**Branch B: Fever, Hypothermia, Chills, Urinary sign, Nuchal Rigidity, Cough, Dyspnea, Cellulitis, Abdominal rigidity → Septic Shock**
- **Interventions**:
  - Antibiotic (preferably after hemoculture)
- **Fluid Therapy**:
  - 500 mL in 20 minutes, up to 30 mL/kg
- **MAP Target**:
  - MAP < 65
- **Vasopressor**:
  - Norepinephrine: 0.5 mg/h IVSE (titrated every 5–10 min)

**Branch C: Bleeding, Polytrauma, Burn, Dehydration, Vomiting, Diarrhea, Pregnancy → Hypovolemic Shock**
- **Interventions**:
  - Fluid therapy: 500 mL in 20 min, up to 30 mL/kg
  - Blood Product Transfusion: RBCs, FFP
  - Hemostasis
- **MAP Target**:
  - MAP < 65 if Severe Head Trauma
  - MAP < 85 if Severe Head Trauma
  - MAP < 65 (general target)
- **Vasopressor**:
  - Norepinephrine: 0.5 mg/h IVSE (titrated every 5–10 min)

**Branch D: Rash, Pruritus, Quincke’s Edema/Angioedema, Stridor, Bronchospasm, Vomiting → Anaphylactic Shock**
- **Interventions**:
  - AIRWAY re-evaluation
  - Epinephrine: 0.3–0.5 mg IM (up to 3 times), then switch to IV
  - Salbutamol Nebulization
  - Solumedrol: 125 mg IV
- **MAP Target**:
  - MAP < 65

---

**Summary of Key Drug Names and Dosages**:
- Norepinephrine: 0.5 mg/h IVSE (titrated every 5–10 min)
- Dobutamine: 2–20 mcg/kg/min
- Furosemide: 1 mg/kg
- Risodan: 1 mg/h
- Epinephrine: 0.3–0.5 mg IM (up to 3 times), then IV
- Solumedrol: 125 mg IV
- Salbutamol: Nebulization
- Antibiotics: Administered after hemoculture
- Fluids: 500 mL in 20 min, up to 30 mL/kg
- Blood Products: RBCs, FFP

---

**Outcomes / Endpoints**:
- All branches converge on MAP targets (<65 or <85 if severe head trauma) and vasopressor use (Norepinephrine).
- Specific interventions are tailored to the underlying cause (e.g., revascularization for cardiogenic shock, antibiotics for septic shock).

This algorithm provides a stepwise approach to shock management, emphasizing early recognition, context-based differential diagnosis, and targeted interventions.

Algorithm 2: Management of anaphylaxis

This is a clinical algorithm for the management of suspected anaphylaxis. It outlines diagnostic criteria, immediate interventions, monitoring, and follow-up steps.

---

**Decision Points & Branches:**

1. **Suspected Anaphylaxis → Diagnosis**
   - Decision point: Look for:
     - Acute onset of illness
     - Life-threatening Airway +/- Breathing +/- Circulation problem
     - Usually skin/mucosal changes
   - Branch: Detailed documentation of potential triggers, symptoms, and response to treatment (parallel action)

2. **Remove or stop allergen** → Mandatory step before medication.

3. **Intramuscular Epinephrine**
   - Dose based on age:
     - Adult: 500 mcg (0.5 mL) of 1:1000 epinephrine
     - Child >12 yrs: 500 mcg (0.5 mL)
     - Child 6–12 yrs: 300 mcg (0.3 mL)
     - Child <6 yrs: 150 mcg (0.15 mL)
   - Repeat dose after 5–15 minutes if needed.

4. **After IM Epinephrine → Two parallel pathways:**
   - **Pathway A: Mast cell tryptase levels**
     - Measure as soon as possible
     - Repeat 1–2 hours later but within 4 hours of onset
   - **Pathway B: Intravenous fluids for hypotension**
     - Adults: 500–1000 mL boluses
     - Children: 20 mL/kg boluses
     - → Then: Nebulised salbutamol – for bronchospasm (2.5–5 mg as needed)

5. **Post-treatment Monitoring & Disposition:**
   - **Adults**: Observe for at least 6 hours
   - **Children**: Admit to paediatric ward

6. **Post-disposition Actions (after observation/admission):**
   - Autoinjector epinephrine pen training
   - Anaphylaxis episode education and resource information
   - Detailed discharge letter to family doctor
   - → Refer to allergy specialist for outpatient follow-up

7. **Adjunctive Medications (administered concurrently or after initial resuscitation):**
   - **Chlorphenamine** (im or iv):
     - Adult: 10 mg
     - Child >12 yrs: 5 mg
     - Child 6–12 yrs: 2.5 mg
     - Child <6 yrs: 250 mcg/kg
   - **Hydrocortisone** (im or iv):
     - Adult: 200 mg
     - Child >12 yrs: 100 mg
     - Child 6–12 yrs: 50 mg
     - Child <6 yrs: 25 mg
   - Continue Cetirizine or Chlorphenamine for ≤3 days
   - Continue prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg for up to 3 days

8. **In refractory cases consider:**
   - IV adrenaline (experienced users only)
   - Alternative vasopressors
   - IM glucagon (if on β-blockers)
   - IV magnesium (beware hypotension)

---

**Summary of Key Drugs and Dosages:**

- **Epinephrine (IM)**:
  - Adult: 500 mcg (0.5 mL)
  - Child >12 yrs: 500 mcg (0.5 mL)
  - Child 6–12 yrs: 300 mcg (0.3 mL)
  - Child <6 yrs: 150 mcg (0.15 mL)
- **IV Fluids**:
  - Adult: 500–1000 mL boluses
  - Child: 20 mL/kg boluses
- **Nebulised Salbutamol**: 2.5–5 mg as needed
- **Chlorphenamine**:
  - Adult: 10 mg
  - Child >12 yrs: 5 mg
  - Child 6–12 yrs: 2.5 mg
  - Child <6 yrs: 250 mcg/kg
- **Hydrocortisone**:
  - Adult: 200 mg
  - Child >12 yrs: 100 mg
  - Child 6–12 yrs: 50 mg
  - Child <6 yrs: 25 mg
- **Cetirizine/Chlorphenamine**: Continue for ≤3 days
- **Prednisolone**: 1–2 mg/kg for up to 3 days
- **Refractory Cases**:
  - IV adrenaline (experienced users only)
  - Alternative vasopressors
  - IM glucagon (if on β-blockers)
  - IV magnesium (with caution for hypotension)

---

**Outcomes:**

- Successful management leads to:
  - Observation/admission as per age group
  - Education and training
  - Discharge with detailed letter
  - Referral to allergy specialist for follow-up

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES
Patients often present with combined forms of shock. Examples include:
- Patients with shock from sepsis or pancreatitis have distributive shock (due to the effects
of inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cascades on vascular permeability and peripheral vasodilation); however, they also often have a hypovolemic component (due to decreased oral intake, insensible losses, vomiting, diarrhea) and a cardiogenic component (due to inflammation-related myocardial depression).
- Patients with underlying cardiomyopathy may present with hypovolemic shock (from
over-diuresis) and cardiogenic shock (from inadequate compensatory tachycardia and/or stroke volume).
- Patients with severe traumatic injury may have hemorrhagic shock from blood loss as
well as distributive shock from SIRS or, less commonly, fat embolism.
- Patients with trauma to the spinal cord can have distributive shock from injury-related
autonomic dysfunction and cardiogenic shock from myocardial depression.
- Patients with a ruptured left ventricular free wall aneurysm can have cardiogenic shock
from primary pump failure, obstructive shock from cardiac tamponade when blood loss is contained by the pericardial sac, and hemorrhagic shock when blood loss is not contained by the pericardial sac.
- Patients with septic shock may transition from a distributive (low systemic vascular
resistance) shock state to multifactorial shock state after massive volume resuscitation that results in abdominal compartment syndrome and/or acute right heart syndrome.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS
Effects of shock are reversible in the early stages and a delay in diagnosis and/or timely initiation of treatment can lead to irreversible changes including multiorgan failure (MOF) and death. Even with treatment, mortality from cardiogenic shock after MI (60 to 65%) and septic shock (30 to 40%) is high. Prognosis depends on the cause, preexisting or complicating illness, time between onset and diagnosis, and promptness and adequacy of therapy.
## X. COMPLICATIONS
As global tissue hypoxia progresses, shock ensues, followed by the multiorgan dysfunction syndrome (MODS), which is manifested by:
- Acute renal failure (ARF)
- Respiratory failure: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)
- Myocardial depression
- Liver failure
- Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
- Anoxic encephalopathy.
Once MODS progresses, in some cases, death is inevitable despite proper eradication of the inciting cause.
## XI. REVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION
For medical professionals:
- Recognize the patients from early stage of shock (pre-shock, shock)
- Rapidly identify the etiology
- Early apply the appropriate interventions and therapy to correct the cause of shock and
prevent MOF and death.
For general population:
- Alert any serious case without delay (SAMU, hospital, etc.)!!! (Time is life)

- Get regular vaccinations against viral infections that may cause sepsis.
- Avoid any contact with the responsible allergen (anaphylactic shock)
- Practice good hygiene.
- Care for and clean any open or gaping wounds.
- Follow medical advice on managing bacterial infections.
- Treat fungal and parasitic infections as soon as symptoms appear.
- Control diabetes, if relevant.
- Avoid smoking.
