## I. DEFINITION
Hemorrhagic shock refers to a state of hypoperfusion due to significant rapid blood loss. Significant and rapid blood loss results in decreased circulating blood volume and therefore inadequate tissue perfusion. This results in severe, life-threatening systemic hypoxia and cellular dysfunction. Without support, hemorrhage may result in hemodynamic instability, end-organ hypoperfusion, and eventually death.
Shock is a physiologic continuum, there are 3 stages of shock:
- Compensated shock (Pre-shock): Patient's physiologic reserve prevents significant alteration in vital signs. Potentially, with timely and appropriate management, deterioration can be prevented, and signs of impending deterioration can be reversed (eg, normalization of heart rate and serum lactate levels).
- Decompensated shock (Shock): Loss of circulating volume overcomes patient's physiologic reserve, resulting in significant alteration in vital signs. The signs and symptoms of organ dysfunction appear (tachycardia, dyspnea, restlessness, diaphoresis, metabolic acidosis, hypotension, oliguria, and cool, clammy skin)

- End-organ dysfunction – Progressive shock leads to irreversible organ damage, multiorgan failure (MOF), and death. During this stage, anuria and acute kidney failure develop, acidemia further depresses CO, hypotension becomes severe and recalcitrant to therapy, hyperlactatemia often worsens, and restlessness evolves into obtundation and coma. Death is common in this phase of shock.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
Hemorrhagic shock in Southeast Asia is a critical public health issue, often resulting from trauma, gastrointestinal bleeding, or ruptured aneurysms.
Incidence and Mortality
High Incidence: Southeast Asia has a high incidence of hemorrhagic shock due to road traffic accidents, natural disasters, and violence.
Mortality Rates: Mortality rates vary by country, but hemorrhagic shock remains a leading cause of death in trauma cases.
## III. ETIOLOGY
- Trauma- penetrating and blunt:
 - Abdominal:
- Splenic injury
- Liver injury
 - Chest:
- Hemothorax
- Aorta or great vessel injury

- Pelvis:
- Pelvic fracture with vascular injury
- Vascular malformations:
 - May lead to thoracic, intraperitoneal, or retroperitoneal bleeding
 - Aneurysms:
- Abdominal aortic aneurysm most common
- Mycotic aneurysm secondary to endocarditis
 - Aortogastric fistula
 - Arteriovenous malformations
- Abortion: Complete, partial, or inevitable
- Ectopic pregnancy
- Epistaxis
- Fractures (especially pelvis and long bones)
- GI bleeding
- Hemoptysis
- Malignancies
- Placenta previa or abruption
- Postpartum hemorrhage
- Retroperitoneal bleeds
- Splenic rupture
- Vascular injuries

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY
In hemorrhagic shock, blood loss exceeds the body's ability to compensate and provide adequate tissue perfusion and oxygenation.
Cellular hypoxia occurs as a result of reduced tissue perfusion/oxygen delivery and/or increased oxygen consumption or from inadequate oxygen utilization. Cellular hypoxia, in turn, causes cell membrane ion pump dysfunction, intracellular edema, leakage of intracellular contents into the extracellular space, and inadequate regulation of intracellular pH. These biochemical processes, when unchecked, progress to the systemic level, resulting in acidosis and endothelial dysfunction, as well as further stimulation of inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cascades.
Compounding this process is a further reduction in tissue perfusion from complex humoral and microcirculatory processes that impair regional blood flow.
Serum lactate levels, when elevated, have traditionally been used as surrogates for hypoperfusion and tissue hypoxia (note that epinephrine-mediated aerobic glycolysis in skeletal muscle contributes to hyperlactatemia as well).
A posttraumatic coagulopathy (trauma-induced coagulopathy) may be resulted from dilutional loss of coagulation factors during hemorrhage and fluid resuscitation, increased chemical mediators like activated protein C, disordered fibrinolysis, and posttraumatic platelet and endothelial dysfunction.
Note: Total blood volume (TBV) is about 7% of ideal body weight = 70ml/kg IBW.
Male (heigh 158.5-168.5cm) whose IBW ~ 60kg, will have TBV= 60 x 70= 4200ml

## V. DIAGNOSIS
Signs and Symptoms
- Class I hemorrhage: Loss of up to 15% of blood volume (up to 630 ml in 60-kg adult).

- HR <100
 - SBP normal
 - Respiratory rate (RR) 14-20
 - Increased or normal pulse pressure
 - Slight anxiety
- Class II hemorrhage: Loss of 15-30% of blood volume (630-1260 ml):
 - Tachycardia: HR >100
 - SBP normal, or minimally decreased
 - Tachypnea: RR 20-30
 - Narrowed pulse pressure
 - Mild anxiety
 - Small decrease in urine output
- Class III hemorrhage: Loss of 30-40% of blood volume (1260-1680 ml):
 - Marked tachycardia: HR >120
 - Hypotension: SBP decreased
 - Marked tachypnea: RR 30-40
 - Marked narrowing of pulse pressure
 - Significant change in mental status: Confusion
 - Delayed capillary refill
 - Marked decrease in urine output
- Class IV hemorrhage: Loss of >40% of blood volume (>1680 ml):
 - HR >140
 - Marked hypotension: SBP decreased
 - RR >35
 - Very narrow pulse pressure
 - Depressed mental status: Confusion, lethargy, loss of consciousness
 - Negligible urine output
 - Cold and pale skin
Note: Female patient with heigh of 156.4-166.4cm, has IBW~55kg their total blood volume is 3850ml. Hemorrhage class I, II, III, IV correspond to the volume loss of < 577ml, 577-1155ml, 1155-1540ml, > 1540ml)

Thorough health and past medical history:
- Underlying disease, risk factors, age
- Medications
- Trauma
Physical Exam
(complete physical exam usually perform after stabilization of A.B.C.)
- Complete physical exam to determine shock class and assess for hemorrhage source
- Vital signs including HR, RR, BP
- Temperature

- Mental status (anxiety, confusion, lethargy, obtundation, coma)
- Pulse character, capillary refill, and skin perfusion
- Pulse pressure

- Abdominal exam
- Pelvic/rectal exam for bleeding as indicated Essential Workup
- Thorough history and physical exam
- IV access for resuscitation
- Blood type and crossmatch Diagnostic Tests and Interpretation
- Ultrasound FAST.
- CBC
- Blood type and crossmatch
- Coagulation studies:
 - PT, PTT
 - International normalized ratio (INR)
- Other measures of tissue hypoperfusion:
 - Base deficit/excess:
 - Can assist in determining class of hemorrhage
 - Arterial blood gas
 - Serum lactate level
 - Serum electrolytes
- Pregnancy test/β-hCG
Imaging
- CXR:
 - Hemothorax:
- Blunt chest injuries
- Thoracic arteriovenous malformation
 - Pelvic x-ray for possible occult fracture
 - Focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST exam):
- Abdominal trauma
- Possible abdominal aortic aneurysm
- Nontraumatic intraperitoneal hemorrhage

- Insert Foley catheter:
 - Monitor urine output
- Nasogastric tube:

- Diagnostic peritoneal lavage:

- For unstable trauma patients when US fails to show intraperitoneal hemorrhage

- Angiography:

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Cardiac tamponade
- Tension pneumothorax
- Cardiogenic shock
- Sepsis
- Adrenal insufficiency
- Neurogenic shock
## VII. MANAGEMENT
a. Objective
Treatment should be initiated as soon as shock state is recognized while simultaneously identifying the underlying bleeding source.
The goal is to restore tissue and organ perfusion and to control the source of hemorrhage to normalize hemodynamic, coagulation, and perfusion parameters.
b. Critical signs
Early recognition and initiate treatment of shock is the key to prevent mortality. Reliance solely on SBP as indicator of shock state can result in delayed recognition Massive blood loss may only result in minimal decrease in Hb or Hct initially A high index of suspicion is necessary for prompt, accurate diagnosis. Probable mechanisms of hemorrhagic shock must be thoroughly and rapidly examined and treated.
- A narrowed pulse pressure is typically present, and often missed owing to a normal systolic value.
- Anxiety or violent behavior may be a sign of shock and can easily be confused for intoxication or isolated brain injury.
- Decreased mental status should be considered an ominous sign of impending decompensation.
- Hypothermia and / or acidosis a key component of the lethal triad (hypothermia, coagulopathy, acidosis), is an independent predictor of mortality in hemorrhaging patients.

- Acute bleeding in previously normal individual, a hemoglobin < 11 g/dL is associated with a mortality rate of nearly 40%
- Patients with a base deficit (BD) greater than 6 are at higher risk of mortality and the need for massive transfusion.

- an international normalized ratio (INR) > 1.5 reliably predicts the need for massive transfusion
c. Mortality risk factors
- Very young and very old people
- Underlying illness or injury
- cardiac arrest (ROSC)
- Craniotomy
- thoracotomy
d. Outpatient management

## Pre-Hospital
- Minimize further blood loss and provide limited fluid resuscitation and other life- saving measures while rapidly transporting the patient to a facility for definitive care.
- Immediate interventions during rapid transport may include:
 - Bleeding site identification and control (strategies may include direct pressure,
tourniquets, hemostatic dressing, and tranexamic acid if possible; use of a pelvic binder for suspected pelvic fracture)
 - Restrictive fluid resuscitation with crystalloid solutions to a target mean
arterial pressure of 50-60 mm Hg in patients without clinical evidence of a traumatic brain injury (TBI); in patients with severe TBI (Glasgow Coma Scale ≤ 8), maintain a mean arterial pressure of ≥ 80 mm Hg.
 - Hypothermia prevention (such as the removal of wet clothing, increasing the
ambient air temperature, and the warming of IV fluids).
 - Endotracheal intubation or other airway management if indicated in trauma
patients.
e. First line treatment
- Every patient who is at risk for hemorrhage should be evaluated by quickly proceeding through the primary survey (A. B. C.), immediate life threats are recognized and treated before a head-to-toe exam and precise diagnosis is made.
- Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma [FAST] for patients with thoracoabdominal injuries (if feasible) should be the first investigation exam.
- Coagulopathy resulting from hemorrhage or resuscitation efforts must be minimized to reduce additional bleeding risk.

## Initial Stabilization/Therapy
- Airway and breathing:
 - Intubation as indicated by patient's respiratory and mental status
 - 100% oxygen via face mask should be administered
- Circulation:
 - 2 large-bore peripheral IV lines (16G or larger)
 - Central venous line or venous cutdown (saphenous) may be necessary
 - Intra-osseous route may be considered
 - Fluid resuscitation with warmed, isotonic crystalloid fluid - total volume
based on patient response to initial fluid bolus (bolus: 1-2L for adult, 20ml/kg

pediatric). Target: MAP of 50-60 mm Hg in absence of TBI, and 80-90 mm Hg in cases of severe TBI.
 - Approach is to balance goal of perfusion and risk of rebleeding and may vary
with patient:
- In blunt trauma, BP maintenance may take precedence to reduce risk
of traumatic brain injury
- In penetrating trauma with hemorrhage, delayed aggressive fluid
resuscitation until definitive control may reduce bleeding risk
- Early transfusion with whole blood or balanced blood products for class Ill or IV shock:
 - Type-specific and cross-matched blood preferred when time permits, often 1
hr
 - Type-specific blood is usually available within 10-15 min
 - Type O blood can be used in immediate, life-threatening situations (type O
Rh-negative blood only for women of child-bearing age)
 - Massive transfusion protocols for patients requiring >4u pRBC in 1 hr, or
> 10 U pRBC / 24 hr

## Ed Treatment/Procedures
- Place patient on continuous monitor
- NPO status, strict bed rest
- Control hemorrhage (direct pressure, pelvic fixation/stabilization, etc.)
- Central venous access may be indicated for CVP monitoring, but placement of such lines should not interfere with resuscitation
- Continually reassess patient for clinical response/deterioration:
 - Vital signs, mental status, and urine output
 - Follow serial blood gas, lactate level, and hemoglobin/hematocrit
measurements
 - Maintain urine output at 50 ml/h
- Response to initial fluid resuscitation is the key to determining subsequent therapy:
 - Rapid response to fluid indicates minimal (<20%) blood loss
 - Transient response indicates ongoing hemorrhage or inadequate resuscitation;
continue fluid and blood administration and obtain necessary studies and consultations
 - Minimal or no response to volume resuscitation indicates ongoing severe
blood loss; immediate angiography or surgical intervention is warranted
- Use fluids warmed (~39°C) by microwave ovens, fluid warmers
- Transfuse whole blood, RBCs, platelets, and other blood products as indicated
- Consider autotransfusion devices with tube thoracostomy treatment of large hemothoraces.
- Monitor closely for coagulopathy particularly with massive transfusion
- Specialty consultation and additional procedures (surgery) as indicated by cause and source of hemorrhagic shock

f. Treatment adjustment
- Antifibrinolytic agents: Tranexamic acid should be given as soon as possible (within 3h of injury) to hemorrhaged patients. Dose: 1g bolus over 10min followed by an infusion of 1g over 8h. Do not use through the transfusion line.
- Initiate damage control surgery in patients with
 - the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy.
 - combined abdominal vascular and pancreatic injuries,
 - severe injuries and signs of ongoing bleeding or
 - coagulopathy, and in those in whom definitive repair is not immediately
feasible.
Provide definitive surgical management in all other patients with traumatic hemorrhage.
- Vasopressors have a limited role and may be used for selected patients in hemorrhagic shock.
- The Assessment of Blood Consumption (ABC) score includes four variables:
 - penetrating mechanism,
 - SBP ≤90 mm Hg in emergency department
 - emergency department heart rate ≥120 beats/minute, and
 - positive fluid on abdominal ultrasonography (FAST) Give 1 point to each positive item. Sum the points to get ABC score. Score ≥ 2, patient is likely to require massive transfusion (≥ 10 units pRBCs) [sensitivity: 75-90%, specificity: 67-88%]

This flowchart details the hospital management of hemorrhagic shock, guiding clinicians through a stepwise algorithm based on clinical assessment and response to interventions.

---

**Starting Point:**
- Patient with hemorrhagic shock being managed in a hospital setting.

---

**Step 1: Initial Actions (Always performed)**
- Institute early mechanical thromboprophylaxis.
- Provide reversal for any patient receiving antithrombotic therapy.

---

**Decision Point 1:**
**Is bleeding source evident, or if death imminent if bleeding is not rapidly controlled?**

- **Yes →** Proceed to:
  - Initiate fluid resuscitation, and immediately institute bleeding control procedures such as:
    - Direct pressure/tourniquets
    - Packing
    - Damage control surgery
    - REBOA (resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta)
    - Definitive surgery

- **No →** Proceed to:
  - Institute initial fluid resuscitation as needed.
  - Immediately institute further investigations and monitoring studies*.
  - Correct hypocalcemia if present.

---

**Decision Point 2 (after initial fluid resuscitation or bleeding control):**
**Is there a rapid response and normalization of hemodynamic vital signs without indications of inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygenation, with initial fluid resuscitation?**

- **Yes →** Proceed to:
  - Provide maintenance fluids.
  - Keep typed and cross-matched blood available.
  - Obtain surgical consultation and evaluation.
  - Provide operative intervention as needed.

- **No →** Proceed to Decision Point 3.

---

**Decision Point 3:**
**Is there a transit response in hemodynamic vital signs to initial fluid resuscitation?**

- **Yes →** Proceed to:
  - Transfuse blood and blood products.
  - Initiate rapid operative or angiographic bleeding control intervention.
  - Consider initiating a massive transfusion protocol to ensure sufficient blood products.

- **No →** Proceed to:
  - Initiate massive transfusion protocol.
  - Provide immediate definitive intervention (operative or angiographic).
  - Consider cardiac ultrasound to identify the cause of shock, and consider non-hemorrhagic shock or pump failure.

---

**Monitoring Studies (*Essential serial blood tests include):**
- Lactate and/or base deficit (BD)
- Hemoglobin or hematocrit
- Coagulation studies (viscoelastic testing or traditional lab)
- Ionized calcium in all patients, especially those receiving transfusions

---

- REBOA: resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES
## 1. Pediatric Considerations
- Children often have greater physiologic reserve than adults and can preserve normal vital signs longer
- Systemic responses to blood loss in the pediatric patient include:
 - Volume loss <25%: Weak, thready pulse and tachycardia; lethargy, irritability,
and confusion; cool, clammy skin; decreased urine output/increased urine specific gravity
 - Volume loss 25--40%: Tachycardia; marked change in consciousness;
dulled response to pain; cyanotic, cold extremities with decreased capillary refill; minimal urine output
 - Volume loss >40%: Hypotension, tachycardia, or bradycardia; comatose;
pale, cold skin; no urine output
## 2. Geriatric Considerations
- Underlying disease, overall deconditioning, and medications may alter responses to hemorrhage and blood loss.
## 3. Postpartum hemorrhage
- In patients with major hemorrhage (blood loss > 1,000 mL and continued bleeding and/or signs of clinical shock), infuse a maximum of 3.5 L of clear fluids (initially 2 L of warmed isotonic crystalloid) while awaiting compatible blood.
- Isotonic crystalloids are preferred over colloids for fluid resuscitation
- Blood Transfusion
 - A blood transfusion is indicated in patients with continued bleeding or signs
of clinical shock and major postpartum hemorrhage.
For patients with major postpartum hemorrhage:
 - In the absence of timely laboratory results, a massive transfusion protocol with

a fixed ratio of 1:1:1 of packed red blood cells (RBC) to fresh frozen plasma to platelets can be used.
 - If immediate transfusion is indicated, give emergency type O, RhD-negative
blood in the form of red cell concentrate and switch to type-specific red cells as soon as possible.
 - Consider transfusion of platelets when the platelet count is < 75 × 10^9/L based
on laboratory monitoring
 - If hemostatic results are unavailable and bleeding continues, infuse fresh
frozen plasma 12-15 mL/kg after 4 units of red blood cells until hemostatic test results are available
 - Consider early fresh frozen plasma if hemostatic results are unavailable
and coagulopathy, such as placental abruption or amniotic fluid embolism, is suspected or detection of postpartum hemorrhage has been delayed.
 - If prothrombin time/activated partial thromboplastin time is > 1.5 times
normal and hemorrhage is ongoing, fresh frozen plasma > 15 mg/kg may be needed to correct coagulopathy.
 - Maintain plasma fibrinogen level > 2 g/L during ongoing postpartum hemorrhage

- Medication:
 - Oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly or 10-40 units IV in 0.5-1 L normal saline as a
continuous infusion [20-40 milliunit/min] (or another uterotonic if IV oxytocin is not available)
 - Avoid undiluted rapid IV infusion as it may cause hypotension.
 - Adverse effects include nausea and vomiting.
 - If oxytocin is not available or for bleeding refractory to oxytocin, alternative
uterotonics may be considered. Options include:
- Ergot alkaloids
- Methylergonovine (Methergine): 0.2 mg intramuscularly every 2-4 hours.
- Ergonovine (ergometrine)
- Ergometrine/oxytocin
- Misoprostol (Cytotec) [oral/sublingual/rectal]

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS
- The prognosis of hemorrhagic shock depends on several factors, including the severity of the blood loss, timeliness of medical intervention, and underlying health conditions of the patient
- Without intervention, severe hemorrhagic shock presents a classic trimodal distribution of deaths:
 - Death occurs within minutes of hemorrhage (immediate exsanguination),
 - Death after 1 to several hours (progressive decompensation),
 - Death occurs days to weeks later (sepsis and organ failure).
- Among survivors, hemorrhagic shock is associated with poor functional outcomes and significantly increased long-term mortality.
- Elevated serum lactate and/or base deficit (BD) at admission is associated with increased mortality and worse outcomes in trauma patients.
- Patients in end-stage/refractory shock will have irreversible cellular damage, resulting in multiple organ failure and most likely death.
## X. COMPLICATIONS
- Major hemorrhage may lead to a "lethal triad" of coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, and hypothermia.
- Without life-saving interventions, complications of hemorrhagic shock and continued bleeding may include cardiac failure, acute kidney injury, lung damage, and poor cerebral perfusion.
- Shock-related hypoperfusion and end-organ damage in the kidneys, liver, intestine, and skeletal muscle may lead to multiorgan failure in survivors.
- Patients with multiple-trauma are at high risk for hospital-acquired venous thromboembolism (VTE),
- Complications of rapid transfusions of blood products and large amounts of fluids.

## XI. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Initial therapy until blood products are available needs to be differentiated to be effective in terms of hemodynamic stabilization and coagulation. Treatment of acidosis and hypothermia can further reduce bleeding complications.
- Early imaging (ultrasonography or contrast-enhanced CT) should be used for detection of free fluid in patients with suspected torso trauma.
- CT assessment should be provided for hemodynamically stable patients.
- Low initial Hb should be considered an indicator for severe bleeding associated with coagulopathy.
- Repeated Hb measurements should be used as a laboratory marker for bleeding, as an initial Hb value in the normal range may mask bleeding.
- Serum lactate and/or base deficit measurements are sensitive tests to estimate and monitor the extent of bleeding and shock.
- Repeated monitoring of coagulation, using a traditional laboratory determination (prothrombin time [PT], activated partial thromboplastin time [APTT], platelet counts, and fibrinogen) and/or a viscoelastic method, should be provided.
- Target systolic blood pressure is 80-90 mm Hg until major bleeding has been stopped in the initial phase following trauma without brain injury.
- In patients with severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) (GCS ≤8), mean arterial pressure ≥80 mm Hg should be maintained.
- Fluid therapy using isotonic crystalloid solutions should be initiated in the hypotensive patient with bleeding trauma.

- Excessive use of 0.9 % NaCl solution should be avoided.
- Hypotonic solutions such as lactated Ringer’s solution should be avoided in patients with severe head trauma.
- Use of colloids should be restricted due to adverse effects on hemostasis.
- Target Hb is 7-9 g/dL.
- In initial management of patients with expected massive hemorrhage, one of the following strategies should be used: Plasma (FFP or pathogen-inactivated plasma) should be provided at a plasma-to-RBC ratio of at least 1:2 as needed, with fibrinogen concentrate and RBC according to Hb level.
- Tranexamic acid should be administered as early as possible to the trauma patient who is bleeding or is at risk of significant hemorrhage, at a loading dose of 1 g infused over 10 minutes, followed by an IV infusion of 1 g over 8 hours.
- Tranexamic acid should be administered to the bleeding patient with trauma within 3 hours after injury.
- Protocols for treatment of bleeding patients should consider administration of the first dose of tranexamic acid en route to the hospital.
- If a plasma-based coagulation resuscitation strategy is used, plasma (FFP or pathogen- inactivated plasma) should be administered to maintain PT and APTT < 1.5 times normal control values.
- Plasma transfusion should be avoided in patients without substantial bleeding.
- Platelets should be administered to maintain a platelet count above 50 × 10^9/L.

- Platelet count above 100 × 10^9/L should be maintained in patients with ongoing bleeding and/or TBI.
- Initial dose is 4-8 single platelet units or 1 apheresis pack
In general, few indications exist to transfer a patient who is in shock to a specialized facility. Ideally, all hospitals and physicians should be prepared to initially treat and stabilize the patient with exsanguinating hemorrhage. After control of the bleeding and reversal of acute shock, patients may be transferred to facilities that can treat additional injuries.
The patient should be transferred by an advanced life support unit with the capability of blood transfusion in route.

## I. DEFINITION
Stroke is defined as any disease process (non-traumatic) that interrupts blood flow to the brain.
## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
Approximately 80 percent of strokes are due to ischemic cerebral infarction and 20 percent to brain hemorrhage.
## III. ETIOLOGY
There are two main subtypes of stroke: (1) Ischemic stroke, (2) Hemorrhagic stroke. Ischemic stroke may be caused by: Thrombosis, Emboli or Systemic hypoperfusion. Hemorrhagic stroke sub-divided into:
- Intra cerebral hemorrhage, usually due to chronic hypertension, and vascular disease (amyloidosis), or complications from cocaine or methamphetamines use.
- Subarachnoid hemorrhage, most frequently caused by rupture of cerebral arterial-venous malformations or cerebral aneurysm.
The transient ischemic attack (TIA): A transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, without acute infarction.
## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY

In ischemic stroke, the lower or absence perfusion to a brain territory due to emboli, thrombosis or systemic hypotension may produce an ischemic zone that evolve to necrosis. The center of the ischemic zone, called “ischemic penumbra” usually stays longer and may survive if the reperfusion was achieved early (before 4.5h). The signs and symptoms of ischemic stroke is related to the damaged zone.
In Hemorrhagic stroke, the hematoma may compress underneath brain causes its dysfunction. The hematoma may extend triggering ICP elevation, blood in the ventricle may block CSF absorption and induce hydrocephalus. In subarachnoid bleeding, the coagulation process of hematoma may trigger cerebral vasospasm and secondary brain ischemic. In the process of intracranial problems (hematoma, cerebral edema, hydrocephalus) the ICP tend to increase, the acute treatment of hypertension may vary also the cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) that tend to decrease. CPP = MAP - ICP

## V. DIAGNOSIS
The diagnosis of stroke in the ED rests on the bedrock of a focused, accurate history and physical examination.
A. Clinic signs & symptoms.
Signs & symptoms of stroke varied to the location of the lesion (anterior cerebral artery circulation, posterior cerebral artery circulation, middle cerebral artery circulation, watershed infarction).
a. Ischemic stroke
The mnemonic BE FAST, is the suspect signs of stroke.
-B: Sudden Balance impairment
-E: Sudden vision loss in one Eye / one field
-F: Facial droop (have patient show teeth or smile)
-A: Arm drift (patient closes eyes and extends both arms straight out, with palm up for 10") -S: Abnormal Speech
-T: Time to call emergency
Clinically, the differentiation of an ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke is not accurate. It is necessary to obtain an emergency non–contrast-enhanced CT for all suspected acute stroke upon arrival. The utility of the first brain CT is primarily to exclude intracranial bleeding, abscess, tumor, and other stroke mimics, as well as to detect current contraindications to thrombolytics.
Physical examination
Assessment of airway, breathing, and circulation is the top priority.
Next, the goals of examination are to confirm the diagnosis of stroke, exclude stroke mimics and identify co-morbidities.
B. Investigation

## VII. MANAGEMENT
1. Objectives
The management of ischemic stroke is time-dependent, different steps need to be done quickly. Find out whether any specific treatment is feasible.
- Eliminate the problems that mimic stroke symptom.
- Differentiate ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke.
- Re-perfusion therapy, if feasible. (Thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy)
- Prevent the expansion of the brain damage, by saving the “ischemic penumbra” and prevent or treat the early complications (re-bleeding, vasospasm, cerebral edema, intracranial hypertension).
- Maintain cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP). In selected patients, surgery or microinvasive procedures is indicated to remove hematoma, drain the hydrocephalus, or to prevent re-bleeding (clipping, stenting, coiling).
2. Severity grading
In Acute phase of stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic), NIHSS is used to grade the severity of stroke and help decide on treatment modality. After treatment, the severity of handicap was commonly measured by modified Rankin Score.

## The National Institutes of Health stroke scale (NIHSS) for Ischemic stroke
It is composed of 11 items. A score of 0 indicates normal function and the higher score indicates impairment with maximum score of 42. Score of more than 25 indicate a severe stroke. (For details, see reference 1).
At the time of presentation, the severity of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is scored by Hunt & Hess scale or The WFNS scale.

Treatment of elevated blood pressure in the first 24 hours of an ischemic stroke is reserved for those with malignant hypertension (> 220 mmHg systolic, 120 mmHg diastolic) or other end-organ failure (e.g., congestive heart failure, renal failure, and hypertensive encephalopathy). The blood pressure typically autoregulates spontaneously with bed rest in the first few days after ischemic stroke; if it remains substantially elevated, it should be carefully lowered daily up to 20% of the mean arterial pressure. Subcutaneous heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin therapy should be considered for immobilized patients with ICVD to reduce the risk of deep venous thrombosis. In

hemorrhagic stroke, use instead the intermittent pneumatic compression device for the first few days.
For patients with evidence of elevated ICP, get head of bed elevation to 30°, analgesia, and sedation is needed.
Indwelling urinary catheters and unneeded IV lines should be avoided, because they can serve as portals of entry for infections.
Elevated temperature should be treated with antipyretics. Looking for causes. Aspiration pneumonia can be avoided by delaying oral feedings until safe swallowing is demonstrated. Early mobilization and rehabilitation should be attempted.
b) Specific treatment for different type of stroke
A. Ischemic stroke:
Hypertension management in acute ischemic stroke depend on the thrombolysis.
- Is not a candidate for thrombolysis, then permissive hypertension is in order (No intervention unless SBP >220mmHg or DBP >120 mmHg.)
- Is a candidate for thrombolytics, then the target blood pressures are SBP ≤185 mmHg and DBP≤ 110mmHg
If blood pressure control is needed, use a titratable IV antihypertensive, Labetalol, starting dose is 10 to 20 mg over 1 to 2 min; continuous infusion at 2 mg/min, (titrated to effect) with a target MAP reduction of 10% to 25%.
Take extreme caution to avoid overcorrection.
Reperfusion therapy:
(1) Intravenous Thrombolysis, (2) Mechanical thrombectomy
a. Intravenous Thrombolysis

Thrombolytic therapy for patients with ICVD is directed at reversing the neurological deficits and preventing progression. The total dose of IV tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) for stroke is 0.9 mg/ kg, given as a 60-minute IV infusion, with 10% of the total dose given as an initial bolus.
Indication & contra-indication of r-TPA (recombinant tissue plasminogen activator) Alteplase®
Alteplase is Contraindicated in:
- Active internal bleeding
- History of cerebrovascular accident (for MI and PE only)
- Recent (within 3 mo) intracranial or intraspinal injury or trauma
- Intracranial neoplasm, arteriovenous malformation, or aneurysm
- Known bleeding diathesis
- Severe uncontrolled hypertension (systolic BP >185 mmHg or diastolic BP >110 mmHg specifically for stroke indication)

- Evidence or suspicion of intracranial hemorrhage on pretreatment evaluation (for stroke indication only)
- Recent (within 3 months) stroke (for stroke indication only)
- History of intracranial hemorrhage (for stroke indication only)
- Seizure at the onset of stroke (for stroke indication only)
- Current use of oral anticoagulants or an INR >1.7 or a prothrombin time >15 sec (for stroke indication only)
- Administration of heparin 48h before the onset of stroke with an elevated aPTT at presentation (for stroke indication only)
- Platelet count <100,000/mm3 (for stroke indication only)
- Hypersensitivity (for central venous access device occlusion indication only). Use Cautiously in:
- Recent (within 10 days) major surgery, trauma, GI or GU bleeding
- Cerebrovascular disease
- Systolic BP ≥175 mmHg and/or diastolic BP ≥110 mmHg
- High likelihood of left heart thrombus
- Hemostatic defects
- Severe hepatic impairment
- Hemorrhagic ophthalmic conditions
- Septic thrombophlebitis
- Previous puncture of a noncompressible vessel
- Subacute bacterial endocarditis or acute pericarditis
- Severe neurological deficit (NIHSS >22) at presentation (for stroke indication only)
- Major early infarct signs on CT scan (for stroke indication only)
- Known or suspected infection in catheter (for central venous access device occlusion indication only)

b. Intra-arterial therapies / mechanical thrombectomy
Using a second-generation stent retriever device is the preferred mode of therapy for eligible patient, whether or not the patient has received intravenous thrombolysis. Patients ≥18 years if they have minimal pre-stroke disability, (modified Rankin Scale < 1), Have a causative occlusion of the internal carotid artery or proximal middle cerebral artery, Have a NIHSS score of ≥ 6, have a reassuring non-contrast head CT (ASPECT score of ≥ 6), And if they can be treated within 6 h of last known normal.

Emergent neurosurgical consultation is indicated.

Strict bed rest in a quiet environment to diminish hemodynamic fluctuations, pain control with titrated doses of opioid analgesics.
Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis with pneumatic compression stockings. Pharmacologic DVT prophylaxis can be added after definitive treatment for the aneurysm. GI ulcer prophylaxis and stool softeners.

Surgical clipping of the neck of the aneurysm and Endovascular aneurysmal obliteration by metal coils are the options available for aneurysmal repair

Management of blood pressure for spontaneous ICH remains controversial. SBP greater than 220 mm Hg, indicate a continuous IV drug infusion and close BP monitoring to lower SBP. The optimal goal blood pressure is uncertain, SBP of 140 to 160 mmHg is a reasonable target. Aggressive reduction can increase renal adverse events. Early neurosurgical consultation is indicated for patients with ICH with evidence of increased ICP or in other conditions where surgical intervention may be indicated, (For example, cerebellar stroke). All non-surgical measures to reduced ICP should be considered. Rapid reversal of anticoagulation to INR < 1.6 may improve survival.
Decompressive craniotomy and evacuation for all patients with ICH is not indicated. For Supratentorial ICH, surgery is usually avoided and should be considered on an individual basis based on assessment of prognosis with or without surgery.

This is a clinical decision tree/algorithm for the initial management of a patient suspected of having a stroke. The flowchart guides clinicians through diagnostic and therapeutic steps based on patient status and imaging findings.

---

**Decision Points and Branches:**

1. **Suspect Stroke**

2. **A.B.C is OK?** (Airway, Breathing, Circulation)

   - **No → Immediate supportive measures:**

3. **Non-contrast brain CT**
   - Followed by:

4. **Stroke mimic conditions?**
   - **Yes → Treat accordingly** (e.g., treat for migraine, seizure, syncope, etc.)
   - **No → Inform & consent; Consider transfer to suitable center**

5. **Non-hemorrhagic** (after ruling out hemorrhage)

       - **No → Supportive treatment**
       - **Yes →**
         - Sometimes + CTA, CTP, or MRI-stroke protocol imaging
         - Check for contraindications and precautions

6. **Hemorrhagic stroke (SAH or ICH)**
   - **Early consult with neurosurgeon**

**Outcomes:**
- **Immediate stabilization** if A.B.C not OK.
- **Treatment of stroke mimics** if non-contrast CT suggests non-stroke causes.
- **Supportive care** for non-eligible patients or those with hemorrhagic stroke not requiring surgery.
- **Reperfusion therapy** (IV r-TPA or thrombectomy) for eligible ischemic stroke patients.

**Note:** This algorithm follows standard acute stroke protocols but does not include time windows (e.g., “within 3 hours” for tPA), which are critical in real-world practice. It also omits specific imaging criteria (e.g., NIHSS score, Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score) that guide eligibility for interventions.

Priority on arrival is making sure that airway (A), breathing (B), and circulation (C) are OK. Maintain SpO2>94%, if need, administer oxygen by mask. Make sure that patient was not hypovolemic, put a good IV line and RL to keep line open. Patient with GCS≤ 8 need intubation and supported ventilation. Hypotension is the worst factors of exacerbation; moderate hypertension is desirable. Inform-consent form should be completed as soon as stroke is clinically diagnosed to catch the time when patient is eligible for the procedures, and if they refuse the intervention, some investigations exam may be omitted. If consented, consider transfer patient to hospital or center where the specific treatments (Thrombolysis, thrombectomy, clip, neurosurgery) are available, as soon as possible.

## VIII. SPECIAL CASES
## 1. Ischemic stroke with concomitant myocardial infarction
Troponin elevation in acute ischemic stroke is not uncommon (prevalence, 0% to 34%), is associated with multiple disease processes (e.g., acute coronary syndrome, congestive heart failure, renal failure, myopericarditis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, atrial fibrillation), and is independently associated with worse all-cause mortality. Troponin elevation in acute stroke is most probably secondary to acute coronary syndrome if other obvious causes are excluded, especially if typical ECG findings for acute coronary syndrome are present. Simultaneous acute ischemic stroke and myocardial infarction can be therapeutically problematic because treating one condition with a procedure may delay a time-dependent indicated procedure for the other. In addition, there are some therapies for acute myocardial infarction (e.g., heparin) that are contraindicated in acute stroke.
“For patients presenting with concurrent AIS [acute ischemic stroke] and acute MI [myocardial infarction], treatment with IV alteplase at the dose appropriate for cerebral ischemia, followed by percutaneous coronary angioplasty and stenting if indicated is reasonable.” (AHA/ASA guidelines, 2018). Obtain emergent neurology and cardiology consults on these patients, but do not delay thrombolysis for stroke if the patient qualifies.
## 2. Transient ischemic attack (TIA)

TIA treatment is important, even all symptoms were disappeared. The patient returned to normal but the risk of developing a real stroke is high especially during the first month. Treatment of TIA primarily focuses on prevention of subsequent stroke.
- Anti-platelet agents
Can select among: Aspirin (75-81mg), clopidogrel (75mg), Dipyridamole (75-100mg qid), alone or combined clopidogrel or dipyridamole with aspirin take every day.
- Anticoagulation
The risk of recurrent stroke in the presence of atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation is low, probably <5% over the next 48 hours; moreover, the risk of hemorrhagic transformation of an acute stroke is also greatest in the first 48 hours.
The use of unfractionated heparin, low molecular-weight heparin, or heparinoids for emergent treatment of a specific stroke subtype or TIA cannot be recommended based on available evidence, even in the presence of atrial fibrillation.

- Carotid artery endarterectomy or stent
In TIA patients with medically treated high-grade internal carotid artery lesions, The Carotid Revascularization Endarterectomy or carotid stenting should be performed promptly, because surgical benefit is greatest within 2 weeks of the TIA. Carotid stenting may be especially useful in patients <70 years old or in patients with higher surgical risks.

## IX. EVOLUTION & PROGNOSIS
The prognosis of stroke depends on: (1) Type of stroke, (2) Location and size of the stroke, (3) Severity of symptoms, (4) Age and overall health.
The prognosis of ischemic stroke is generally better than for hemorrhagic stroke. Strokes affecting the speech center or motor cortex, are more likely to cause lasting disabilities. Larger strokes also tend to have a worse prognosis than smaller strokes.
People with mild symptoms are more likely to make a good recovery than those with severe symptoms. Prompt diagnosis and treatment of an acute cerebral vascular accidents can improve the chances of a good recovery.
The recovery aspect of stroke:
- 1-3 months: the brain exhibits the most remarkable plasticity and potential for improvement. During this time, most patients undergo intensive rehabilitation in hospitals or specialized centers, focusing on regaining lost function in movement, speech, and cognitive skills. Significant progress is often observed during this phase.
- 3-6 months: the rate of recovery slows down but can still be substantial
- 6-12 months: The improvement becomes less dramatic,
- 1 year and beyond: While some individuals achieve near-complete recovery, others may have permanent disabilities.
## X. COMPLICATIONS

The main complications of SAH:
- Re-bleeding (within the first 24h, particularly within 6h).
- Vasospasm and delay cerebral ischemia (3-4day after rupture, peak at 7-10d and resolves by 14-21d).
- Raise ICP and hydrocephalus (within 3 days of rupture, in 20% of patient) Other complication:
- Seizure 20% (mostly at first 24h); risk: thick clot, ICH, prior seizure, middle cerebral artery aneurisms, delayed infarct.
- Hyponatremia (SIADH, and Salt-wasting sd.).
- Cardiac change (neurogenic stunned myocardium).
- Neurogenic pulmonary edema (NPE), usually resolves in 48-72h.

The early complications of ICH are Intracranial pressure (ICP) elevation causing local neuronal damage, and vasoconstriction mediated by blood breakdown products or neuronal mechanisms causing remote perfusion changes.

## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMANDATION
- Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease (pre-stroke): control the chronic hypertension, Diabetes, dyslipidemia; life-style change.
- Early seek medical advice when suspect a stroke. Stroke is time-dependent disease.
- Do no harm to patient (multiple-transfers, waiting-treatment), “time is brain”
- Important of rehabilitation therapy immediately after stroke
- Secondary prevention of cardiovascular diseases (post-stroke)

## I. DEFINITION
Altered mental status and coma are broad clinical categories used to describe disorders of arousal (awake) and content of consciousness (aware). Arousal behaviors include wakefulness and basic alerting. Content of consciousness includes awareness, memory, language, reasoning, spatial relationship integration, emotions, complex attention, and the myriad integration processes that make us human.
Coma is characterized by failure of both arousal and content functions of consciousness. A coma is the most severe of consciousness altered.

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY
The function of the brainstem and/or both hemispheres must be impaired for unresponsiveness to occur. Coma can result from
- deficiency of substrates needed for neuronal function (as with hypoglycemia or hypoxia).
- a brainstem disorder such as hemorrhage or
- bilateral cortical dysfunction.
- Cerebral edema and infection of the brain and/or surrounding
Cerebral blood flow is constant at mean arterial pressures of 50 to 100 mm Hg due to the process of cerebral autoregulation. Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is the pressure that maintain the blood flow to the brain. It is the net pressure gradient between mean arterial pressure (MAP) and intracranial pressure (ICP): CPP = MAP- ICP
In extreme uncontrolled elevation of the ICP, cerebral perfusion pressure is diminished which may causes brain ischemia. The Cushing reflex (Hypertension and bradycardia in a comatose patient): may be observed with increased ICP.
## V. DIAGNOSIS
## a. Signs & symptoms
The clinical features of a coma vary with both the depth of coma and the cause. Examination, laboratory procedures, and neuroimaging allow differentiation between structural and metabolic causes of coma in almost all patients in the ED
- Structural Coma
Patient may have hemiparesis, the eyes may conjugately deviate toward the side of brain lesion.
- Toxic-metabolic coma

The diffuse CNS dysfunction is reflected by the lack of focal physical examination findings that point to a specific region of brain dysfunction. Pupillary response is generally preserved in toxic- metabolic coma.
A posterior fossa or infratentorial expanding lesion, such as cerebellar hemorrhage or infarction, may cause abrupt coma, abnormal extensor posturing, loss of pupillary reflexes, and loss of extraocular movements.
A Pseudo coma or psychogenic coma is occasionally encountered.
General examination may reveal signs of trauma or suggest other diagnostic possibilities for the unresponsiveness. However, asymmetric findings on examination of cranial nerves through pupillary examination, assessment of corneal reflexes, and testing of oculovestibular reflexes may suggest focal CNS lesions. Asymmetric muscle tone or reflexes raise the suspicion of a focal lesion. The goal of the physician is to rapidly determine if the CNS dysfunction is from diffuse impairment of the brain or if signs point to a focal (and perhaps surgically treatable) region of CNS dysfunction.
Liberal use of CT scanning is encouraged because exceptions to the tentative clinical diagnosis are frequent.
The Glasgow Coma Scale (Table-2) is a widely used clinical scoring system for alterations in consciousness. GCS stratify consciousness altered from 15 (alert) to 3 (deep coma). Typically, a score of 8 or below is indicative of coma.

## b. Investigation
CT is the neuroimaging procedure of choice. Acute hemorrhage is readily identified, as is midline shift and mass lesions. Consider lumbar puncture if CT scan findings are unremarkable and subarachnoid hemorrhage or CNS infection is suspected.
Suspect basilar artery thrombosis in a comatose patient with “normal” results on head CT, in which the only finding may be a hyperdense basilar artery. MRI or cerebral angiography is needed to make the diagnosis of basilar artery thrombosis.
## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Delirium, dementia, and coma may each affect consciousness, but their clinical presentations are distinct. Prompt and accurate differentiation between the three conditions is essential for appropriate management in the ED setting.
Delirium, acute encephalopathy, refer to an abrupt disorder characterized by impairment of attention and cognition. The literature suggests that at least 1 out of 10 elderly ED patients and at least 1 out of 4 elderly hospitalized patients have delirium at the time of admission. Delirium typically develops over days. Disordered attention and acute fluctuating course are the hallmarks of the condition, which may also affect cognition, level of consciousness, language, and perception. Activity levels may be either increased or decreased.

## VII. MANAGEMENT
1. Objectives of Management
Maintain vital function, in the same time, find and correct the possible reversible causes Treat and prevent the structural and functional derangement caused by coma (elevation ICP, respiratory depression) and treat its cause.
2. Critical signs
Depth of coma, GCS lower or egal 8, the lower is the more severe
Coma secondary to prolong shock, hypoxia or hypoglycemia
Coma on Cardiac arrest with return of spontaneous circulation post resuscitation (CPR) Coma which GCS drops abruptly (secondary deterioration of brain injury, herniation)

3. Mortality risk factor
Age and medical conditions of patient
Coma associated with condition that deteriorates hemodynamic (hypotension/ bleeding) Coma associated with condition that deteriorates oxygenation (pneumonia, chest trauma) Systemic factors that exacerbated the secondary brain injury: fever, agitation, hypoxia, hypercapnia, hypotension, hyponatremia.
Localize factors that exacerbated the secondary brain injury: expansion of intracranial hematoma, cerebral edema, intracranial herniation, cerebral vasospasm, Intracranial Pressure elevation.
4. Outpatient management
All patient with acute loss of consciousness should be evaluated and follow-up in emergency department. Coma is a Medical Emergency. While waiting for, and during the transport, be cautious about aspiration pneumonia (patient may vomit).
Check breathing and pulse. If breathing OR pulse is absent then start first aid CPR. If breathing AND pulse is present then put the patient on recovery position.
5. First-line treatment
Treatment of coma involves identification of the cause of the brain failure and initiation of specific therapy directed at the underlying cause.
Attend to airway, ventilation, and circulation. Evaluate and treat for readily reversible causes of coma, such as hypoglycemia and opioid toxicity.

Rapid point-of-care glucose determination can identify the need for dextrose. Give D50% 50ml IV in once or divided in two doses followed by D10% infusion, check glycemic again 10-15min after the bolus. Give Thiamin 100mg IM/IV if suspect vitamin B1 deficiency. In case coma with bradypnea and myosis, suspect opioids overdose, give Naloxone 0.4-2mg IV repeat every 2- 3min, or put into IV infusion with rate adjusted to patient response. In patient who is opioids dependent, too quick to reverse may trigger withdrawal syndrome.
The patient suspect to have intracranial hypertension (severe headache, nausea-vomiting, blur vision, secondary altered consciousness, pupillary dilated or unequal) need to be managed immediately:
- Raise Head of Bed (reduce veinous volume) to 30degree
- Hyperosmolar (NS 3%, mannitol) [Reduce (remove) some water from brain tissue]
- Hyperventilate (Vasoconstriction, reduce cerebral blood flow)
- Sedation (reduce sympathetic nervous system tone)
- Control fever / seizure (Reduce cerebral oxygen demand, reduce the cerebral blood flow)
- Ventriculostomy [Remove (Reduce volume of CSF)
- Intracranial Hematoma removal. (hematoma with midline deviated)

## VIII. SPECIAL CONSIDERATION
1. Head trauma & coma.
If trauma is suspected, maintain stabilization of the cervical spine during assessment. If protection of the airway is in doubt or the coma state is likely prolonged, then protect the airway by intubating the patient.
2. For children,
For children consider ingestions (intoxication), infections, and child abuse in the appropriate clinical setting.
3. nonconvulsive status epilepticus or subtle status epilepticus
A state of electromechanical dissociation of the brain and body after seizure. If the motor activity of the seizure stops and the patient does not awaken within 30 minutes, then consider nonconvulsive status epilepticus. Obtain neurologic consultation and electroencephalography.
Fig. 3_ Decisional tree of initial management

This is a flowchart titled “Initial management of patient with Coma.” It outlines a stepwise approach to managing a comatose patient, starting from basic life support and progressing through assessment for elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score, and reversible causes.

---

**Decision Points and Branches:**

1. **Starting Point:** “Coma” → leads to initial ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation).

2. **First Decision Point:**
   - **“Suspect ICP Elevated*?”**
     - **Yes →** Manage elevated ICP:
       - Head of bed elevated 30°, head in neutral position.
       - Mannitol: 0.5–1.0 g/kg IV or
       - Hypertonic saline: 3% 1.5–3 ml/kg given as bolus infusion over 10–20 min
       - Dexamethasone: 10 mg IV (in tumoral edema)
       - Hyperventilation (PaCO₂ ≤ 35 mmHg) first 24h post brain injury
     - **No →** Proceed to next decision point.

3. **Second Decision Point:**
   - **“GCS ≤ 8?”**
     - **Yes →** Intubate + Ventilate
     - **No →** Proceed to next decision point.

4. **Third Decision Point:**
   - **“Suspect reversible causes?”**
     - **Yes →** Treat specific reversible causes:
       - Alcoholism/denutrition: Thiamine 100 mg IV
       - Hypoglycemia: Dextrose 50% 50 ml IV
       - Opioids overdose: Naloxone 0.2–2.0 mg IV
       - Overdose BZD: Flumazenil 0.2 mg IV (for selected case)
     - **No →** Proceed to final step.

5. **Final Step:**
   - “Cause of coma? Specific Treatment”

---

**Drug Names, Dosages, and Outcomes:**

- **Mannitol**: 0.5–1.0 g/kg IV
- **Hypertonic saline**: 3% 1.5–3 ml/kg as bolus infusion over 10–20 min
- **Dexamethasone**: 10 mg IV (specifically for tumoral edema)
- **Hyperventilation**: Target PaCO₂ ≤ 35 mmHg for first 24 hours after brain injury
- **Thiamine**: 100 mg IV (for alcoholism/denutrition)
- **Dextrose**: 50% 50 ml IV (for hypoglycemia)
- **Naloxone**: 0.2–2.0 mg IV (for opioid overdose)
- **Flumazenil**: 0.2 mg IV (for benzodiazepine overdose — selected cases)

---

**Outcomes:**

- Immediate stabilization via ABCs.
- Management of elevated ICP with positioning, osmotic agents, steroids (if applicable), and hyperventilation.
- Intubation and ventilation if GCS ≤ 8.
- Reversal of identifiable causes (e.g., thiamine, dextrose, naloxone, flumazenil).
- Final step directs to identifying the underlying cause of coma and initiating specific treatment.

The flowchart emphasizes rapid identification of life-threatening conditions and targeted interventions before determining the etiology of coma.

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS
The evolution and prognosis of coma is varied to its cause. Toxic and metabolic coma usually has better prognosis than structural coma. However, with the delay of treatment metabolic coma will transform to structural coma, e.g., hypoglycemia. In other condition that coma resulted from severe organ dysfunction, e.g., liver encephalopathy, multi-organs system dysfunction, the prognosis is poor.

## X. COMPLICATIONS
Coma with GCS lower than 8 usually had a depressed ventilation; The resulting hypercapnia induced cerebral vasodilatation and elevation of intracranial pressure. In acute phase of head trauma patient often had a vomit that risks aspirated and compromised the airway. Other complications included, cerebral edema, aspiration pneumonia, bed-sore, deep-vein thrombosis infections, long-term handicaps, and complications link to the cause of coma.
## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMANDATION
Acute coma is a medical emergency. Coma may be a sign of cardiac arrested; identify early, the first 10-15min is precious time for cardiorespiratory resuscitation (CPR). Coma patient may lose control on his airway and had high risk of aspiration (airway obstruction, pneumonia), put the patient on recovery position or other preventive measures taken. In poisoning, coma is the latest stage of any poison, treat early may prevent it from happen.

Dr. IM Virya, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Asst. TAING Sovanna, Dr. Pen Phallkun, Dr. Krouch Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara.
## I. DEFINITION
Allergic reaction is a various conditions caused by hypersensitivity of the immune system to typically harmless substances in the environment.
It can be classified into different types based on the underlying mechanisms involved. The four main types of allergic reactions are:
1. Type I (Immediate Hypersensitivity) Reactions:
- These reactions occur rapidly, within minutes to hours of exposure to the allergen.
- Examples include allergic rhinitis (hay fever), asthma, food allergies, and anaphylaxis.
2. Type II (Cytotoxic) Reactions:
- These reactions involve antibodies targeting and attacking cells within the body, leading to cell destruction.
- Examples include certain drug-induced hemolytic anemia and blood transfusion reactions.
3. Type III (Immune Complex-Mediated) Reactions:
- These reactions involve the formation of immune complexes that get deposited in tissues, triggering inflammation and damage.
- Examples include serum sickness and certain autoimmune diseases like lupus. 4. Type IV (Delayed-Type) Reactions:
- These reactions typically occur 48-72 hours after exposure to the allergen and involve T-cell activation.

- Examples include contact dermatitis (e.g., poison ivy rash) and certain drug hypersensitivity reactions.
Anaphylaxis is defined as a serious allergic or hypersensitivity reaction that is usually rapid in onset and may cause death.
The term “anaphylaxis” is derived from the Greek words “ana” (against) and “phylaxis” (protection). Anaphylaxis requires urgent recognition and treatment.

## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
The incidence and prevalence of anaphylaxis vary worldwide, with differences dependent on a number of variables. Anaphylaxis is likely underreported as well.
Worldwide incidence: recent studies estimate that the global incidence of anaphylaxis ranges from 50 to 112 episode per 100 000 person-years. Additionally, a population-based analysis found approximately 46 cases of anaphylaxis per 100 000 populations per year.
## III. ETIOLOGY
- IgE Mediated
1. Food Triggers: Most commonly peanuts or other nuts, fish or shellfish, eggs and cow’s milk. Asthma and others atopic diseases are a risk factor for food-based anaphylaxis.

2. Drug triggers:
- Antibiotics: Penicilin-related antibiotics and sulphonamides. Reactions are twice as likely to occur after intravenous or intramuscular administration when compared to the oral route.
- Other antivirals, antihelminthics and TB medications
- Muscle relaxants
- Antineoplastic/cytotoxic/immunomodulators.
3. Insect venom triggers: Bees, wasps, yellow jackets, hornets and fires ants. Venoms-allergic patients respond well to immunotherapy
4. Other triggers
- Latex
- Horse derived antitoxins (snake antivenoms)
- Helminths
- Non-IgE Mediated
1. Immune complex: Blood products, immunoglobulins and dextrans 2. Non-immunological mast cell activators: Radiocontrast media 3. Modulators of arachidonic acid metabolism: Aspirin and NSAIDs 4. Idiopathic
5. Exercise

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY
The mechanism responsible for most cases of human anaphylaxis involves immunoglobulin E (IgE). Possible alternative mechanisms remain incompletely understood.
The term "anaphylaxis" has traditionally been reserved for IgE-dependent events, and the term "anaphylactoid reaction" has been used to describe IgE-independent events, although the two reactions are often clinically indistinguishable.
Instead, the World Allergy Organization has proposed that anaphylactic reactions be categorized as immunologic and non-immunologic.
- Immunologic anaphylaxis is typically described as IgE mediated. The traditional IgE- mediated mechanism of anaphylaxis begins with an antigen binding to an allergen- specific IgE. Antigen-bound IgE in turn binds to the receptor Fc-epsilon-RI on mast cells and/or basophils. This causes these cells to degranulate, releasing a number of inflammatory mediators.
- Non-immunologic anaphylaxis being a result of sudden basophil or mast cell degranulation in the absence of immunoglobulins.
## V. DIAGNOSIS
1. Clinical features

Anaphylactic reactions vary in duration and severity but typically are rapid in onset with most occurring within 2 hours of allergen exposure. Clinical presentations depend on the degree of hypersensitivity, the quantity, route, and rate of antigen exposure, as well as the target organ sensitivity and responsiveness. Presentations include a combination of clinical characteristics, affecting an array of organ systems including the skin, respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, cardiovascular, or the central nervous system.

| ENT | Oropharyngeal or throat fullness Tongue swelling |
| Respiratory | Uvular edema/hydrops Shortness of breath and/or wheezing Pharyngeal or laryngeal edema Stridor |
| Cardiovascular | Rhinitis Hypotension Chest pain |
| Skin | Urticarial and/or angioedema Flushing Pruritus only |
| GI | Nausea, emesis, cramps, or diarrhea |
| Neurologic | Headache Seizure |

content: Anaphylaxis is predominately a clinical diagnosis. Criteria for defining anaphylaxis were developed in 2004 by a panel of experts at the National Institutes of Health, which resulted in the publication of the NIAID/Anaphylaxis Network Definition of Anaphylaxis.

## Clinical criteria for diagnosis anaphylaxis
1. Acute onset of an illness (minutes to several hours) with involvement of the skin, mucosal tissue, or both (e.g., generalized hives, pruritus or flushing, or swollen lips-tongue-uvula) and at least one of the following:
a. Respiratory compromise (e.g., dyspnea, wheeze-bronchospasm, stridor, or hypoxemia) b. Reduced BP or associated symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (e.g., hypotonia [collapse], syncope, or incontinence)
2. Two or more of the following that occur rapidly after exposure to a likely allergen for that patient (minutes to several hours):
a. Involvement of the skin-mucosal tissue (e.g., generalized hives, itch-flush, or swollen lips- tongue-uvula)
b. Respiratory compromise (e.g., dyspnea, wheeze-bronchospasm, stridor, or hypoxemia) c. Reduced BP or associated symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (e.g., hypotonia [collapse], syncope, or incontinence)
d. Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., crampy abdominal pain or vomiting)
3. Reduced BP after exposure to a known allergen for that patient (minutes to hours): a. Infants and children: low systolic BP (age specific) or greater than 30% decrease in systolic BP
b. Adults: systolic BP of <90mmhg or greater than 30% decrease from that person’s baseline
2. Investigation
- There are currently no biomarkers or laboratory tests that can resolutely confirm or refute the diagnosis and no biomarker that increases in concentration irrespective of trigger.
- Tryptase levels

- These are now recommended for patients presenting with anaphylaxis, but this
only needs to be done for one episode.

- When present, the degree of rise in tryptase does correlate with severity of the
symptoms, but a rise may not be found in all patients.
- Skin prick tests and allergen-specific serum IgE levels can be performed by the allergy specialist after 3–4 weeks to avoid false-positive results.
- Challenge or provocation tests can be performed but should be done with caution in a facility that has the resources to manage any subsequent anaphylaxis.

## VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
## VII. MANAGEMENT
1. Objectives
Prompt recognition and initiation of the appropriate interventions remain key in avoiding adverse outcomes. Treatment delays, even by a few minutes, could potentially lead to hypoxia, circulatory collapse, and even death. It is also important to treat anaphylaxis promptly because it appears to be most responsive to treatment in its early phases, based on the observation that delayed epinephrine injection is associated with fatalities.
2. Critical sign
- Cardiovascular system:
- Myocardial depression
- Arrhythmias
- Myocardial ischemia
- Respiratory system:
- Bronchospasm
- Laryngeal edema
- Asphyxia

3. Mortality risk factor
Risk factors for increased anaphylaxis severity and mortality:
- Very young (under-recognition)
- Elderly (Decrease physiologic reserves)
- Comorbid conditions
- Cardiovascular disease (heart failure, ischemic heart disease, hypertension)
- Pulmonary disease (asthma, obstructive airway disease)
- Others:
- Concurrent use of anti-hypertensive agents, specifically beta-blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors
- Concurrent use of cognition-impairing drugs (e.g., alcohol, recreational drugs, sedatives, tranquilizers)
- Recent anaphylaxis episode
- Upright posture at the onset of symptoms
4. Outpatient Management
The cornerstones of initial management are the following.
- Removal of the inciting cause, if possible (stop infusion of a suspect medication).
- Call for help
- Intramuscular (IM) injection of epinephrine at the earliest opportunity, followed by additional epinephrine by IM or intravenous (IV) injection as needed.
- Placement of the patient in the supine position with the lower extremities elevated, unless there is prominent upper airway swelling prompting the patient to remain upright (and often leaning forward). If the patient is vomiting, placement of the patient semi recumbent with lower extremities elevated may be preferable. Place pregnant patients on their left side.
- Supplemental oxygen.
- Volume resuscitation with IV fluids.
5. First line treatment

- The first and most important treatment in anaphylaxis is epinephrine. There are no absolute contraindications to epinephrine in the setting of anaphylaxis.
- Air way – Immediate intubation if evidence of impending airway obstruction from angioedema. Delay may lead to complete obstruction. Intubation can be difficult and should be performed by the most experienced clinician available. Cricothyrotomy may be necessary.
- IM epinephrine
- Adult: give epinephrine 0.3 to 0.5 mg IM in the mid-outer thigh. Can repeat every 5 to 15 minutes (or more frequently), as needed. If epinephrine is injected promptly IM, most patients respond to 1, 2, or at most, 3 doses. If symptoms are not responding to epinephrine injections, prepare IV epinephrine for infusion.
- Pediatric: 0.01mg/kg (0.01ml/kg of 1:1000 dilution).
- Position – Place patient in recumbent position, if tolerated, and elevated lower extremities
- Oxygen – Give 8-10l/MN via facemask or up to 100% oxygen, as needed.

- Normal Saline or Ringer lactate rapid bolus – Rapid infusion of 1 to 2 liters IV or 10-20ml/kg in pediatric. Repeat, as needed. Massive fluid shifts with severe loss of intravascular volume can occur. Monitor urine output.
6. Treatment adjustment
- Albuterol (salbutamol) – For bronchospasm resistant to IM epinephrine.
- Adult: 2.5-5mg in 3 mL saline via nebulizer, or 4 to 6 puffs by metered dose inhaler (MDI). Repeat every 20mn as needed.
- Pediatric: 1.25-2.5mg nebulized, or 4-6 puffs from MDI with holding chamber. Repeated every 20mn as needed
- H1 antihistamine – for relief of urticarial and itching only.
- Adult: Cetirizine (Zyrtec) 10 mg IV or chlorpheniramine 10mg IM/IV or diphenhydramine (Polaramine) 25 to 50 mg IV/IM/PO.
- Pediatric: Diphenhydramine (Polaramine) 1mg/kg IV/IM/PO.
- H2 antihistamine – for relief of urticarial and itching only.
- Adult: Famotidine 20 mg IV or cimetidine 300mg or Ranitidine 50mg IV.
- Pediatric: Ranitidine 0.5mg/kg IV or Cimetidine 4-8mg/kg IV.
- Glucocorticoid – for prevention of protracted and biphasic reactions.
- Adult: Methylprednisolone 80-125mg IV or hydrocortisone 250-500mg IV.
- Pediatric: Methylprednisolone 1-2mg/kg IV or hydrocortisone 5-10mg/kg IV.
- Magnesium sulfate – for treatment of bronchospasm.
- Adult: 2g IV over 20mn.
- Pediatric: 25-50mg/kg IV.
- Glucagon – for treatment of patient on beta-blockers with refractory hypotension.
- Adult: 1mg IV every 5mn until hypotension resolves followed by 5-15 mcg/mn infusion.

- Pediatric: 50mcg/kg every 5mn.
- Monitoring – Continuous noninvasive hemodynamic monitoring and pulse oximetry monitoring should be performed. Urine output should be monitored in patients receiving IV fluid resuscitation for severe hypotension or shock.

This is a clinical management flowchart for suspected anaphylaxis. It outlines the diagnostic criteria, immediate interventions, monitoring, and follow-up steps.

---

**Decision Points & Branches:**

1. **Suspected Anaphylaxis → Diagnosis - look for:**
   - Acute onset of illness
   - Life-threatening Airway +/- Breathing +/- Circulation problem
   - And usually skin/mucosal changes
   - ➝ Branch: Detailed documentation of potential triggers, symptoms, and response to treatment

2. **After diagnosis → Remove or stop allergen → Intramuscular Epinephrine**
   - Dose by age:
     - Adult: 500 mcg (0.5 mL) of 1:1000 epinephrine
     - Child >12 yrs: 500 mcg (0.5 mL)
     - Child 6–12 yrs: 300 mcg (0.3 mL)
     - Child <6 yrs: 150 mcg (0.15 mL)
   - ➝ Repeat dose after 5–15 minutes if needed

3. **After IM epinephrine → Two parallel branches:**
   - **Left branch: Mast cell tryptase levels**
     - As soon as possible
     - 1–2 hours later but within 4 hours of onset
   - **Right branch: Intravenous fluids – for hypotension**
     - Adults: 500–1000 mL boluses
     - Children: 20 mL/kg boluses
     - ➝ Then: Nebulised salbutamol – for bronchospasm (2.5–5 mg as needed)

4. **After mast cell tryptase levels → Observation/admission:**
   - **Adults:** Observe for at least 6 hours
   - **Children:** Admit to paediatric ward

5. **After observation/admission → Post-anaphylaxis care:**
   - Autoinjector epinephrine pen training
   - Anaphylaxis episode education and resource information
   - Detailed discharge letter to family doctor
   - ➝ Refer to allergy specialist for outpatient follow-up

6. **After IV fluids/salbutamol → Two parallel branches:**
   - **Chlorphenamine (im or iv):**
     - Adult: 10 mg
     - Child >12 yrs: 5 mg
     - Child 6–12 yrs: 2.5 mg
     - Child <6 yrs: 250 mcg/kg
   - **Hydrocortisone (im or iv):**
     - Adult: 200 mg
     - Child >12 yrs: 100 mg
     - Child 6–12 yrs: 50 mg
     - Child <6 yrs: 25 mg
   - ➝ Continue Cetirizine or Chlorphenamine for ≤3 days
   - ➝ Continue prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg for up to 3 days

7. **In refractory cases consider:**
   - iv adrenaline (experienced users only)
   - alternative vasopressors
   - im glucagon (if on β-blockers)
   - iv magnesium (beware hypotension)

---

**Drug Names and Dosages:**

- **Epinephrine (IM):**
  - 1:1000 concentration
  - Adult: 500 mcg (0.5 mL)
  - Child >12 yrs: 500 mcg (0.5 mL)
  - Child 6–12 yrs: 300 mcg (0.3 mL)
  - Child <6 yrs: 150 mcg (0.15 mL)

- **Intravenous Fluids:**
  - Adults: 500–1000 mL boluses
  - Children: 20 mL/kg boluses

- **Nebulised Salbutamol:**
  - 2.5–5 mg as needed

- **Chlorphenamine:**
  - Adult: 10 mg (im or iv)
  - Child >12 yrs: 5 mg
  - Child 6–12 yrs: 2.5 mg
  - Child <6 yrs: 250 mcg/kg

- **Hydrocortisone:**
  - Adult: 200 mg (im or iv)
  - Child >12 yrs: 100 mg
  - Child 6–12 yrs: 50 mg
  - Child <6 yrs: 25 mg

- **Cetirizine / Prednisolone:**
  - Continue Cetirizine or Chlorphenamine for ≤3 days
  - Continue prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg for up to 3 days

- **Refractory Cases:**
  - iv adrenaline (experienced users only)
  - Alternative vasopressors
  - im glucagon (if on β-blockers)
  - iv magnesium (beware hypotension)

---

**Outcomes:**

- Immediate: Remove allergen, administer IM epinephrine, monitor vital signs, provide IV fluids and nebulised salbutamol as indicated.
- Intermediate: Measure mast cell tryptase levels, observe or admit based on age, continue antihistamines/corticosteroids.
- Long-term: Autoinjector training, patient education, discharge letter, referral to allergy specialist.

This flowchart provides a structured, age-based approach to managing anaphylaxis from initial recognition through to post-event care and specialist follow-up.

## VIII. SPECIAL CASE
1. Urticarial and Angioedema
Urticarial is commonly encountered in the ED. It is characterized by the presence of wheals, angioedema, or both. Urticarial appears as papules or wheals that consist of central swelling with surrounding reflex erythema and is associated with itching or a burning type sensation. These lesions are a result of mediators (predominately histamine) released from mast cells. They tend to occur on the extremities and are usually transient, with skin often returning to its normal appearance within 24 hours. Urticarial can be classified based on its duration, with acute urticarial lasting less than 6 weeks and chronic episodes lasting longer than 6 weeks. There are also several types of inducible urticarial including cold contact, delayed pressure, heat contact, solar, aquagenic, or cholinergic.

Angioedema is characterized by edema of the subcutaneous or submucosal tissues, commonly involving the face, mouth, lips, tongue, extremities, or genitalia. It is a result of abrupt vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, allowing fluid to move from the vascular to the interstitial space. As the swelling is located in the deeper layers of the skin, the appearance is often normal in color and patients often complain of pain or a pressure sensation, rather than an itch. Of particular concern is when the tongue, posterior pharynx, or larynx is involved, which could progress to airway obstruction and compromise. Angioedema can be mediated by an allergic mechanism in response to exposure to foods, drugs, or physical stimuli or by a nonallergic mechanism such as Hereditary Angioedema (HAE), acquired angioedema, or ACE-inhibitor- induced angioedema.
2. Management
Angioedema with urticarial without airway threatening:
- H1-Antihistamine: cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine or Diphenhydramine
- H2-Antihistamine may also beneficial: Famotidine, Ranitidine or Cimetidine.
- Corticosteroids: prednisone as a second-line therapy
- Epinephrine: anaphylactic dosing for severe symptoms and no cardiac risk factors.
- Avoid exposure to potential triggering agents.
Angioedema with airway-threatening:
- Epinephrine at anaphylactic doses.
- Antihistamines
- Intubation if situation required and paralytics should be utilized with caution.
- Prepared for difficult airway algorithm using alternative measures (fiber optic laryngoscopy, surgical airway).

## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS
- Biphasic reaction: reoccurrence of anaphylactic symptoms without re-exposure to the triggering agent within 8 hours to 72 hours.
- Prevention by administer corticosteroids but recent studies have failed to show significant effect.
- Risk factor for biphasic reactions include
- Hypotension
- Wide pulse pressure
- Unknown trigger
- Greater than 1 dose of epinephrine
- Cutaneous signs and symptoms, prior anaphylaxis
- And delayed epinephrine administration.

- Patients should be monitored for a minimum of 6 h after resolution of symptoms. This observation period may need to be longer depending on the presence of any of the following high-risk features:
- Extremes of age
- Significant co-morbidity
- Severe reaction with slow onset
- Severe asthma
- Likely continued absorption
- History of significant biphasic reaction
- Evening or night presentation
- Difficulty accessing emergency care
- Hospitalization should be strongly considered for patients who present with protracted anaphylaxis, hypotension, or airway involvement; receive more than two doses of IM epinephrine; or have poor outpatient social support, or inability to acquire an auto-injectable epinephrine device.

## X. COMPLICATION
The main complications which can occur following an anaphylactic reaction include:
- Wheeze
- Stridor
- Hypoxemia
- Hypotension
- End-organ dysfunction
- Death
## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION
Anaphylaxis is a potentially life-threatening allergic condition which can present with multiple symptoms.
Anaphylaxis should be treated with intramuscular epinephrine, supportive management, and adjunct medications as needed. The mainstay of management is avoidance of triggers and to carry an epinephrine auto-injector.
A prescription for an epinephrine auto-injector should be provided following treatment of anaphylaxis, and training should also be provided regarding its use. Patients should also be assessed and followed by an allergist.

## I. DEFINITION
Poisoning or intoxication is a serious condition that occurs when a person or an animal is exposed to a substance that can harm their health or even kill them.
## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
An epidemiological Surveillance report 2011 in Thailand found that the incidence of environmental pesticide poisoning is 3.20 per 100.000 person. The incidence of prescribed drugs poisoning is 3.81 and the intentional ingestion of toxic substances is 5.91 per 100.000. In Singapore, the incidence of alcohol consumption-related ED visit was remarkably increased from 48.7 per 100.000 person (in 2007) to 79.1 per 100.000 person (in 2016).
## III. ETIOLOGY

Poisoning may be “acute” (occurs a few hours to few days after exposure) or “Chronic” (problems occur after repeated and long-time exposure). In emergencies most of the intoxication cases was acute poisoning. Intoxication or poisoning may be intentional or non- intentional. Intentional poisoning: suicide attempt, self-harm, abuse, misuse. Non-intentional poisoning: error dose, accidental, environmental toxics (air pollution, arsenic in water...), occupational poisoning, food, drink (methanol poisoning), animal bites. Poison can be a drug that is used in clinic (overdose), food, drink, chemical that use in industrial / agricultural works, or household-use, or biologic (mushroom, some fishes). Exposure route may be inhalation, skin contact, mucous membrane contact, ingestion, or injection. Animals or snakebites were also a kind of poisoning in which the poison or venom were injected into the subcutaneous tissue or muscle during the bite.

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY
To initiate the poisoning, the organism is exposed to the toxic chemical. When a toxic level of the chemical is accumulated in the cells of the target tissue or organ, the resultant injury to the cells disrupts their normal structure or function. Symptoms and toxic signs then develop, and, if the toxicity is severe enough, death may result. Different groups of substances may have different mechanisms of toxicity to human. It may be a Systemic poisoning (Cyanide, lead, warfarin, pesticides), specific organ poisoning (paracetamol-liver, gentamycin-kidney, snake Viperidae-venom-hematologic / snake Elapidae-venom- neurologic), local poisoning (caustic, acid, snake Viperidae-venom), some substances may cause endocrine disruption (DDT, Bisphenol A, Dioxins), some other may be cancerogenic (arsenic-skin, Asbestos-lung, tobacco- lung). Substances belonging to a particular pharmaceutical or chemical class often produce a cluster of symptoms and signs, or
“toxidrome”, enabling the identification of potential toxins when a clear history is unavailable.

## V. DIAGNOSIS
The diagnosis of poisoning is based on the meticulous history, physical examination and/or toxidrome found in physical exam.
## 1. Signs & symptoms
