Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan,
Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. MEN Sengleap,
Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour
## I. DEFINITION
Aortic dilatation, in clinical practice, aortic root dilatation can be suspected in male adults when aortic diameter is >40 mm and in females at >36 mm or with an indexed diameter/BSA (aortic size index [ASI]) >22 mm/m2.
Arterial aneurysm is defined as a diameter >1.5 times (>50%) larger than the predicted one.
Aneurysm is a pathologic dilation of a blood vessel, affecting all three layers of the vessel wall. An aneurysm is a permanent, localized arterial dilation to more than 50% of the normal diameter. True aneurysms involve all three layers, while pseudoaneurysms disrupt intimal and medial layers.
Aneurysms can be classified by appearance, fusiform or saccular aneurysm.
- Fusiform: Circumferential widening of the artery
- Saccular: Localized, typically asymmetric, outpouchings of the artery wall. Ectasia is an arterial dilatation <150% of normal arterial diameter.
## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
## A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA)

Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA) have an estimated incidence of at least 5 to 10 per 100,000 person-years. Aortic root or ascending aortic aneurysms are most common (approximately 60%), followed by aneurysms of the descending aorta (approximately 35%) and aortic arch (<10%).

## B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA)
AAAs occur in 3% to 9% of men older than 50 years and are the most common form of aortic aneurysms. Most AAAs (>80%) arise in the infrarenal aorta.
- 90% of all abdominal aortic aneurysms >4.0 cm is related to atherosclerotic disease.
- Risk of rupture increases with size: the 5-years risk of aneurysms < 5cm is 1-2%; whereas it is 20-40% for aneurysms > 5 cm in diameter.
## III. PATHOGENESIS AND ETIOLOGY
Aortic aneurysms result from conditions that cause degradation or abnormal production of the structural components of the aortic wall: elastin and collagen.
The causes of aortic aneurysms may be broadly categorized as degenerative disorders, genetic or developmental diseases, vasculitis, infections, and trauma.
## A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA)
*Aortic root or ascending aorta:
- Syndromic: Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Turner syndrome.
- Non-Syndromic: Bicuspid aortic valve, Sporadic TAA, Familial TAA. *Descending aorta:

- Atherosclerosis
- Aortitis (non-infectious): vasculitis disorders (eg, giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis).
- Aortitis (infectious): Syphilis, Infected (mycotic) TAA cause by systemic or local infections (eg, sepsis, pneumonia), lymphangitic spread (eg, tuberculosis).

## B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA)
- Atherosclerosis (majority cause): risk factor: Smoking, age, HTN, Hyperlipidemia, Male sex; Family history of AAA, other cardiovascular disease
- Inflammatory aneurysm
- Infectious aneurysm
- Inherited connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome).
## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
A wide variety of pathological factors are associated with aortic aneurysms. These include degenerative diseases, inherited disorders, infections, inflammatory conditions (i.e., vasculitis), and trauma.
## V. DIAGNOSIS
## 1. Clinic
## A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA):
Most TAAs are asymptomatic and are discovered incidentally. Less frequently revealed by clinical symptoms:
- Pain - tearing, radiating to back
- Heart failure - due to AR
- Thromboembolic (stroke, painful/parenthesis of limbs)
- Hoarseness of voice (compression of recurrent laryngeal nerve), dysphagia, plethora and edema from superior vena cava compression
- Aorto-esophageal fistula and hemoptysis can also be seen.
- Can mimic other acute disorders (AMI, renal colic, pancreatitis)
## B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA):
- Asymptomatic
- Incidental finding on abdominal imaging examination: as a palpable, pulsatile, expansile, and nontender mass, frank ecchymosis.
- Acute abdominal pain and hypotension occur with rupture of the aneurysm, which requires an emergency operation or endovascular repair.
## 2. Investigation
## A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA):

- Chest x-ray: widening of the mediastinal shadow and displacement or
compression of the trachea or left main stem bronchus
- Echocardiogram or transesophageal echocardiography, can be used to
assess the proximal ascending aorta and descending thoracic aorta
- Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI are sensitive and specific tests for
assessment of aneurysms of the thoracic aorta and involvement of branch.

## B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA):
- Abdomen x-ray: demonstrate the calcified outline of the aneurysm; 25% not calcified.
- Ultrasonography: screening and surveillance.
- CT or MRI: gold standard’s in the pre-operative and post-operative evaluation of AAA.
- Since the presence of mural thrombi may reduce the luminal size, aortography may underestimate the diameter of an aneurysm.
## VI. DIFFERENCIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Chest pain
 - Acute myocardial infarction
 - Pulmonary embolism
 - Spontaneous pneumothorax
 - Esophageal rupture
- Abdominal pain
 - Renal/biliary colic
 - Bowel obstruction/perforation
 - Non-dissection-related mesenteric ischemia
- Back pain
 - Renal colic
 - Musculoskeletal pain
 - Intervertebral disc herniation
- Focal neurologic deficit
 - Primary ischemic cerebrovascular accident
 - Cauda equina syndrome
## VII. MANAGEMENT
## 1. Objective
The goal is to slow the growth of the aneurysm and prevent the rupture or dissection.
## 2. Critical signs
*Risk of dissection:
- Diameter > 60mm of ascending aorta
- Diameter > 70mm of descending aorta.
## A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA):
## a. Medical therapy:
 - Control blood pressure: (target BP< 130/80 mmHg for non-diabetic patient and BP < 140/90mmHg for diabetic; target HR: 60bpm.)
- Beta blocker (Atenolol; Bisoprolol, Metoprolol…)
- ACEi or ARB
 - Statin for dyslipidemia target LDL cholesterol <70 mg/dL.

- Screening 6 months after initial scan then every 12 months unless symptomatic or increased rate of expansion or if size is 4.5cm - 5.5cm.
 - Smoking Cessation

## b. Percutaneous or surgical intervention:
Indication for surgery:
 - Instable Hemodynamic
 - Symptomatic

- Diameter ≥ 55mm or rate of growth ≥ 1.0cm per year.
 - Causing bronchial compression, aortobronchial or aortoesophageal fistulas
 - Traumatic, Mycotic
*Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair (TEVAR) or Open surgery repair.

## B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA):
- AAA diameter of 25-29 mm, Ultrasound imaging should be considered 4 years later.
- Patient with small diameter (30-55mm), The interval for imaging should be considered:
 - Every 3 years for AAA of 30-39mm.
 - Every 2 years for AAA of 40-44mm diameter.
 - Every year for AAA of > 45mm diameter.
## a. Medical Therapy:
- Control blood pressure: (target BP< 130/80 mmHg for non-diabetic patient and BP < 140/90mmHg for diabetic or CKD; target HR: 60bpm.). Beta blocker is 1st line in HTA drug with AAA. ACEi, ARB and other Antihypertension is drug of choice.
- Statins: reduce the risk of cardiovascular events related to atherosclerosis
 - cardiovascular disease and rupture.
- Antiplatelet to reduce intraluminal mural thrombus is controversial but usually use in
 - others indication of CVD.
- Smoking Cessation
## b. Surgical Therapy Indication:
- Asymptomatic AAA:
 - Diameter >55mm.
 - Aneurysm growth >10mm per year.
- Symptomatic AAA
 - In case of ruptured AAA, emergency repair is indicated.
 - In case of symptomatic but non ruptured AAA, urgent repair
is indicated.
## AAA repair methods:
- Open aortic aneurysm repair
- Endovascular aortic aneurysm repair (EAVR)
## VIII. SPECIAL CASES
Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is the most common congenital cardiac abnormality. A thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is present ≈ 50% of BAV patients, who also have an 8-fold higher risk of aortic dissection than the general population.
## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS

- Thoracic abdominal aneurysms (TAA) enlarge an average of 3 to 5 mm/year.
- Risk factors for rapid enlargement include larger size of aneurysm, location in the descending aorta, and presence of mural thrombi.
- The risk of rupture appears to rise abruptly as TAAs reach 6 cm in diameter.
- Survival rate of patients with untreated large TAAs is 54% at 5 years.
- TAA rupture has a mortality of 97%.
- Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) typically enlarge at a rate of 10%/year, but some
enlarge exponentially; about 20% remain the same size indefinitely.

## X. COMPLICATIONS
- Rupture or Dissection
- Thrombus embolism.
- Lower Limb ischemia.
- Infected (mycotic) aneurysms
- Aorto-enteric fistulas, Aorto-caval fistulas
## XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION
- Stringent control of hypertension
- Lipid profile optimization
- Smoking cessation
- Other atherosclerosis risk reduction measures.
- Avoid isometric exercises
## XII. REFERECES
1. 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of peripheral arterial and aortic diseases. 2. Mark A. Creager, J. L. (2022). Disease of aorta, Harrison's_Internal Medicine 21th Edition (pp. 2101-2104).
3. Schermerhorn, A. C. (2019). Diseases of the Aorta, Braunwald’s Heart Disease Edition 11^th (pp. 1295-1305).
4. Mark A. Farber, Federico E. Parodi, MD. 2023, Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms, Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms
5. E. Ladich, J. Butany and R. Virmani (2016), Aneurysms of the aorta: ascending, thoracic, and abdominal and their management, Cardiovascular Pathology 4^th Edition, (pp. 169-211).

## MITRAL REGURGITATION (MR)
Asst. Prof. CHHUN Lay Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr.
MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM
Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof CHAN Sokha, Prof. SOK Chour
## I. DEFINITION
Is the heart valve condition in which the flaps of the mitral valve do not close properly, causing a backward flow of blood back to the left atrium.
## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
MR is the most common valvular abnormality worldwide, affecting over 2 to 3% of the total population and has a prevalence that increases with age.
## III. ETIOLOGY
A. Primary MR:
a. Infectious/Rheumatic:
- Rheumatism valvular heart disease is most common cause of VHD, more than 95% of total VHD in the developing country,
- Endocarditis
b. Degenerative:
- Mitral valve prolapses,
- Myxomatous degenerative,
- Maorfanc syndrome
c. Congenital:
- Congenital malformations of the mitral valve, B. Secondary MR:
a. Papillary Muscle Rupture:
- Papillary muscle rupture is a very rare condition seen in 1% to 2% of patients after myocardial infarction (MI)
- or infective endocarditis. It leads to severe mitral regurgitation due to dysfunction of the papillary muscles,
b. Ischemic MR (IMR):

- IMR results from prior MI associated with normal mitral valve leaflets and chordae. Ischemia of the segments underlying the papillary muscles results in remodeling. This phenomenon causes papillary muscle displacement, which results in a more apical position of the leaflets known as a “seagull sign”.
c.  Congestive heart failure (CHF) Associated:
- Cause by annulus dilation
- Remodeling of left LV
d. Chronic Atrial Fibrillation,

## e. Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
f. Other rare causes of MR such as prolonged use of certain medications can
cause MR,

## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY
A. Pathophysiology mechanism:
- The definition of mitral regurgitation is a retrograde flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium.
- Mitral regurgitation leads to left ventricular volume overload due to increased stroke volume, caused by an increase in blood volume within the left atrium and hence an increased preload delivered to the left ventricle during diastole.
- In chronic progressive MR, ventricular remodeling occurs, allowing maintenance of cardiac output, and an initial increase in ejection fraction (EF) is usually observed. - --
- However, depending on the regurgitant fraction, the effective EF can be considerably lower. Over time, there is a positive feedback loop by which volume overload from MR causes ventricular dilatation, widening of the mitral annulus, and diminished coaptation of leaflets, leading to further worsening of MR.
- Eventually, volume overload becomes so severe that excitation-contraction coupling becomes impaired and wall stress-related afterload on the left ventricle leading to dilatation and decreased contractility, resulting in a reduction of EF. B. Anatomy pathology: Any disease affection these anatomies can cause MR,
- Mitral leaflets (anterior and posterior)
- Mitral valve annulus,
- Chordae teninease
- Papillary muscle
- LV remodeling,
C. Carpentier classification:
- Type I: Normal leaflet motion
+ annular dilation, leaflet perforation + regurgitation jet directed centrally
- Type II: Excessive leaflet motion

This is a detailed anatomical diagram of the mitral valve, viewed from the left ventricular side (i.e., the ventricular aspect). The diagram illustrates the structural components of the mitral valve, including its leaflets, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, annulus, and commissures.

Key labeled components:

1. **Anterior leaflet** – The larger, more prominent leaflet of the mitral valve, which is attached to the anterior annulus. It has a smooth, thin structure and forms the majority of the valve’s surface area.

2. **Posterior leaflet (3 lobes)** – The posterior leaflet is divided into three distinct lobes (anterior, middle, and posterior) and is attached to the posterior annulus. It lies behind the anterior leaflet and is less visible from this perspective.

3. **Chordae tendineae** – Thin, fibrous cords that connect the free edges of the mitral valve leaflets to the papillary muscles. These prevent prolapse of the leaflets during ventricular contraction.

4. **Medial papillary muscle** – A muscular structure located on the medial (central) side of the left ventricle, attaching to the posterior leaflet via chordae tendineae.

5. **Lateral papillary muscle** – Located laterally (to the side), also attaching to the posterior leaflet via chordae tendineae.

6. **Anterior annulus** – The ring-like structure at the base of the anterior leaflet, forming part of the mitral valve’s fibrous ring.

7. **Posterior annulus** – The ring-like structure at the base of the posterior leaflet, completing the mitral valve’s annular framework.

8. **Anteromedial commissure** – The junction point between the anterior and posterior leaflets on the medial side of the valve.

9. **Posterolateral commissure** – The junction point between the anterior and posterior leaflets on the lateral side of the valve.

10. **Lateral capillary muscle** – This label appears to be a misnomer or error; there is no such structure as “lateral capillary muscle” in standard cardiac anatomy. It may refer to the lateral papillary muscle, but the term “capillary” is incorrect — papillary muscles are not capillary structures. The correct term should be “lateral papillary muscle,” which is already labeled elsewhere.

The diagram provides a clear view of how the mitral valve functions mechanically: during diastole, the valve opens to allow blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle; during systole, the valve closes tightly to prevent backflow into the atrium. The chordae tendineae and papillary muscles ensure proper coaptation of the leaflets.

This diagram is useful for understanding mitral valve anatomy, pathology (e.g., prolapse, regurgitation, stenosis), and surgical repair/replacement procedures.

This is a detailed anatomical diagram of the aortic valve and adjacent structures of the heart, viewed from the ventricular side. The illustration depicts the aortic valve’s three cusps and associated leaflets, commissures, and surrounding anatomy.

Key labeled components:

1. Aortic Valve — The overall structure at the exit of the left ventricle into the aorta.
   - Left Coronary Cusp — One of the three cusps of the aortic valve; it is the cusp that opens toward the left coronary artery.
   - Noncoronary Cusp — The cusp that does not directly correspond to any coronary artery origin.
   - Aortic Mitral Curtain — A thin, membranous structure located between the aortic valve and the mitral valve annulus; also known as the aortic curtain or aortic valve curtain.

2. Leaflets of the Mitral Valve — Although technically part of the mitral valve, these are shown here for anatomical context relative to the aortic valve.
   - Anterior Leaflet — Divided into three segments labeled A1, A2, and A3.
     - A1 — The segment closest to the anterior commissure.
     - A2 — The middle segment.
     - A3 — The segment closest to the posterior commissure.
   - Posterior Leaflet — Divided into two segments labeled P1 and P2.
     - P1 — The segment closest to the anterior commissure.
     - P2 — The middle segment.

3. Commissures — Points where the mitral valve leaflets meet.
   - Anterior Commissure — Junction point between the anterior leaflet and the posterior leaflet on the anterior side.
   - Posterior Commissure — Junction point between the anterior leaflet and the posterior leaflet on the posterior side.

4. Blood Flow — Indicated by a blue arrow showing blood flowing from the left ventricle through the aortic valve into the aorta.

Algorithm:

This is a clinical decision-making algorithm titled “Management of patients with severe chronic primary mitral regurgitation.” It outlines a stepwise approach to managing patients based on symptoms, hemodynamic parameters, surgical risk, and anatomical suitability.

---

**Decision Points and Branches:**

1. **Initial Decision Point: Symptoms**
   - **Y (Yes)** → Proceed to evaluate “Operative risk judged by the Heart Team.”
   - **N (No)** → Evaluate “LVEF ≤ 60% or LVEDD ≥ 40 mm.”

2. **Branch from “LVEF ≤ 60% or LVEDD ≥ 40 mm”**
   - **N (No)** → Evaluate “New onset of AF or SPAP > 50 mmHg.”
     - **Y (Yes)** → “High likelihood of durable repair, low surgical risk, and LA dilatation.”
       - **N (No)** → “Follow-up”
       - **Y (Yes)** → “Surgical mitral valve repair”
   - **Y (Yes)** → “Inoperable or at high surgical risk.”
     - **N (No)** → “Surgery (repair whenever possible)”
     - **Y (Yes)** → “TEER if anatomically suitable/extended HF treatment”
   - **(Note: The branch labeled “High risk of futility” is reached only if operative risk is judged high by the Heart Team and the patient is deemed not suitable for surgery.)**

3. **Branch from “Operative risk judged by the Heart Team”**
   - Leads to two outcomes:
     - “Inoperable or at high surgical risk” → Further branching as above.
     - “High risk of futility” → Outcome: “Palliative care”

---

**Key Clinical Parameters:**
- **LVEF**: Left Ventricular Ejection Fraction (≤ 60% indicates reduced function)
- **LVEDD**: Left Ventricular End-Diastolic Dimension (≥ 40 mm indicates dilation)
- **SPAP**: Systolic Pulmonary Artery Pressure (> 50 mmHg indicates pulmonary hypertension)
- **AF**: Atrial Fibrillation (new onset is a marker of disease progression)

---

**Outcomes:**
- **Follow-up**: For patients without symptoms, preserved LV function, no new-onset AF or elevated SPAP, and no indication for immediate intervention.
- **Surgical mitral valve repair**: Recommended for patients with high likelihood of durable repair, low surgical risk, and LA dilatation.
- **Surgery (repair whenever possible)**: For patients deemed inoperable or at high surgical risk but still candidates for repair.
- **TEER**: Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair — indicated if anatomically suitable and/or extended heart failure treatment is needed.
- **Palliative care**: For patients with high risk of futility due to poor prognosis despite intervention.

---

**Important Notes:**
- The algorithm does not include any specific drug names, dosages, or pharmacological interventions.
- The term “LA dilatation” refers to left atrial enlargement, which is a key predictor of surgical success.
- “Extended HF treatment” implies advanced heart failure therapies (e.g., devices, medications) may be considered alongside TEER.

This algorithm is designed to guide multidisciplinary decision-making, particularly involving the Heart Team, to optimize outcomes in patients with severe chronic primary mitral regurgitation.

## I. DEFINITION
Mitral stenosis (MS) is a form of valvular heart disease, characterized by narrowing of mitral valve orifice in diastole. Today, the most common cause of MS is rheumatic fever, but the stenosis usually appears clinically relevant only after several decades.
## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
The prevalence of rheumatic disease in developed countries is declining, with an estimated incidence of 1 in 100000. The prevalence is higher in developing nations than in US. In Cambodia, the prevalence is more than 35 case per 100000.
## III. ETIOLOGY
- Rheumatic fever more than 95%,
- Calcification of mitral valve leaflets,
- Congenital heart disease,
- Mitral annular calcification,
- Endomyocardial fibroelastosis,
- Malignant carcinoid syndrome,
- Myxom of mitral valves
- Systemic lupus erythematosus, Whipple disease, Fabry disease, and rheumatoid arthritis.
## IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY

- The normal mitral valve orifice area is 4 to 6cm2. If mitral valve areas less then 2cm2 cause and impediment to the blood flow from the LA int LV. This creates a presser gradient across the MV. As the gradient across the MV increases, the LV requires the atrial kick to fill with blood.
- MS causes an increase int LA pressure. The normal LV diastolic pressure is 5 mmHg. A pressure gradient across the MV of 20 mmHg due to severe MS will cause a LA pressure of about 25 mmHg. This LA pressure is transmitted to the pulmonary vasculature resulting in pulmonary hypertension.
- A LA pressure remains elevated, the LA will increase in size. As the LA increases in size, there is a greater chance of developing Afib. If Afib develops, the atrial kick is lost.
- Thus, the LV filling depends on the atrial kick in severe MS. With the loss of the atrial kick, there is a decrease in cardiac output and sudden development of CHF.
- MS progresses slowly from initial signs of mitral stenosis to NYHA functional class II symptoms to Afib to NYHA functional class III or IV symptoms.

This is a detailed pathophysiological diagram illustrating the progression of mitral stenosis and its downstream effects on cardiac function and systemic symptoms.

Components and Labels:

1. Starting Point: “Mitral Stenosis (↓ MVA)” — indicates reduced mitral valve area.
   - Arrows lead to:
     - “↑ Mitral Valve Gradient” — increased pressure gradient across the stenotic valve.
     - “Shortened diastole (Tachycardia), Loss of AV Synchrony (AFib, heart block), ↑ Pulmonary Venous Flow (Volume loading)” — compensatory mechanisms and hemodynamic changes.

2. From “↑ Mitral Valve Gradient”:
   - Leads to “↑ LVDP” (Left Ventricular Diastolic Pressure) — indicating increased pressure during ventricular filling.
   - Also leads to “↑ Left Atrial Pressure” — primary consequence of impaired left ventricular filling.

3. “↑ Left Atrial Pressure” branches into two main pathways:
   - Left: “Left Atrial Enlargement” → “Atrial Arrhythmias” → “Symptoms”
   - Right: “↑ Pulmonary Venous Pressure” → “Pulmonary Edema” → “Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension” → “RVH and RV Hypertension, TR and RVE” → “Symptoms”

4. Additional Pathways:
   - “↑ Pulmonary Venous Pressure” also directly contributes to “Pulmonary Edema.”
   - “Pulmonary Edema” leads to “Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension,” which then leads to “RVH and RV Hypertension, TR and RVE” (Right Ventricular Hypertrophy and Right Ventricular Failure, with Tricuspid Regurgitation and Right Ventricular End-Diastolic Volume increase).

5. Final Outcome: All pathways converge at “Symptoms,” representing clinical manifestations such as dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, and pulmonary edema.

## Mitral Valve Anatomy According to the Wilkins Score
## Grade 1
- Mobility: Highly mobile valve with only leaflet tips restricted
- Thickening: Leaflet near normal in thickness (4 mm to 5 mm)
- Calcification: A single area of increased echo brightness
- Subvalvular Thickening: Minimal thickening just below the mitral leaflets
## Grade 2
- Mobility: Leaflet mid to base portions have normal mobility
- Thickening: Mid leaflets normal, considerable thickening of margins (5 to 8 mm)
- Calcification: Scattered areas of brightness confirmed to leaflet margins
- Subvalvular Thickening: Thickening of chordal structures extending to one of the chordal lengths
## Grade 3
- Mobility: Valve continues to move forward in diastole, mainly from the base
- Thickening: Thickening extending through the entire leaflet (5 mm to 8 mm)
- Calcification: Brightness extending into the mid portions of the leaflets
- Subvalvular Thickening: Thickening extended to the distal third of the chords
## Grade 4
- Mobility: No or minimal forward movement of the leaflets in diastole
- Thickening: Considerable thickening of all leaflet tissue (more than 8 mm to 10 mm)
- Calcification: Extensive brightness throughout much of the leaflet tissue
- Subvalvular Thickening: Extensive thickening and shortening of all chordal structures extending down to the papillary muscles.

## MANAGEMENT AND SURVEILLANCE OF PROSTHETIC
## VALVES
Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap,

Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour
## I. DEFINITION
Prosthetic heart valves are designed to replicate the function of native valves by maintaining unidirectional blood flow and can be separated into two broad categories, mechanical and bioprosthetic (also called tissue) valves, each with different advantages and disadvantages.
Mechanical heart valves (MHV) are made entirely from non-biological (artificial) materials including metals (titanium, cobalt), pyrolytic carbon, and polymers in order to provide mechanical stability and durability.
Bioprosthetic valves (BPV) are, at least in part, made from animal (e.g., porcine, bovine or equine) (heterograft or xenograft) or human (homograft or allograft) tissue mounted onto a metal or polymer supporting structure with three pillars (also called struts or posts) and have a trileaflet configuration that resembles the geometry of a native aortic valve.
## II. SELECTION OF PROSTHETIC VALVES
The choice between a mechanical and a bioprosthetic valve is a complex decision based on prosthetic valve characteristics, patient-related factors (e.g., comorbidities) and patient preferences such as wishes and expectations.

## III. BASELINE ASSESSMENT AND FOLLOW-UP
All patients with prosthetic valves require lifelong follow-up to detect early deterioration in prosthetic function or ventricular function, or progressive disease of another heart valve. Clinical assessment should be performed yearly or as soon as possible if new cardiac symptoms occur. TTE should be performed if any new symptoms occur or if complications are suspected. After transcatheter, as well as surgical implantation of a BHV, echocardiography, including measurement of transprosthetic gradients, should be performed within 30 days after valve implantation (i.e. baseline), at 1 year, and annually thereafter.

content:
This is a detailed antithrombotic therapy algorithm for patients with valve prostheses, based on guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and the European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS).

---

**Main Decision Point:**
Antithrombotic therapy for valve prostheses → splits into two major branches:

1. **Mechanical heart valve**
2. **Bioprosthetic heart valve**

---

**Branch 1: Mechanical Heart Valve**

- **Primary Recommendation:** VKA lifelong (Class I)
    - This is indicated for all patients with mechanical valves.

- **Additional Consideration: CAD (Coronary Artery Disease)**
    - Add low-dose ASA in selected patients at low risk of bleeding (Class IIb)

- **If VKA therapy interrupted for major planned invasive procedure:**
    - Minimize time with subtherapeutic INR
    - Bridging anticoagulation with UFH or LMWH (not required for minor surgeries) (Class I)

---

**Branch 2: Bioprosthetic Heart Valve**

This branch further splits into three types of procedures:

1. **MVR/TVR (Mitrvalve Replacement / Tricuspid Valve Replacement)**
2. **SAVR (Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement)**
3. **TAVI (Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation)**

Each of these has a common decision point:

→ **Other indications for oral anticoagulation?** (Yes/No)

- **If “N” (No other indications):**
    - MVR/TVR → OAC for 3 months (Class IIa)
    - SAVR → SAPT or OAC for 3 months (Class IIa)
    - TAVI → SAPT long-term (Class I)

- **If “Y” (Yes other indications):**
    - MVR/TVR → OAC long-term (Class I)
    - SAVR → OAC long-term (Class I)
    - TAVI → OAC long-term (Class I)

---

**Drug Names and Dosages Mentioned:**

- **VKA (Vitamin K Antagonist):** Lifelong (no specific dosage given, but INR monitoring implied)
- **ASA (Aspirin):** Low-dose (exact mg not specified, but “low-dose” is stated)
- **UFH (Unfractionated Heparin)**
- **LMWH (Low Molecular Weight Heparin)**
- **OAC (Oral Anticoagulant):** Generic term; specific agents (e.g., warfarin, DOACs) are not named, but context implies use of VKA or DOACs depending on indication.
- **SAPT (Short-term Anticoagulation Therapy):** Not defined by specific agent, but implies short-term use (e.g., rivaroxaban, apixaban, or warfarin) for 3 months.

---

**Outcomes and Classifications:**

- All recommendations are labeled with ESC/EACTS class levels:
    - **Class I:** Strong recommendation (evidence-based)
    - **Class IIa:** Weak recommendation (some evidence)
    - **Class IIb:** Weak recommendation (limited evidence)

---

**Summary of Key Clinical Decisions:**

- Mechanical valves → lifelong VKA.
- Bioprosthetic valves → depend on procedure type and presence of other indications for OAC.
    - Without other indications: short-term OAC/SAPT (3 months).
    - With other indications: long-term OAC.
- Bridging therapy recommended only for major invasive procedures with VKA interruption.
- Low-dose ASA may be added for CAD patients at low bleeding risk.

This algorithm provides a structured approach to antithrombotic management post-valve replacement, tailored to prosthesis type, procedure, and comorbidities.

- Combination of oral anticoagulant (OAC) with antiplatelet drugs: this combination may be considered in patients with coexistent atherosclerotic (e.g., peripheral artery, coronary artery or cerebrovascular) disease (Class IIb)

morbidity due to the risk of MHV thrombosis and high risk of bleeding during pregnancy and delivery.
 - The potentially teratogenic VKAs cross the placenta and have a dose-
dependent relationship with adverse outcomes, including foetal wastage and embryopathy.
 - It is very challenging to manage the anticoagulant during pregnancy for the
safety of mother and child as well as avoiding the complications.

## VI. COMPLICATIONS
- Structural failure (bioprosthetic valves): resulting in thickening, calcification, tearing, or disruption of the prosthetic valve (PV) with eventual haemodynamic dysfunction, manifesting as stenosis, regurgitation or a combination of both.
- Thrombosis and thromboembolism: leading to prosthetic valve dysfunction and embolism.
- Pannus formation: leading to prosthetic valve dysfunction
- Paraprosthetic regurgitation
- Bleeding related to antithrombotic therapy
- Intravascular haemolysis
- Infectious endocarditis
- Heart failure
## VII. PATIENT EDUCATION
Patients should be educated about
- Prosthetic valve outcomes,
- The need for proper care (including optimal dental care, the need for antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures, and when required, appropriate antithrombotic therapy)
- Seeking prompt medical attention for any new sign or symptom that might be related to a valve complication such as a significant change in the audible click of a mechanical prosthesis, persistent or recurrent fever, decrease in exercise tolerance, ischemic cerebral events, or palpitations.
- The relation of VKA and diet
- Follow-up and checking PT and INR regularly with his/her doctor.
- Not to start, stop, or change the dose of any medicine or supplement without checking with his/her doctor.

## DEEP VENOUS THROMBOSIS
Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha,
Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour
## I. DEFINITION
Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of blood clot (thrombus) in a deep vein, typically in the legs.
## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
DVT is a significant global health issue, affecting around 1 in 1000 people annually. The incidence increases with age and risk factors include immobility, surgery, trauma, cancer, and genetic clotting disorders. DVT is more common in women due to risk factors like pregnancy and oral contraceptive use.
## III. ETIOLOGY
The etiology of DVT involves a combination of factors that promote blood clotting in the veins. These include immobility (e.g after surgery or long flights), trauma to the vein, hypercoagulability (due to genetic disorders like Factor V Leiden), and vascular injury. Additional risk factors include cancer, use of oral contraceptives, pregnancy and obesity.
## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

The pathophysiology of DVT involves Virchow’s triad, which consists of three key mechanisms: venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. Venous stasis, often caused by prolonged immobility, reduces blood flow, promoting clot formation. Endothelial injury from trauma or surgery triggers clotting at the injury site, while hypercoagulability – whether from genetic disorders, cancer or hormonal changes – increases the blood’s tendency to clot. Together, these factors lead to thrombus formation in deep veins, usually in the legs.

## V. DIAGNOSIS
1. Clinical assessment:
- Assess symptoms (leg pain, swelling) and use a clinical prediction tool like the two-level modified Well’s Score (Annex 1) to determine the likelihood of DVT
2. D-dimer Test:
- For patients with DVT unlikely, a D-dimer blood test is performed. If the D-dimer is negative, DVT is ruled out. If positive, further imaging is required.
3. Imaging with Venous Ultrasound:
- For patients with DVT likely or positive D-dimer, compression venous ultrasound is the first-line imaging test.
4. Further Imaging:
- If the ultrasound results are unclear or DVT involves unusual locations (e.g. pelvic veins), advanced imaging like CT venography or MR venography may be used.

5. Follow-up:
- In patients where initial tests are inconclusive but suspicion remains,

## repeat ultrasound after 5 – 7 days may be performed to confirm or
exclude DVT.
## Vl. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
Several conditions that present with similar symptoms such as leg pain and swelling:
1. Cellulitis: a bacterial skin infection that cause redness and swelling 2. Muscle strain or tear: injury to muscle can lead to localized pain and swelling 3. Baker’s cyst: a fluid-filled cyst behind the knee that can rupture, causing pain and swelling
4. Lymphedema: swelling due to lymphatic obstruction can mimic DVT 5. Chronic venous insufficiency: persist swelling and skin changes due to poor vein function, often confused with acute DVT
## Vll. MANAGEMENT
1. Initial assessment: risk stratification is crucial. Categorize patients as low, intermediate or high risk based on clinical presentation and underlying conditions
2. Initial treatment (first 5 – 21 days)
- Initiate anticoagulation in most patients unless contraindicated
- Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) such as apixaban or rivaroxaban are preferred for most non-cancer patients
- LMWH (Low molecular weight heparin) or unfractionated heparin (UFH) is used for certain patients (e.g. cancer, renal impairment, high bleeding risk).
- VKA (Vitamin K antagonists): second-line therapy. VKA are often considered when DOACs are contra-indicated or unsuitable, such as
- In patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30 ml/min)
- In patients on certain medications that interact with DOACs,
reducing their efficacy or increase bleeding

- Compression stockings are recommended to reduce symptoms like swelling and prevent post-thrombotic syndrome.

This is a clinical decision algorithm for the diagnosis and management of suspected lower limb deep vein thrombosis (DVT). The flowchart begins with suspicion of DVT and guides through diagnostic and therapeutic steps based on clinical probability, imaging, and risk stratification.

---

**Decision Points and Branches:**

1. **Initial Decision Point:**
   - **Input:** Lower limb DVT suspicion
   - **Action:** Clinical probability assessment using two-level modified Wells score
   - **Branches:**
     - DVT unlikely → Proceed to D-dimer test
     - DVT likely → Proceed to Venous US

2. **Branch: DVT Unlikely**
   - **Action:** D-dimer test
   - **Branches:**
     - D-dimer Negative → No DVT → No anticoagulation (No AC)
     - D-dimer Positive → Proceed to Venous US (Note: This branch merges into the “DVT likely” pathway’s Venous US step)

3. **Branch: DVT Likely**
   - **Action:** Venous US
   - **Branches:**
     - Proximal DVT → Anticoagulation (AC) and compression therapy
     - IDDVT (Inferior Deep DVT — likely meaning distal DVT or isolated distal DVT) → Further stratified by risk

4. **Branch: Proximal DVT**
   - **Actions:**
     - At least 3-months AC (NOACs in non-cancer patients)
     - Immediate (<24 hrs) compression
     - Assess indication to reperfusion
   - **Follow-up:** 3-months assessment
     - Includes: Venous US, risk/benefit, compliance, patient’s preference, PTS (Post-Thrombotic Syndrome)
   - **Branches from 3-months assessment:**
     - Stop AC → Continue or not compression
     - Extend AC → Yearly evaluation → Continue or not compression

5. **Branch: IDDVT**
   - **Stratification by Risk:**
     - High risk patient → 3-months AC
     - Low risk patient → 
       - Short term LMWH (full or lower dose)
       - OR venous US surveillance

---

**Drug Names and Dosages:**

- **NOACs**: Non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (specific drugs not named, e.g., apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran; dosage unspecified per algorithm)
- **LMWH**: Low molecular weight heparin (e.g., enoxaparin, dalteparin); specified as “full or lower dose” — no specific mg/kg or daily dose given
- **Anticoagulation (AC)**: General term for anticoagulant therapy; duration specified as 3 months (proximal DVT) or short-term (IDDVT low-risk)

---

**Outcomes:**

- **No DVT**: No anticoagulation
- **Proximal DVT**: 3-month anticoagulation + compression + reperfusion assessment → followed by 3-month reassessment leading to stop or extend AC
- **IDDVT high risk**: 3-month anticoagulation
- **IDDVT low risk**: Short-term LMWH or surveillance (no anticoagulation required)

---

**Key Clinical Terms:**

- DVT: Deep Vein Thrombosis
- D-dimer: Biomarker for fibrin degradation products
- Venous US: Ultrasound of veins
- AC: Anticoagulation
- NOACs: Novel Oral Anticoagulants
- LMWH: Low Molecular Weight Heparin
- PTS: Post-Thrombotic Syndrome
- Compression: Mechanical compression therapy (e.g., graduated compression stockings)
- Reperfusion: Assessment for potential thrombolysis or thrombectomy if indicated
- Risk stratification: Based on clinical factors (not detailed in algorithm)

---

**Summary Flow:**

Suspicion → Wells Score → DVT Unlikely (D-dimer) → No DVT → No AC  
or DVT Likely → Venous US → Proximal DVT → 3-month AC + compression → 3-month reassessment → Stop or Extend AC  
or IDDVT → High risk → 3-month AC; Low risk → Short-term LMWH or surveillance

This algorithm integrates clinical probability, diagnostic testing, imaging, and risk-based treatment decisions for DVT management.

## Vlll. SPECIAL CASES
- Pregnancy-Related DVT: due to physiological changes and compression of pelvic veins. Use Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) for treatment.
- Cancer-Related DVT: due to increased coagulability associated with malignancy, treatment (chemotherapy) and immobility. Management often involves long-term anticoagulation with LMWH or DOACs.
- Post-surgical DVT: Common in orthopedic and abdominal surgeries. Prophylactic measures (e.g. early mobilization, compression stockings) and anticoagulation may be initiated perioperatively.
- Upper extremity DVT: often associated with central venous catheters or repetitive trauma. Management focus on catheter removal and anticoagulation.
- May-Thurner Syndrome: compression of the left common iliac vein by the right common iliac artery leading to DVT. Management includes stenting or surgical intervention alongside anticoagulation.

## lX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS
- Immediate risk: DVT can lead to serious complications such as pulmonary embolism (PE) especially in acute phase
- Long-term outcomes: many patients may experience resolution of symptoms, but some develop post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS), characterized by chronic pain and swelling
- Recurrence: the risk of recurrent DVT varies based on individual risk factors (e.g. cancer, history of thrombosis), with rates ranging from 10 – 30% in 10 years
- Appropriate anticoagulation and monitoring improve outcomes, reducing the risk of complications and recurrences.
## X. COMPLICATIONS
- Pulmonary embolism (PE)
- Post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS): resulting from damage to veins and valves
- Recurrent DVT
- Chronic venous insufficiency: long-term damage to veins lead to varicoses veins and skin ulcer
- Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens: a rare, severe condition where extensive thrombosis causes blue discoloration of the limb, leading to tissue ischemia and necrosis.
- Venous gangrene: a rare but critical complication (death of tissue due to compromised blood flow)
## Xl. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION
- Identify individuals at high risk (e.g. surgery patients, those with cancer, or prolonged immobilization) to tailor prevention strategies
- Use compression stocking to promote venous return during hospitalization or surgery
- Pharmacological prophylaxis: administer anticoagulant (LMWH or DOACs) for high- risk patients

- Early mobilization: encourage early mobilization after surgery or during prolonged hospitalization
- Patient education: inform patients about DVT symptoms and the important of prevention measures particularly after surgery or during long travel.

The prevention of deep venous thrombosis (DVT), a common and potentially serious condition, is a critical component of clinical care.
Effective DVT prevention begins with identifying patients at risk:

- IMPROVE Bleeding Risk Score (risk assessment for bleeding)

## IV. ISK ASSESSMENT FOR BLEEDING
1. Improve Bleeding Risk Score
The IMPROVE bleeding risk score is a validated tool for assessing the risk of bleeding in hospitalized patients who may require pharmacological prophylaxis for DVT / PE
2. Scoring and Risk category
- Score ≥ 7 : High risk of bleeding (pharmacological prophylaxis should be used cautiously or avoided). Mechanical prophylaxis may be alternative.
- Score < 7: Low risk of bleeding (pharmacological prophylaxis is safe and recommended)
## V. METHOD OF PROPHYLAXIS
1. Mechanical Prophylaxis:
Mechanical methods promote venous blood flow and are primarily used for patients at high bleeding risk or as an adjunct to pharmacological prophylaxis
- Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC): inflatable sleeve applied to the legs to promote venous return and useful in surgical and ICU patients with high bleeding risk
- Graduated Compression Stocking (GCS): Elastic stockings that apply pressure to the legs, reducing venous stasis.
2. Pharmacological prophylaxis
- Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH):
- Enoxaparin 40 mg (SC) daily
- Enoxaparin 20 mg (SC) daily (for renal impairment with eGFR
15 – 30 ml/min)
- Unfractionated Heparin (UFH): 5000 units (SC) every 8 – 12 h, preferred in patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR< 30 ml/min)
- Direct Oral Anticoagulant (DOA):
- Rivaroxaban: 10 mg orally once daily (avoid if eGFR < 15
ml/min)
- Apixaban: 2.5 mg orally twice daily (avoid if eGFR < 15
ml/min)

Dr. SOK Monghak, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KHUON Rithy, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap,      Dr.

## I. DEFINITION
Infectious Endocarditis (IE) refers to infection of the endocardial surface of the heart; it usually refers to infection of one or more heart valves or infection of an intracardiac device.
## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
- The incidence of infective endocarditis is estimated between 30 and 80 cases per million inhabitants and per year in the general population in industrialized countries.
- Incidence increases after the age of 60 and Staphylococcus is now the most frequent responsible microorganism.
- Infective endocarditis was native (NVE) in 1764 (56.6%) patients, prosthetic (PVIE) in 939 (30.1%), and device-related (CDRIE) in 308 (9.9%). Infective endocarditis was community-acquired in 2046 (65.66%) patients.
## III. ETIOLOGY AND RISK FACTORS
- Risk factors for native valve infective endocarditis (IE) include cardiac factors or non-cardiac risk factors.
- It is most often from bacteria and more rarely a fungus from

| Bacteria | Source of Infection |
|---|---|
| Staphylococcus aureus | Skin |
| Oral Streptococcus, HACEK | Oral, dental |
| Group D Streptococcus | Gastro-intestinal tract (Coloscopy) |
| Enterococcus | Gastro-intestinal tract (Coloscopy), Urinary tract |

| Cardiac risk factors | Non-cardiac risk factors |
|---|---|
| • Previous infective endocarditis | • Central venous catheter |
| • Valvular heart disease | • People who inject drugs |
| • Prosthetic heart valve | • Immunosuppression |
| • Central venous or arterial catheter | • Recent dental or surgical procedures |
| • Transvenous cardiac implantable electronic device • Congenital heart disease | • Recent hospitalization Haemodialysis |

The differential diagnosis for endocarditis is broad and should be considered based on two clinical categories: presence of bacteremia in the absence of valvular vegetation and presence of valvular vegetation(s) in the absence of bacteremia.

This is a detailed surgical timing algorithm for patients with left-sided infective endocarditis (IE). The flowchart guides clinicians through decision-making pathways to determine whether surgery should be performed, and if so, whether it should be emergency, urgent, or non-urgent, based on clinical criteria.

---

**Main Decision Points & Branches:**

The flowchart begins at the top with three primary initial conditions:

1. **Heart failure**
   - → Leads to “Cardiogenic shock or pulmonary oedema”?
     - **Yes (Y)** → “Emergency surgery (Class I)”
     - **No (N)** → “Poor haemodynamic tolerance”?
       - **Yes (Y)** → “Urgent surgery (Class I)”
       - **No (N)** → “Non-urgent surgery (Class I)”

2. **Uncontrolled infection**
   - → Leads to “Local complications (abscess, false aneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation)”?
     - **Yes (Y)** → “Urgent surgery (Class I)”
     - **No (N)** → “Persistent positive blood culturesᵃ”?
       - **Yes (Y)** → “Urgent surgery (Class IIa)” (highlighted yellow)
       - **No (N)** → “Resistant bacteriaᶜ or fungi”?
         - **Yes (Y)** → “Urgent or non-urgent surgery (Class Iᵈ)” (green box with note)
         - **No (N)** → “PVE caused by S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negative bacilli”?
           - **Yes (Y)** → “Urgent surgery (Class IIa)” (yellow)
           - **No (N)** → “Non-urgent surgery (Class I)”

3. **High risk of embolism or established embolism**
   - → Leads to “Vegetation ≥10 mm and emboli despite appropriate antibiotic therapy”?
     - **Yes (Y)** → “Urgent surgery (Class I)”
     - **No (N)** → “Vegetation ≥10 mm and other reason for surgeryᵇ”?
       - **Yes (Y)** → “Urgent surgery (Class I)”
       - **No (N)** → “Vegetation ≥10 mm and no evidence of embolus”?
         - **Yes (Y)** → “Urgent surgery (Class IIb)” (orange)
         - **No (N)** → “Antibiotic therapy and continued observation”

---

**Key Notes & Annotations:**

- **ᵃ Persistent positive blood cultures**: Implies ongoing bacteremia despite antibiotics.
- **ᵇ Other reason for surgery**: Includes indications such as valve dysfunction, prosthetic valve infection, or recurrent IE not related to embolism.
- **ᶜ Resistant bacteria or fungi**: Refers to organisms that are not susceptible to standard antibiotic regimens.
- **ᵈ Urgent or non-urgent surgery (Class I)**: Indicates that timing depends on additional factors not specified in this chart (e.g., patient stability, availability of resources).
- **Class I**: Emergency or urgent surgery; Class IIa/IIb: Urgent but less immediately life-threatening; Class I also used for non-urgent surgery in some branches.

---

**Outcomes:**

- **Emergency surgery (Class I)**: Immediate intervention required due to hemodynamic instability or life-threatening complications.
- **Urgent surgery (Class I)**: Required within 24–72 hours due to significant complications or high-risk features.
- **Urgent surgery (Class IIa)**: Urgent but may allow for more planning; often due to persistent infection or specific pathogen profiles.
- **Urgent surgery (Class IIb)**: Urgent but less immediately critical than Class I or IIa; often due to large vegetations without active embolism.
- **Non-urgent surgery (Class I)**: Can be scheduled after stabilization; typically for low-risk patients with large vegetations and no active complications.
- **Antibiotic therapy and continued observation**: No immediate surgery indicated; monitoring for clinical deterioration or new complications.

---

**Color Coding:**

- **Green boxes**: Indicate surgery is recommended (emergency, urgent, or non-urgent).
- **Yellow boxes**: Indicate urgent surgery with specific sub-classification (Class IIa).
- **Orange box**: Indicates urgent surgery with specific sub-classification (Class IIb).
- **Blue boxes**: Indicate non-surgical management (antibiotics and observation).

---

**Clinical Implications:**

This algorithm emphasizes that surgical timing in IE is highly dependent on the presence of complications, vegetation size, embolic events, and microbiological findings. It aligns with guidelines from major cardiology societies (e.g., ESC, AHA) and helps standardize decision-making across institutions.

Note: Drug names, dosages, and specific antibiotic regimens are not included in this flowchart — they are managed outside the surgical decision pathway and depend on local protocols and microbiology reports.

VIII.

## EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS
- Relapse is a repeat episode of IE caused by the same microorganism and represents a failure of treatment and mandates a search for a persistent focus of infection and an evaluation towards surgical therapy.
- Reinfection is an infection caused by a different microorganism, usually more than 6 months after the initial episode.
- Once antibiotic treatment has been completed, blood cultures should be performed.
- Patients discharged after the first episode of IE should remain under close surveillance for potential long-term complications.

## IX. COMPLICATIONS
Complications of infective endocarditis (IE) include cardiac, metastatic, neurologic, renal, musculoskeletal, and pulmonary complications as well as complications related to systemic infection (including embolization, metastatic infection, and mycotic aneurysm). More than one complication can occur simultaneously.
## X. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION
Measures for prevention of IE include:
- Maintenance of oral hygiene
- Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to invasive dental or invasive oral procedures
- Timely treatment of infections with pathogens likely to cause endocarditis
- Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to surgery reduces the risk of surgical site infection, as discussed separately, and has been postulated to reduce the risk of subsequent endocarditis.
- Closure of a patent ductus arteriosus or ventricular septal defect.

## I. DEFINITION
Infectious Endocarditis (IE) refers to infection of the endocardial surface of the heart; it usually refers to infection of one or more heart valves or infection of an intracardiac device.
## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
- The incidence of infective endocarditis is estimated between 30 and 80 cases per million inhabitants and per year in the general population in industrialized countries.
- Incidence increases after the age of 60 and Staphylococcus is now the most frequent responsible microorganism.
- Infective endocarditis was native (NVE) in 1764 (56.6%) patients, prosthetic (PVIE) in 939 (30.1%), and device-related (CDRIE) in 308 (9.9%). Infective endocarditis was community-acquired in 2046 (65.66%) patients.
## III. ETIOLOGY AND RISK FACTORS

cardiac risk factors.

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
## V. DIAGNOSIS
1. Clinical Manifestations
- Symptoms: Fever is the most common symptom of IE
- It is often associated with chills, anorexia, and weight loss.
- Other common symptoms: Malaise, headache, myalgias, arthralgias, night sweats, abdominal pain, tooth pain and dyspnea.
- Signs: A new or changing cardiac
- Supportive signs: splenomegaly, petechiae or splinter hemorrhages.
- Relatively uncommon manifestations highly suggestive of IE:
- Janeway lesions
- Osler nodes
- Roth spots
2. Investigation for Endocarditis
- Blood cultures: At least two sets of blood cultures should be obtained from separate venipuncture sites prior to initiation of antibiotic therapy.
- Cardiac imaging:
- Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the first diagnostic test for patients with suspected IE.
- Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) has higher sensitivity than TTE and is better for detection of cardiac complications.
- Cardiac CT: May be helpful for cases in which definitive evidence of IE and its complications cannot be demonstrated with TEE, and/or for planning surgery in patients with extra valvular complications.
- Additional evaluation for IE source or complications: ECG, chest radiography, other radiographic imaging tailored to clinical manifestations, and dental evaluation.

This image displays a clinical guideline table for antibiotic treatment of infective endocarditis (IE) or native valve endocarditis (NVE) / prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) caused by different types of resistant Enterococcus species. The table is divided into three main sections based on the resistance profile of the causative organism.

---

**Section 1: High-level aminoglycoside resistance (HLAR) Enterococcus spp.**

*Clinical scenario:* NVE or PVE due to HLAR Enterococcus spp.
*Recommended regimen:* Combination of ampicillin or amoxicillin and ceftriaxone for 6 weeks.
*Level of evidence:* I (Strong recommendation), B (Moderate quality of evidence).

**Adult antibiotic dosage and route:**
- Ampicillin: 12 g/day i.v., in 4–6 doses
- Amoxicillin: 200 mg/kg/day i.v., in 4–6 doses
- Ceftriaxone: 4 g/day i.v. or i.m., in 2 doses

**Paediatric antibiotic dosage and route:**
- Ampicillin: 300 mg/kg/day i.v., in 4–6 equally divided doses
- Amoxicillin: 100–200 mg/kg/day i.v., in 4–6 doses
- Ceftriaxone: 100 mg/kg i.v. or i.m., in 2 doses

---

**Section 2: Beta-lactam resistant Enterococcus spp. (E. faecium)**

*Clinical scenario:* IE due to beta-lactam resistant Enterococcus spp. (E. faecium)
*Recommended regimen:* Vancomycin for 6 weeks combined with gentamicin for 2 weeks.
*Level of evidence:* I (Strong recommendation), C (Low quality of evidence).

**Adult antibiotic dosage and route:**
- Vancomycin: 30 mg/kg/day i.v., in 2 doses
- Gentamicin: 3 mg/kg/day i.v. or i.m., in 1 dose

**Paediatric antibiotic dosage and route:**
- Vancomycin: 30 mg/kg/day i.v., in 2–3 equally divided doses
- Gentamicin: 3 mg/kg/day i.v. or i.m., in 1 dose

---

**Section 3: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus spp.**

*Clinical scenario:* IE due to vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus spp.
*Recommended regimen:* Daptomycin combined with beta-lactams (ampicillin, ertapenem, or ceftaroline) OR fosfomycin.
*Level of evidence:* I (Strong recommendation), C (Low quality of evidence).

**Adult antibiotic dosage and route:**
- Daptomycin: 10–12 mg/kg/day i.v., in 1 dose
- Ampicillin: 300 mg/kg/day i.v., in 4–6 equally divided doses
- Fosfomycin: 12 g/day i.v., in 4 doses
- Ceftaroline: 1800 mg/day i.v., in 3 doses
- Ertapenem: 2 g/day i.v. or i.m., in 1 dose

**Paediatric antibiotic dosage and route:**
- Daptomycin: 10–12 mg/kg/day i.v., in 1 dose (age-adjusted)
- Ampicillin: 300 mg/kg/day i.v., in 4–6 equally divided doses
- Fosfomycin: 2–3 g/day i.v., in 1 dose
- Ceftaroline: 24–36 mg/kg/day i.v., in 3 doses
- Ertapenem: 1 g/day i.v. or i.m., in 1 dose [if younger than 12 years, 15 mg/kg/dose (to a maximum of 500 mg) twice daily]

This is a detailed surgical timing algorithm for patients with left-sided infective endocarditis (IE). The flowchart guides clinicians through decision-making pathways to determine whether surgery should be performed, and if so, whether it should be emergency, urgent, or non-urgent, based on clinical criteria.

---

**Decision Points and Branches:**

The flowchart begins at the top with the main title: “Surgical timing for patient with left-sided infective endocarditis.”

It branches into three primary initial conditions:

1. **Heart failure**
   - → If YES (Y) to “Cardiogenic shock or pulmonary oedema”: → Emergency surgery (Class I)
   - → If NO (N) to “Cardiogenic shock or pulmonary oedema”: → Proceed to “Poor haemodynamic tolerance”
     - → If YES (Y) to “Poor haemodynamic tolerance”: → Urgent surgery (Class I)
     - → If NO (N) to “Poor haemodynamic tolerance”: → Non-urgent surgery (Class I)

2. **Uncontrolled infection**
   - → If YES (Y) to “Local complications (abscess, false aneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation)” → Urgent surgery (Class I)
   - → If NO (N) to “Local complications”: → Proceed to “Persistent positive blood culturesᵃ”
     - → If YES (Y) to “Persistent positive blood culturesᵃ”: → Urgent surgery (Class IIa)
     - → If NO (N) to “Persistent positive blood culturesᵃ”: → Proceed to “Resistant bacteriaᶜ or fungi”
       - → If YES (Y) to “Resistant bacteriaᶜ or fungi”: → Urgent or non-urgent surgery (Class Iᵈ)
         - → If YES (Y) to “PVE caused by S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negative bacilli”: → Urgent surgery (Class IIa)
           - → If NO (N) to “PVE caused by S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negative bacilli”: → Non-urgent surgery (Class I)
         - → If NO (N) to “Resistant bacteriaᶜ or fungi”: → Proceed to “Vegetation ≥ 10 mm and no evidence of embolus”
           - → If YES (Y) to “Vegetation ≥ 10 mm and no evidence of embolus”: → Urgent surgery (Class IIb)
             - → If NO (N) to “Vegetation ≥ 10 mm and no evidence of embolus”: → Antibiotic therapy and continued observation
           - → If NO (N) to “Vegetation ≥ 10 mm and no evidence of embolus”: → Antibiotic therapy and continued observation

3. **High risk of embolism or established embolism**
   - → If YES (Y) to “Vegetation ≥ 10 mm and emboli despite appropriate antibiotic therapy”: → Urgent surgery (Class I)
   - → If NO (N) to “Vegetation ≥ 10 mm and emboli despite appropriate antibiotic therapy”: → Proceed to “Vegetation ≥ 10 mm and other reason for surgeryᵇ”
     - → If YES (Y) to “Vegetation ≥ 10 mm and other reason for surgeryᵇ”: → Urgent surgery (Class I)
     - → If NO (N) to “Vegetation ≥ 10 mm and other reason for surgeryᵇ”: → Proceed to “Vegetation ≥ 10 mm and no evidence of embolus” (same branch as above)

---

**Outcomes (Surgery Types):**

- **Emergency surgery (Class I)** — Indicated for cardiogenic shock or pulmonary oedema due to heart failure.
- **Urgent surgery (Class I)** — Indicated for local complications, vegetation ≥ 10 mm with emboli despite antibiotics, poor haemodynamic tolerance, or vegetation ≥ 10 mm with other surgical indications.
- **Urgent surgery (Class IIa)** — Indicated for persistent positive blood cultures or PVE caused by S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negative bacilli when not meeting Class I criteria.
- **Urgent surgery (Class IIb)** — Indicated for vegetation ≥ 10 mm with no evidence of embolus but other compelling reasons for surgery.
- **Non-urgent surgery (Class I)** — Indicated for stable patients without acute complications or resistant organisms.
- **Antibiotic therapy and continued observation** — For patients with vegetation ≥ 10 mm and no embolus, and no other indication for surgery.

---

**Notes (Footnotes):**

- ᵃ Persistent positive blood cultures — implies cultures remain positive after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotic therapy.
- ᵇ Other reason for surgery — includes recurrent embolic events, valve dysfunction, or other structural issues.
- ᶜ Resistant bacteria or fungi — includes methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE), or other multidrug-resistant organisms.
- ᵈ Urgent or non-urgent surgery — depends on clinical context; may require individualized assessment.

---

**Color Coding:**

- Green boxes: Surgery indicated (emergency or urgent).
- Yellow boxes: Urgent surgery (Class IIa).
- Orange box: Urgent surgery (Class IIb).
- Blue box: Antibiotic therapy and continued observation.
- Purple boxes: Decision nodes or intermediate criteria.
- Red circles: “No” (N) decision paths.
- Green circles: “Yes” (Y) decision paths.

---

**Clinical Implications:**

This algorithm helps standardize surgical decision-making in IE, prioritizing life-threatening complications (e.g., embolism, heart failure) while also considering microbiological factors (e.g., resistant organisms) and vegetations size (>10 mm). It aligns with guidelines from the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and American Heart Association (AHA).

Note: No specific drug names, dosages, or brand names are listed in the flowchart. The focus is on clinical indicators and surgical urgency classification.

## VIII. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS
- Relapse is a repeat episode of IE caused by the same microorganism and represents a failure of treatment and mandates a search for a persistent focus of infection and an evaluation towards surgical therapy.
- Reinfection is an infection caused by a different microorganism, usually more than 6 months after the initial episode.
- Once antibiotic treatment has been completed, blood cultures should be performed.
- Patients discharged after the first episode of IE should remain under close surveillance for potential long-term complications.
## IX. COMPLICATIONS
Complications of infective endocarditis (IE) include cardiac, metastatic, neurologic, renal, musculoskeletal, and pulmonary complications as well as complications related to systemic infection (including embolization, metastatic infection, and mycotic aneurysm). More than one complication can occur simultaneously.
## X. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION
Measures for prevention of IE include:
- Maintenance of oral hygiene
- Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to invasive dental or invasive oral procedures
- Timely treatment of infections with pathogens likely to cause endocarditis
- Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to surgery reduces the risk of surgical site infection, as discussed separately, and has been postulated to reduce the risk of subsequent endocarditis.
- Closure of a patent ductus arteriosus or ventricular septal defect.

## I. DEFINITION
Pericarditis refers to the inflammation of the pericardial layers with or without pericardial effusion.
## Type of pericarditis
## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
Acute pericarditis is diagnosed in 0.2% of all cardiovascular in-hospital admissions and is responsible for 5% of emergency room admissions for chest pain.
## III. ETIOLOGY
- Idiopathic is most common: presumed to be viral
- Infectious
 - Tuberculosis
 - Viral: Coxsackie virus A, B (most common), echovirus
 - Bacterial: S. pneumoniae, S. aureus
- Post-MI: acute (direct extension of myocardial inflammation, 1-7 d post-MI), Dressler’s syndrome (autoimmune reaction, 2-8 weeks post-MI)
- Post-cardiac surgery (e.g. CABG), other trauma
- Metabolic: uraemia/CKD, hypothyroidism
- Neoplasm: Hodgkin’s, breast, lung, renal cell carcinoma, melanoma
- Collagen vascular disease: SLE, polyarteritis, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma
- Other: drugs (e.g. hydralazine), radiation, infiltrative disease (sarcoid)

content: Due to the parietal layer's rich innervation, any inflammatory process mediated by an infectious, autoimmune or traumatic insult can result in severe retrosternal chest pain, as is commonly seen in acute pericarditis. This explains why the vast majority of presentations (>90%) have chest discomfort. In cases of pericardial effusion, the pericardial compliance can increase in response to slowly

accumulating fluid, allowing the pericardial sac to dilate over time without compressing the cardiac chambers. This means that the rate of fluid accumulation (and resulting pressure changes, as in pericardial compliance) is often more important than the volume in determining the hemodynamic sequela affecting the heart.

## V. DIAGNOSIS
## Symptoms
Chest pain is the most common symptom of pericarditis (>95%). It usually feels sharp or stabbing, and some patients having achy or pressure-like chest pain. The pain:
- Usually occurs behind the breastbone or on the left side of the chest
- Spread to the left shoulder and neck
- Get worse when coughing, lying down or taking a deep breath
- Get better when sitting up or leaning forward
Other signs and symptoms of pericarditis may include:
- Cough
- Fatigue or general feeling of weakness or being sick
- Leg swelling
- Low-grade fever
- Palpitation
- Shortness of breath when lying down
- Swelling of the belly (abdomen)
## Investigations
- ECG: initially diffuse elevated ST segments ± depressed PR segment, the elevation in the ST segment is concave upwards → 2-5 d later ST isoelectric with T wave flattening and inversion
- Chest X-ray
- Heart ultrasound: performed to assess for pericardial effusion
- CT or MRI: when located pericardial effusion, pericardial thickening or masses, constrictive pericarditis

This is a clinical diagram illustrating the four stages of evolution of an electrocardiogram (ECG) pattern typically seen in acute myocardial infarction (AMI), particularly in the context of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI). The diagram visually depicts the progression of ECG changes over time, from initial injury to resolution or normalization.

Components and Labels:

1. Stage 1:
   - Shows early ECG changes.
   - Key features labeled below:
     • PR depression
     • Generalized ST segment elevation
   - The waveform shows a prominent QRS complex with elevated ST segments that are not yet inverted.

2. Stage 2 (Transitional):
   - Divided into “early” and “late” phases.
   - Early phase: J point begins to move toward baseline.
   - Late phase: J point is on or near the baseline before T waves begin to flatten.
   - This stage represents the transition from injury to ischemic necrosis.

3. Stage 3:
   - Key feature labeled: T wave inversion.
   - The ST segment may be flat or slightly elevated, but T waves are clearly inverted.
   - This reflects the onset of necrosis and repolarization abnormalities.

4. Stage 4:
   - Key feature labeled: Normalization of ECG.
   - The ECG returns to baseline morphology, with ST segments normalized and T waves returning to upright configuration.
   - This indicates healing or resolution of the infarct, though some residual changes may persist.

Clinical Significance:
This diagram outlines the classic ECG evolution in STEMI, which is critical for diagnosis and timing of interventions such as thrombolytics or percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). The progression helps clinicians determine the age of the infarct and guide management decisions.

- Anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs/ASA, steroids)
- Colchicine
- Treat the underlying disease
* Tapering once inflammatory markers have normalized
## VIII. SPECIAL CASES
- Inpatient investigation and more intensive evaluation for a non-viral etiology should be considered where there is:
 - Any fever >38°C
 - Gradual onset
 - Large effusion (>20 mm) or tamponade
 - Lack of response to 1 week of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
 - Any history of trauma, immunosuppression/deficiency or oral
anticoagulant use
- If pericarditis is caused by a bacterial infection, treatment may include antibiotics and drainage, if necessary.
- If pericarditis causes fluid buildup around the heart, a surgery or other procedure may be needed to drain the fluid (pericardiocentesis).
## IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS
The prognosis of acute pericarditis largely depends on the underlying aetiology. It is excellent in cases of idiopathic pericarditis. Prompt diagnosis and appropriate treatment of acute pericarditis may reduce the risk of acute complications and recurrences.
## X. COMPLICATION
- Pericardial effusion
- Constrictive pericarditis
- Cardiac tamponade (this life-threatening condition requires emergency treatment)

## I. DEFINITION
Constrictive pericarditis (CP) is a chronic inflammatory process, often characterized by chronic scarring, fibrosis and calcification of the pericardium associated with diastolic dysfunction, eventually leading to low cardiac output and heart failure.
## II. EPIDEMIOLOGY
Complication of acute CP is a relatively rare complication of viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis (<0.5%) but, in contrast, is relatively frequent for specific etiologies, especially bacterial. In Asian series, TB pericarditis is reported to be the underlying etiology in 20-80% of cases
## III. ETIOLOGY
## 1. Common causes:
- Complication of acute idiopathic pericarditis
- Post cardiac surgery or post chest radiotherapy
- Infection (viral or bacterial)
- Tuberculosis
- Bacterial infections that lead to purulent pericarditis
## 2. Less common causes:
- Infection (fungal)
- Neoplasms
- Uremia
- Connective tissue disorders
- Drugs (e.g: procainamide and hydralazine)
- Trauma
- Myocardial infarction (with past medical history of Dressler syndrome and hemopericardium)

## IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY
Pericardial non-compliance creates a stiff ventricular-pericardial unit,
limiting ventricular relaxation and determines ventricular diastolic pressure, resulting in
elevated, equalized diastolic pressures in all chambers
decreasing the LV end diastolic volume (LV preload) and therefore left-sided stroke volume.
Clinically, predominantly as right-sided congestion (jugular venous distention, edema, and ascites) as well as elevation in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and a decreased cardiac
output response to exercise (given inadequate ventricular filling) results in dyspnea and
effort intolerance
## IV. DIAGNOSIS
1. Initial assessment:
- The low prevalence of CP makes identifying key physical examination and historical features an important initial step in the diagnostic process.
- History of cardiac surgery, radiation or tuberculosis should heighten clinical suspicion in the presence of edema, abdominal distention and exertional dyspnea.
- In early stage: symptoms secondary to a reduction in cardiac output including fatigue and exertional dyspnea
- In late stage, the filling pressures become significantly elevated, and systemic venous pressure rises, signs of overt RHF develop such as jugular venous distention, edema, ascites, pleural effusion.
- Elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP) is present in virtually all patients:
- Kussmaul's sign
- Rapid x- and y-descents seen in the JVP of a patient with

constrictive pericarditis. These are appreciated as rapid inward “flicking”/collapsing deflections in the presence of an elevated JVP.
- Other findings: diastolic apex beat or diastolic precordial impulse, high- pitched early diastolic pericardial knock in heart auscultation. 2. Investigations:
a. Laboratory testing:  nonspecific in constrictive pericarditis. b. Echocardiography: As an initial diagnostic test, echocardiography can
confirm the diagnosis of CP in most cases if pre-test probability is sufficiently high.
- The pathognomonic finding is respirophasic septal shifting, detected by either M mode or 2D imaging and abnormal beat-to-beat septal motion, or "shudder," due to differential rapid early diastolic filling of the right and then left ventricle.

- The inferior vena cava is universally plethoric in the absence of hypovolemia; a sensitive but nonspecific feature of CP.
- The exaggerated respiratory preload changes are also exemplified by an inspiratory decrease in mitral valve inflow Doppler and an increase in tricuspid valve inflow Doppler.
c. Cardiac radiology:
- In CP, chest x-rays can demonstrate pericardial calcification, a pathognomonic finding in the presence of clinical heart failure and elevated JVP. Chest CT is more sensitive for pericardial calcification than chest x-ray.
- Chest CT and MRI allow for precise measurement of pericardial thickness, with MRI in particular demonstrating excellent accuracy (93%) in detection of pericardial thickening >4 mm.

## Vl. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
The differential diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis (CP) includes conditions with similar symptoms such as restrictive cardiomyopathy, cardiac tamponade, systolic or diastolic congestive heart failure (CHF), Right-sided valvular abnormalities, Right-sided atrial tumors, and Superior vena cava syndrome and nephrotic syndrome. Theses can present with dyspnea, edema, ascites, pleural effusion, jugular vein distention mimicking CP. Careful evaluation of clinical history, laboratory finding and diagnostic imaging (echocardiography, cardiac CT or MRI) is essential to differentiate CP from these conditions.
## Vll. MANAGEMENT
1. Objective:
- Improving cardiac function, reducing inflammation and congestion.
- The primary etiology be identified and managed accordingly
- The definitive cure for CP is primarily surgical in the form of complete pericardiectomy, where feasible.
2. Critical signs:
End-stage disease can include cachexia, markedly reduced resting cardiac output (cardiac index ≤1.2 L/m2 per min), hypoalbuminemia due to protein-losing enteropathy, and/or congestive hepatopathy including cardiac cirrhosis.
## 3.  Outpatient management

Outpatient care may be appropriate during the early stages of the disease, particularly when the diagnosis is still uncertain and symptoms are relatively stable. It is important to emphasize and encourage a low salt and fluid-restricted diet as these are probably beneficial in order to avoid congestion and exacerbations of heart failure symptoms. Although no specific restrictions are needed, activity can often be severely limited by symptoms. However, decreased daily activities may be recommended in some patients.
4. Pharmacologic therapy:
Medical treatment may be considered as a trial of two to three months as conservative treatment if it is transient CP. The following specific treatment modalities should be considered for each of the special situations highlighted.
- Subacute CP may respond to steroids if treated before pericardial fibrosis develops.
- Diuretics, particularly loop diuretics, are the mainstay to relieve congestion and to
optimise clinical volume status; however, they may decrease preload to the point of reducing cardiac output and thus require closer monitoring.
- Any other medications used to treat patients with CP should be specifically directed
to the underlying aetiology of the pericardial disease.

- Any therapy directed towards the causative disease, e.g., antituberculosis therapy, is
appropriate.
- CP-related complications require their own specific therapy as appropriate, e.g., atrial
arrhythmias.
- In general, beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers should be avoided.
- Patients with advanced cardiac symptoms related to constriction may derive little
benefit from surgery, as these are often the high surgical risk group.

## 5. Pericardiectomy
Pericardiectomy: a pericardiectomy remains the definitive therapy and a potential cure in most CP patients
Indication — We suggest pericardiectomy for patients with chronic constrictive pericarditis who meet all of the following criteria:
- Symptoms and signs have persisted despite at least 4 to 12 months of IL-1 inhibitor therapy.
- Symptoms are moderate to severe (New York Heart Association [NYHA] functional class III or IV (table 2).
- Constrictive pericarditis has not progressed to "end-stage." (See 'Patients unlikely to benefit from pericardiectomy' below.)
- There is no concomitant restrictive cardiomyopathy
Patients unlikely to benefit from pericardiectomy: Due to the complex nature of the surgery and the associated operative mortality, surgery should be carefully considered in patients who may not benefit from the procedure.
- Mild disease
- End-stage disease
- Mixed constrictive-restrictive disease
- Other high-risk groups – Mortality after pericardiectomy is also high in individuals with end-stage kidney disease or ventricular systolic dysfunction.
## 6. Mortality risk factors of pericardiectomy
Detrimental outcomes of pericardiectomy include progressive heart failure or advanced heart failure symptoms (NYHA III-IV), sepsis, renal failure, respiratory failure, arrhythmia, prior mediastinal radiotherapy as the primary cause of constriction, and other concomitant severe comorbidities.

Preoperative myocardial atrophy or fibrosis is as well one of the causes of peri-operative mortality due to reduced ventricular mobility, particularly the RV free wall, are associated with acute RV dilatation related to subsequent increased preload to the RV, to increased venous return which then leads to acute RV failure and decreased cardiac output, function and subsequent death. Extensive pericardial calcification might have prognostic implications, which make pericardiectomy more extensive and complex.
